#5525. Beyond Beauty: Kitchens That Work as Well as They Look

A kitchen at Skyline by Toll Brothers in Summit at Orchard Hills in Irvine, California.

Gena Kirk had a couple of non-negotiables when she renovated her Southern California kitchen: a Moroccan door that would open to the pantry and a touchless faucet that she “couldn’t live without.” Turns out, Kirk’s design decisions are in lockstep with many homeowners today who prioritize multifunctional kitchens that are inherently personal.

“Home buyers are less afraid of taking some risk and making their kitchens more curated to feel like it’s their own,” says Kirk, vice president of KB Home Corporate Design Studio.

In fact, today’s more nuanced kitchen is reflected in the 2027 National Kitchen and Bath Association’s Kitchen Trends Report, released in October. Among the findings are expanding kitchen floor plans with more clearly defined zones and a growing preference for personalized gathering spaces over bland, impersonal kitchens designed with resale in mind.

A kitchen at Toll Brothers at Thornebrook in Bulverde, Texas.

“While the kitchen has always been the ‘heart of the home,’ that idea has taken on new meaning,” said Bill Darcy, global president and CEO of NKBA, commenting on the report. “We’ve entered a new era of what the kitchen can do for homeowners—solving real problems … and elevating the way we live.”

We ask more of our kitchens today. Beyond meal preparation, they serve as gathering places for everything from homework and family dinners to entertaining. As their role expands, so does their connection to surrounding spaces. Mudrooms, pantries, and back kitchens are becoming more common, along with dedicated coffee and beverage stations, baking centers, and pet areas.

“[Kitchen] design is becoming more intentional to reflect how people cook, entertain, and connect,” says Lisa McClelland, senior vice president of the Toll Brothers Design Studio. “The emphasis is on creating spaces that feel open and welcoming while providing distinct areas for preparation, dining, and conversation.”

According to the NKBA report, kitchen footprints are expected to continue growing over the next three years. Yet even as kitchens get larger, their layouts are becoming simpler, “with less clutter and a more spacious feel,” the report states. The traditional kitchen work triangle remains important, along with multifunctional features that support a wider range of activities.

“People are thinking about how they operate in their kitchen,” Kirk says. She also predicts continued growth in products designed to simplify everyday tasks, such as motion-activated faucets, workstation sinks that combine a cutting board and built-in strainer, and countertop cabinets and drawers to store small appliances.

“It’s really about form and function,” Kirk says. “People want to be organized so everything is in one place versus spread throughout the kitchen.”

A kitchen at KB Home’s Primrose community in Lancaster, California.

Kitchen islands have evolved beyond their strictly utilitarian roots, too, becoming larger and more central to everyday living. Features such as “thoughtful seating, storage, and room to work” enhance their role as gathering spaces, McClelland says. “The goal is a kitchen that feels effortless, whether you’re making breakfast or hosting a large celebration with family and friends.”

Although kitchens are working harder, homeowners want them to look as good as they cook. Furniture-like cabinetry, layered lighting, and handcrafted, artisanal details help seamlessly bridge kitchens with the rest of the home.

“Faucets, cabinet hardware, and lighting can coordinate without matching exactly, creating a layered, collected look that feels personal rather than overly designed,” McClelland says.

Kirk notes a marketplace shift toward using more natural materials, including quartzite countertops and backsplashes and woods such as walnut that show natural graining. The NKBA report highlights this shift, with quartzite and quartz as the top two countertop materials that will be a key design feature in the coming years.

“Consumers are more interested in natural products, period. Not only in what they’re putting in their mouths, but what they’re putting around them,” Kirk says.

A kitchen at Toll Brothers at Sedona in Sedona, Arizona.

Lighting is emerging as a key design element, as well. “Good kitchen lighting gives you useful choices, and placement is critical, especially at work surfaces,” lighting designer Nathan Orsman notes in the NKBA report. Layered lighting designs include undercabinet, task, and decorative lighting, all part of the recipe that helps “shape a space that feels both practical and inviting throughout the day,” McClelland says.

Layered lighting designs include under-the-counter and built-in cabinet, task, and decorative lighting, all part of the recipe that helps “shape a space that feels both practical and inviting throughout the day,” McClelland adds.

Mixed metal hardware and plumbing fixtures that blend finishes, from brushed brass and gold tones to matte black, nickel, and stainless, are another way homeowners are expressing their individual styles, McClelland says. Likewise, she adds, “blending natural wood tones, creamy neutrals, and rich textures creates spaces that feel both refined and welcoming.”

Beyond the visible design elements, technology and wellness features are playing an increasingly important role in kitchen design. Solutions that enhance natural light, improve ventilation, and filter water are helping create healthier, more comfortable spaces. Multifunctional appliances are also gaining traction as homeowners look for greater convenience and versatility.

“Consumers are looking for convenience, form, and functionality,” Kirk says.

A kitchen at KB Home’s Gateway community in El Cajon, California.

According to the NKBA report, top appliance features include ovens with air-frying and steam-cooking capabilities, dedicated beverage units, and refrigerators with zoned storage that supports healthy habits.

“Manufacturers are getting smarter about the products they are producing that follow the health and wellness trends the consumers are after,” Kirk says.

Kitchens have long commanded a significant share of homeowners’ design budgets. More and more, though, their influence extends well beyond the kitchen itself, shaping design decisions throughout the home.

“We’re building the kitchen first, and then that’s leading to the rest of their home design,” Kirk says.

Although design preferences vary by region, the desire for kitchens tailored to homeowners’ lifestyles remains consistent. “The common thread is a desire for kitchens that feel warm, functional, and highly personalized,” McClelland says. “Buyers want spaces that support everyday living while still delivering the craftsmanship and luxury details that make a home special.”

Kelly Ryan Kegans is a Minneapolis-based writer and editor with more than 25 years of experience covering home design, architecture, and lifestyle topics. #5524. The Home Insurance Move That Could Save You $440 a Year

When you’re planning a move, every monthly cost counts. That’s why it can be frustrating to see home insurance keep creeping up. According to Intercontinental Exchange, it now makes up 9.6% of the average monthly mortgage payment.

But the latest numbers show some progress on that front – as the increases start to slow down. Here’s what you need to know and what you can do about it.

A look at the past two years shows how much things have cooled down. In mid-2024, home insurance premiums rose 4.3% in a single quarter. By the second quarter of this year, that was down to 1.8%. That’s the smallest quarterly growth in almost 3 years – and that’s a good thing (see graph below):

As Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at Intercontinental Exchange, explains:

“Property insurance has been a fast-growing component of the monthly mortgage payment, but this quarter’s data shows the pace of increase is finally slowing.”

While your premium will likely still go up over time, it may not climb as quickly as it did a couple of years ago. And that’s, at the very least, a step in the right direction.

Here’s where you have some say in what you pay. Let’s take current homeowners as an example. Intercontinental Exchange found that when homeowners shopped around and switched insurance companies, their premiums went down 6.6% on average. Those who stayed with their current company saw an increase of 10.4% (see graph below):

Think about that. That’s a big difference and it goes to show that looking for a new provider can literally pay off.

That works out to about $440 a year in savings for the people who switched. And they didn’t have to give up coverage to get it. Their deductibles dipped 1.4%, and their coverage limits actually rose 7.3%.

While this example is current homeowners, the same general idea applies for first-time buyers too. Shop around and get multiple quotes before you pick your insurance provider. Then, once you’re settled in, review your policy each year when it comes up for renewal. You’re not locked into the first price you get.

The home itself plays a role as well. According to John Burns Research and Consulting (JBREC), newly built homes are 10% to 15% less expensive to insure than older ones nationally.

And while a brand-new home won’t necessarily be the right fit for every buyer, if you’re open to one, it could be one more way to keep your monthly insurance costs down.

Home insurance is certainly a bigger part of the monthly costs than it used to be, and that can feel like just one more thing to juggle when you’re buying a home or moving. But knowing you have ways to keep it in check can take some of the pressure off. Compare a few options before you buy, revisit your policy each year, and lean on trusted local professionals as you plan for your next move.

#5523. What Experts Forecast for Mortgage Rates and Home Prices in 2027

When it comes to housing, two of the biggest questions on everyone’s mind right now are:

And if you’re weighing whether to move in the next few months or wait until 2027, here’s what you should know.

When experts look ahead to 2027, they see a steady housing market. No wild swings. No big surprises. Just a calmer, more balanced market.

And steady makes planning a whole lot easier. Let’s break it down.

Lots of people are holding out for lower rates. But the latest forecasts from Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo show rates holding fairly flat through 2027 (see graph below):

Lenders see it the same way. In a recent survey from HousingWire, 70% of mortgage executives said they expect rates to be around 7.5% or higher six months from now (see graph below):

And if you’re wondering why, the answer is fairly simple. Chen Zhao, Head of Economics Research at Redfin, says:

“Until the underlying economic fundamentals—everything from oil prices to AI–that are keeping rates high change, mortgage rates are unlikely to fall significantly.”

So what does that mean for you? Instead of trying to guess where rates go next, focus on what you can control. Even if rates don’t budge, there are still ways to get the best rate possible. When you talk with your lender, ask about:

Your credit score. Even a small bump in your score could help lower your rate.

Different loan types. Some programs offer lower rates or smaller down payments than you might expect.

Buying down your rate. Paying a little more upfront (called “points”) can lower your rate and your monthly payment.

That way, you’ll know exactly where you stand and what a comfortable monthly payment looks like for you.

But what about prices? Here’s where steady really works in your favor.

Experts don’t see a home price drop coming. On average, forecasts from Fannie Mae, MBA, and Wells Fargo show prices rising about 1% to 1.5% a year through 2027 (see graph below):

In plain terms, in most places prices are still going up, just not as fast. For sellers, that means your home should hold onto its value. For buyers, slower growth gives you a little more breathing room. Just don’t count on prices getting cheaper while you wait.

But keep in mind, these are national forecasts. Prices can look very different from one area to the next, so what matters most is what’s happening where you live.

When the market is steady, you don’t have to try to time it perfectly. There’s no big swing to wait out.

That puts the focus back on you. Maybe you need more space for a growing family. Maybe you’re ready for less upkeep. A steady market makes it easier to plan for either one.

If you’re asking yourself should you move now or wait? You should know experts see a steady market through 2027, with rates holding near today’s levels and prices rising slowly. So, rather than waiting for a big shift that may not come, connect with a local real estate agent and run the numbers on what a move looks like at today’s rates and prices, so you can decide based on your goals instead of the headlines.

#5522. Alex Trebek’s Former 578-Acre California Ranch and Winery Heads to Auction for $6.45 Million

A sprawling California ranch where Alex Trebek helped run a winery is heading to auction, giving buyers a chance to purchase nearly 578 acres of the Central Coast once owned by the longtime “Jeopardy!” host.

Known as Creston Manor, the property in San Luis Obispo County near Paso Robles is listed for $6.45 million.

In a press release shared with Realtor.com®, Concierge Auctions revealed bidding is scheduled to open on Dec. 4 and conclude live on Dec. 16 at The Dominick in New York City, where the ranch will be offered as part of the company’s year-end sale.

Lindsey Harn of Christie’s International Real Estate and Mike Goldfarb of Coldwell Banker Residential Brokerage Company are working with the auction house on the sale.

Creston Manor is the second former Trebek property in the area to come up for auction through the company this year.

Earlier in 2026, Concierge Auctions sold Windfall Farms, a nearly 724-acre property in nearby Paso Robles, for $16.9 million. The auction house said it marketed that property for 39 days before the sale.

Creston Manor was established in 1900, decades before Trebek became a partner in Creston Manor Vineyards and Winery in 1987.

According to the auction house, the game show host used the property primarily for ranching and wine production.

One vintage detail from the auction announcement ties the ranch to Washington, DC. Concierge Auctions says wine from the estate was served at President George H.W. Bush’s inauguration.

The vineyard and winery are still operational, according to the sale announcement.

The estate also retains parts of its ranching history, including a preserved blacksmith shop and the original Highway 58 bridge.

Those structures sit on the same property as the barns, stables, and livestock facilities that support its current agricultural use.

The ranch covers approximately 577.65 acres, with rolling pastureland and mountain views. Livestock pens are set up to accommodate cattle, horses, sheep, and pigs, and the stables provide dedicated space for horses.

The existing agricultural facilities are a central part of the offering, particularly for buyers who want to continue ranching or producing wine on the property.

Beyond the agricultural buildings, the property has five residences and a separate private suite. Together, the living quarters span approximately 7,550 square feet and contain 14 bedrooms and 14 full bathrooms.

According to Concierge Auctions, the estate can accommodate more than 30 guests.

Harn pointed to the combination of housing, winemaking facilities, and equestrian infrastructure as a distinguishing feature of the property.

The ranch is in Creston, a community in northern San Luis Obispo County with agricultural ties of its own. Goldfarb highlighted the estate’s seclusion and its proximity to Paso Robles, where the surrounding wine region is home to more than 200 wineries.

Paso Robles also has a downtown dining scene and the Tin City tasting district. Nearby Santa Margarita Lake offers kayaking, fishing, and hiking.

Concierge Auctions is handling the sale through its division focused on wineries, vineyards, and other wine country real estate.

Creston Manor brings those uses together on a single property, with the working winery and vineyard sharing the acreage with livestock facilities and multiple homes.

Chad Roffers, the auction house’s CEO and co-founder, said the company hopes to draw international bidders to Creston Manor, just as it did when it brought Windfall Farms to auction earlier this year.

The auction house also says a closing will trigger a contribution toward building homes for families in need through its Key for Key program, a partnership with Giveback Homes.

#5521. What the Silver Tsunami Means if You’re Planning To Sell

If you’re following the housing market, you may have heard the term “silver tsunami” lately. It’s the idea that millions of homes owned by older Americans could come onto the market as more homeowners reach retirement age and make their next move.

And when you hear a phrase like that, it’s easy to picture a flood of houses hitting the market all at once. But that picture doesn’t match the data.

And if you’re planning to sell, it’s not a reason to put your plans on hold. Let’s look at what the research actually says.

According to Realtor.com, about 13.9 million homes owned by older Americans are expected to change hands by 2036. Sure, that’s a big number. But these homes aren’t all expected to come onto the market at once.

The projections show this happening gradually over the next decade, with roughly 1.3 to 1.5 million homes changing hands each year (see graph below):

Rather than a sudden wave of houses flooding the market, this is a gradual shift as longtime homeowners make decisions about where and how they want to live.

The term silver tsunami makes for a dramatic headline, but the actual data tells a much less dramatic story. And there’s another reason these homes won’t overwhelm the market.

After the 2008 housing crash, builders significantly slowed construction. And for years afterward, they didn’t build enough homes to keep up with demand. That led to a housing shortage we’re still dealing with today.

And just how big a gap are we talking about? Estimates vary, but many experts say the U.S. is still millions of homes short. For example, a recent report from the White House Council of Economic Advisers explains:

“If homebuilding and the growth of the single-family housing stock had continued at their historical pace instead of falling dramatically after 2008, there would be 10 million or more additional single-family homes today.”

As more longtime homeowners sell, those homes will help a gap that’s already there. But they won’t push us over the edge. That’s because, at the same time, more households are expected to form in the decade ahead, and they’ll need homes, too.

So, more homes becoming available over time isn’t automatically a bad thing. It can give buyers more options and help create a more balanced housing market moving forward.

Here’s the takeaway if you’re thinking about selling your house. The silver tsunami isn’t something you need to plan your move around. What’s happening in your local market is far more important than a national projection about the next decade.

That’s because real estate is local. Some markets have more homes for sale than others. Some are seeing houses sell relatively quickly, while others are taking longer.

And those are the conditions that matter when you’re deciding how to price, prepare, and market your house.

For example, an agent who knows your area can help you understand:

How many homes are for sale nearby. This tells you how much choice buyers have and how your house will compare.

What similar houses are actually selling for. That’s one of the most important factors in setting a competitive asking price.

What buyers are looking for right now. Knowing which features and improvements matter most can help your house make a strong first impression.

And that’s something you can act on today, regardless of what happens with the silver tsunami over the next decade.

The right strategy starts with understanding your local market and making decisions based on what’s happening there, not what a dramatic national headline suggests might happen years from now.

The silver tsunami may sound like a major wave of homes coming onto the market, but the research points to a gradual shift over the next decade, not a sudden flood of listings.If you're thinking about selling, don't let that headline make you second-guess your plans. Talk to an agent about what's happening in your local market.

#5520. Job Growth Slows Nationally, but Some Local Markets Tell a Different Story

Job growth is one of the most important signals for home builders, as employment security helps shape consumer confidence, household formation, and the willingness to make a major purchase. And right now, the latest employment picture is a mixed one for the housing industry.

While employment growth remained positive, the U.S. added just 29,000 positions in September 2026, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Meanwhile, unemployment edged up to 4.2%. The slowdown fits a broader pattern of relatively modest hiring rather than a sharp deterioration in the labor market.

The composition of growth is equally important. Education and health services remained the strongest employment engine, expanding 1.7% from a year earlier. Information employment, by contrast, fell 4% year over year, while financial activities declined 1.1% over the same period.

These differences matter for builders. Two markets can add a similar number of jobs but generate different levels of housing demand depending on the industries driving growth and the incomes associated with those positions.

The national slowdown also masks significant geographic variation.

Salt Lake City led the major markets tracked by Zonda with 2.8% year-over-year employment growth in September, followed by Raleigh at 2.1% and Las Vegas at 1.9%.

The picture changes when looking at the number of jobs created since last year. Dallas added 36,200 positions despite employment growing a more modest 0.8%. New York City added 29,800, Los Angeles 28,600, Houston 25,100, and Phoenix 24,400.

That distinction is also important: percentage growth can identify accelerating economies, while absolute job creation provides another measure of the potential scale of household demand.

At the other end of the spectrum, Washington, D.C., lost 66,800 jobs and employment declined 2% since September 2025. Indianapolis fell 1.1%, Portland 0.9%, and Atlanta 0.3%. Still, several markets with declining employment have not experienced unusually high unemployment rates, suggesting builders should avoid treating negative job growth as a standalone demand signal.

For builders making multiyear land decisions, the outlook through 2031 may be even more important. The strongest projected employment gains cluster in Texas, the Mountain and Desert region, and the Carolinas, per Moody’s. Raleigh is forecast for 9.9% total employment growth from December 2026 through December 2031, followed by Austin at 9.7%, Orlando at 8.4%, and Las Vegas at 7.9%.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s Apartment Outlook subscription.

#5519. Selling Your Home? What You Should Know About Price Cuts vs. Rate Buydowns.

In today’s market, a growing number of sellers are opting to do something called a price cut – especially when their house has been on the market for a while without any bites.

According to HousingWire Data as many as 4 in 10 (43%) sellers are going this route – that’s the highest it’s been in 4 years. But what if there’s another (potentially better option) for your bottom line? And it’s just as appealing, if not more so, to today’s buyers?

First, let’s set the stage on why some compromise may be necessary in today’s market.

In September, Redfin says there were 63% more sellers than buyers in the market. And with so many sellers active and relatively few buyers by comparison, those purchasers are realizing they have more power. And as mortgage rates continue to put a squeeze on their budgets, they’re leaning in and using it.

One of the most common negotiation points? The price.

That’s because they want to feel like they’re getting a deal and they want to see their monthly payment drop. And since buyers can’t control rates, the price feels like the most obvious lever to pull.

But the savviest sellers realize being flexible doesn’t always mean a lower price, paying for a buyer’s rate buydown might work better.

A buydown is money paid at closing to lower the buyer’s mortgage rate. When you pay it as the seller, you are paying some of the buyer’s interest ahead of time, so the buyer gets a lower rate and monthly payment. And that’s especially appealing to today’s buyers.

Temporary buydowns lower the rate for the first few years, then it goes back to the full rate. The more years a buydown covers, the more it costs. These work well for buyers who expect to refinance within a certain amount of time.

A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the whole loan. These are paid for with “discount points.” One point costs 1% of the loan. According to FICO, each point generally lowers the rate by about a quarter of a percent. This type of buydown works well for buyers who plan to stay in the home for a long time.

And here’s why these can be a win-win for both buyers and sellers. Rate buydowns help sellers stand out in a crowded market and they can have a bigger impact on your buyer than a price cut would.

Here’s an example to show you what that could look like.

Let’s say you’re willing to make a $10,000 concession to help get the deal done. Take a look at these three ways to spend that money and the impact they could have on a buyer’s $420,000, 30-year fixed loan at 7%:

It’s the same $10,000 from the seller. But a 2-1 buydown saves the buyer about eight times more each month in the first year.

And since most buyers shop by monthly payment, that’s what grabs their attention.

That’s what makes a rate buydown worth considering. Instead of reducing your asking price, you may be able to use that same money to have a bigger impact on your buyer’s monthly payments. And depending on what matters most to that buyer, the immediate savings could be more appealing than a price reduction.

The key is working with your agent and the buyer’s lender to compare the options and see which one makes the most sense.

Loan programs cap how much a seller can pay toward a buyer’s costs.

Money toward buydowns doesn’t limit what else a buyer may ask a seller to pay for. Buyers may still ask for repairs or other concessions.

Putting the buydown offer in your listing lets agents and buyers know it’s an option.

Your agent can run scenarios on buydowns and other costs of selling in advance so you’re prepared when an offer comes in.

As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers.”

And sellers who offer solutions like buydowns can make meaningful impact where home buyers need it most: in their wallets.

When you're looking for ways to make your house more appealing to buyers, a price reduction isn't your only option. A mortgage rate buydown could help a buyer save more each month, especially in the early years of their loan.Talk to your agent or a trusted lender which incentives could make the biggest difference for buyers in our market, while still protecting your bottom line.

#5518. Shoppable Model Homes Bring New Convenience to Buyers

Homeowners are becoming more practical in nearly every aspect of homeownership. This pragmatic mindset is also influencing the model home experience. For today’s home shopper, inspiration has greater value when buyers can actually put it to use.

Although buyers are drawn to the blank-canvas opportunity of a new build, decision fatigue is real, and tools that build confidence and save time are a welcome relief.

“We are seeing a lot of interest in making models actionable through features like the shoppable model home,” says Ali Richert, enterprise sales, head of home builder at Wayfair Professional.

In addition to shoppable models, furnished homes are popular too. A Zonda survey showed that 73% of buyers would be open to buying a furnished or partially furnished home.

With affordability still a challenge, buyers are looking closely at the overall value of a new-home purchase, including what builders can offer beyond the home itself.

“Regardless of why someone is buying a house, most home buyers will have one thing in common after getting the keys. They will need to furnish the home,” says Richert.

“Historically, the relationship between a builder and buyer ended at closing. Now builders are asking how they can help make the full journey easier.”

“This is one of the ideas that drive innovations like our shoppable model homes or even alternative closing incentives, like home buyer Wayfair gift cards. Instead of furnishing a model to inspire buyers, builders are beginning to view furnishing as an extension of the home buying experience itself,” she says.

In shoppable models, features like scannable QR codes, product links, online storefronts, or other purchasing arrangements simplify the process and bridge the gap between inspiration and real-life functionality, a pragmatic benefit that saves time and builds confidence when envisioning what life will look and feel like at home.

Various buyer groups see benefit in these features, explains Richert.

Investors may need to furnish a whole home quickly to go to market. A second-home buyer might want their home furnished immediately, so that vacations can be taken. First-time and move-up buyers may not have enough existing furniture to fill a space.

But regardless of why you are buying a home, “having a turnkey option for furnishing solutions can remove time, stress, and uncertainty from a process that can seem overwhelming,” she says.

“For a lot of buyers, especially after the long process of choosing a builder, a lender, a community, finishes, cabinets, flooring, and countless other decisions, the appeal of having to skip another major project full of decisions can be incredibly appealing.”

Love the look and the vibe of the model? Model home merchandisers make it look easy, but the aesthetic and the experience are the result of a highly curated, researched process that requires training, talent, and access to products.

Model homes not only display the latest trends and demonstrate how to make the best use of various spaces, but their design details are also selected to appeal to the target market. It’s no wonder that buyers find the aesthetic compelling.

“We focus heavily on purposeful merchandising and thoughtful space planning, showing buyers how each room can function, including multifunctional spaces and ideas they can realistically incorporate into their own home,” says Megan Calmes, director of sales and marketing with Creative Design.

“Additionally, we think about the buyer’s journey beyond the purchase. We want the model to feel aspirational, but also attainable.”

Models aren’t like generic furniture showrooms. The specifics of the floor plan guide the selection of furnishings, which means buyers are seeing pieces chosen for the very spaces they may soon call home.

For example, a buyer might choose a sofa on their own for the new living room, but that’s only a small part of the overall design. Accents like tables, rugs, and artwork matter too. The model demonstrates how these pieces work together, both aesthetically and within the room’s dimensions.

The model shows you how to assemble a look, not just admire it.

A flex room has a ton of potential, but will various uses work comfortably in real life? A model can demonstrate the size and placement of furniture and accents to support a particular purpose, or even multiple functions, within the available space.

Having shoppable tools, or the option to purchase the home furnished as demonstrated, can make those possibilities easier to recreate.

The vast majority of house hunters aren’t designers, so having access to professionally selected furnishings and decor gives buyers a practical head start.

Personalization is always possible, of course. Buyers might purchase the larger anchor pieces, such as a sofa, rug, and dining table, then bring in their own artwork, textiles, or accessories to make the space their own.

#5517. Low Rates or Lots of Leverage? Buyers Rarely Get Both.

If you’ve been watching mortgage rates lately, you might feel a little stuck. Rates climbed above 7% this year, and a lot of buyers have decided to sit tight and wait for them to come back down.

But rates are only half the story. When you buy a home, you usually get one of two things: low rates or negotiating power. It’s rare to get both at the same time. And right now, you have a lot more of that second one than you might think.

Think back to 2020 and 2021. Rates were near 3%, and buyers rushed into the housing market. Those low rates sounded great, but they came with a catch. There were a lot of buyers just like you that you had to compete with – and there weren’t enough homes for sale to meet that demand.

That’s why homes got multiple offers, buyers paid over asking or waived inspections, and sellers held all the cards. Jake Krimmel, Senior Economist at Realtor.com, shows just how one-sided things got:

“Seller’s markets peaked at 98 of 100 metros in spring 2022 after two years of mortgage rates near 3%.”

Then, in the second half of 2022, rates went up. As a result, the number of people buying homes went down, inventory grew, and the balance slowly started tipping from sellers back to buyers. Fast forward to today, and that flip is officially here.

In a recent report, Realtor.com found about two-thirds (66) of the top 100 metros now lean in favor of buyers (see graph below):

And while you may want lower rates, this shift in power has its own perks.

There are more homes for sale than there have been in years. And in a more buyer-friendly market like that, it means sellers have to work harder to get their homes sold. As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Higher inventory and lengthening days on market give buyers improved negotiating power.”

That shows up in the deals buyers are getting. According to Redfin, nearly half of buyers now get some kind of concession from the seller – like help with closing costs, money for repairs, or even the seller paying to buy down your mortgage rate (see graph below):

So when you find a home you love, even if the rate isn’t what you necessarily wanted, there are other levers to pull. Ask about a price cut or a seller-paid rate buydown, too. It could take some of the sting out of today’s rates.

And just in case you’re still thinking you’ll just hold off until rates drop, here’s what you should know. Experts at Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo don’t expect rates to fall much through 2027 (see graph below):

And here’s the whole point. Even if rates did drop in a big way, a lot of buyers would rush back in. More competition means fewer deals, fewer concessions, and sellers getting the upper hand again.

So waiting comes with a trade-off. You might land a better rate down the road, but you’d probably give up the bargaining power you have today.

That doesn’t mean you have to move right now. You should only buy when the numbers work for you. But if you’ve got a real reason to move, today’s leverage could help make your numbers work – even at today’s rates.

#5516. Builder Sentiment Falls to 14-Year Low in November

Builder confidence fell sharply in November as higher mortgage rates, persistent affordability challenges, and rising construction costs continued to weigh on the new-home market, according to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB).

The NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index fell four points to 25 in November, its lowest reading since April 2012. The index stood at 29 in October. Any reading below 50 indicates more builders view market conditions as poor than good.

“Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today’s economy,” says Bill Owens, chairman of the NAHB. “Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction.”

All three components of the HMI declined during the month. The index measuring current sales conditions fell six points to 28, while the component measuring sales expectations over the next six months declined two points to 30. Prospective buyer traffic dropped two points to 16, its lowest level in 15 years excluding the onset of the pandemic in 2020.

In response to weaker demand, builders continued to rely heavily on incentives and price reductions to attract buyers. The share of builders cutting home prices increased to 46% in November, the highest level of the post-Covid period. The average price reduction remained at 6% for the eighth consecutive month.

Meanwhile, 68% of builders offered sales incentives, also a post-Covid high. November marked the 20th consecutive month in which at least 60% of builders reported using incentives. That represents a further deterioration from October, when 43% of builders reported cutting prices and 65% used incentives.

“The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges, including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability,” says Robert Dietz, NAHB chief economist. “Mortgage rates above 7%, softer consumer confidence, and an uncertain economic outlook are holding buyers back.”

On a three-month moving-average basis, builder confidence declined in every region. The Northeast fell four points to 34, the Midwest declined five points to 35, the South dropped three points to 27, and the West fell three points to 23.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5515. Abandoned Property for Sale: How To Buy an Abandoned Home

Buying an abandoned property can be a bargain for homebuyers—if you can actually find such a property.

Properties that are unclaimed by their owners are potential low-cost purchases that might be attractive to prospective homebuyers. They certainly have become all the rage on TikTok, with influencers snatching up properties left and right and sharing their renovation journeys.

Still, "abandoned house for sale" isn't a sign you're likely to see on the roadside. (There might actually be laws against that!)

An abandoned property is usually a property whose original owner is no longer in possession of the home. Due to the owner's financial difficulties, the house is typically run-down and in desperate need of repair. If the law in your area allows you to claim this type of home and you're handy, it might be worth investigating.

However, some abandoned homes for sale can turn out to be in good condition, with the owner hoping to unload the property before foreclosure. This could provide the right buyer with an opportunity to purchase the abandoned property or unclaimed home at a discount—and possibly a significant return on investment if you later flip it.

Purchasing an abandoned or unclaimed property involves following the same procedures as buying any other piece of real estate. Before setting out on your journey to find an abandoned home, review your financial situation.

Remember, there will be additional expenses over and above the original sale price of the property. A pre-qualification from your bank or lender will help you estimate what mortgage amount you qualify for. Many banks also require pre-approval letters, so you can make quick decisions on the property you wish to purchase.

Most abandoned homes for sale are on their way to foreclosure, but the bank has not yet initiated the process. Various lists of abandoned properties or unclaimed properties are available, or you can search for abandoned foreclosures or pre-foreclosures online.

Check for listings of homes for sale with certain phrases that might indicate an abandoned property, such as "immediate possession," "must sell," "below market value," or "under appraisal." Don't forget to add "near me."

Real estate agents will usually have valuable knowledge of abandoned properties in the area and the law relating to claiming them, and can provide you with a selection of homes about to be foreclosed on by the bank.

Some properties might look abandoned but are not listed for sale. You might also check into the laws regarding unclaimed property and whether there is a statute of limitations on its return.

If you find an interesting unclaimed property like this, visit your county clerk’s office. It will have information about the homeowners, the home's current appraised value, liens, or tax problems.

You could then try tracking down the owners and asking them to sell their property. If the property has had liens or tax problems, the owners might be more willing to sell.

Abandoned homes will almost always have issues. Due to months (or years) of neglect, a lack of maintenance, and overall aging, vacant homes are far from pristine. They are often sold as is, which means what you see is what you get.

One major risk? Abandoned homes usually have had their utilities turned off. With no way to check the water, electricity, gas, heating and cooling systems, or appliances, even a professional home inspector will be unable to thoroughly evaluate the house. There could be wiring problems, water leaks, or gas leaks—any of which would be extremely costly to repair.

It might be possible to have utilities turned on temporarily, but that requires paying a deposit and putting the utilities in your name. Even if utilities are turned on, you'll likely have to accept some elements of the abandoned home as is. But remember, forgoing major system inspections is a huge gamble.

A second major risk factor is the deferred maintenance involved with the purchase of a property that's been left to the elements. If previous owners abandoned the home or lost it to foreclosure, they probably didn't pay attention to routine maintenance tasks. Costly repairs will crop up sooner than expected, and you'll have to budget for future repairs.

And to top it off, obtaining home insurance on an abandoned home is difficult. Most insurance agencies won't insure a vacated house without an inspection from one of their agents. And that agent might require you to make costly repairs before issuing a policy.

If the insurer issues a policy, premiums for an unoccupied structure will likely be significantly higher. Because no one has watched over the home, it's more likely to have suffered vandalism or fire damage. Vacant homes often have broken pipes or leaking roofs with resulting water damage, stolen copper wiring, mold, pest issues, and damaged appliances.

Assuming you have found a potential abandoned property for sale and been pre-approved, you will want to factor in costs that will be needed to get the home into solid condition. Get a thorough maintenance inspection performed on the property, and note what needs to be fixed and how much it will cost.

Claiming a property like this also involves adding in the cost of the appraisal fee, pest and lead inspection fees, title insurance, closing costs, and other legal fees.

Crunch the numbers before you consider a bid. A real estate agent can also accompany you to the abandoned property for sale and point out the extra expenses you will incur after the purchase of this property. The agent can also help you figure out how high your bid should be. Look for the right opportunities, and you might find a home that is just right for your budget.

Angela Colley writes about real estate and all things renting and moving for Realtor.com. Her work has appeared in outlets including TheStreet, MSN, and Yahoo.

#5513. Today's Market Could Be a Win for Veterans Looking To Buy a Home

If you’re a veteran or active-duty service member who’s been hoping to buy a home, you may have more going for you in today’s housing market than you realize.

VA home loans already come with some pretty powerful benefits. But now, with more homes for sale and buyers having more room to negotiate in many markets, those benefits could go even further.

And if you’ve ever heard that buying with a VA loan is harder, takes longer, or puts you at a disadvantage, there’s something else you should know… a lot of what people believe about VA loans simply isn’t true.

Today, nearly 4 million service members and veterans have an active VA home loan. And according to the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), more than 343,000 homes were purchased using VA loan benefits in its most recent reported fiscal year. And it’s easy to see why.

For eligible veterans and service members, VA loans offer advantages that can make buying a home more affordable, including:

No down payment required for many eligible borrowers.

No monthly mortgage insurance, even with no down payment.

Competitive mortgage rates that can help lower monthly payments.

Benefits like this are powerful in any market – and even more so today. That may be why VA loan usage has grown for the last two years in a row.

A few years ago, when homes were getting multiple offers and buyers were competing for nearly every listing, VA buyers sometimes had a harder time getting their offers accepted.

A 2021 survey from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), found 89% of sellers were likely to accept an offer from a buyer using a conventional loan. But only 30% were likely to accept one using an FHA or VA loan.

The reason? Some sellers were concerned that VA financing would take longer, be more difficult to close, and require them to pay more in costs and repairs. But those concerns don’t necessarily reflect how VA loans actually perform.

A white paper from Vetted VA based on 2025 mortgage data busted a lot of VA loan myths:

Myth #1: VA loans get denied more often than other loans.

The Reality: VA loans actually have the lowest denial rate. Just 8.2% of VA purchase applications were denied, compared to 15.0% for conventional loans, 12.8% for FHA loans, and 12.5% for USDA loans.

The Reality: 90% of VA home loan applications that reached underwriting made it to closing, compared to 81% for conventional loans.

The Reality: VA loan appraisals typically take 7–10 business days, similar to conventional and FHA loans.

Myth #4: Sellers have to pay all the closing costs for VA buyers.

The Reality: VA buyers can pay many standard closing costs themselves. Buyers and sellers can also negotiate which eligible costs the seller will cover.

Since there are more homes for sale and fewer buyers competing in many areas, sellers may be more open to different financing options than they were a few years ago. And the opportunity doesn’t stop at getting your offer accepted.

Depending on the house and your local market, you may also be able to negotiate a lower price, ask for repairs, or request help with closing costs.

VA guidelines allow sellers to cover the buyer’s normal closing costs, plus concessions of up to 4% of the home’s value.

Think about what that combination could mean. You may be able to buy with no down payment, avoid mortgage insurance, and negotiate help with some of the other expenses that come with buying a home.

That could mean keeping thousands of dollars in your savings instead of spending them upfront, giving you more breathing room after you get the keys.

If you're active duty, you've served, or you know someone who has, connect with a local agent and a trusted VA-approved lender to see what you qualify for.Your VA home loan benefit and today's market could be a powerful combination.

#5512. The Housing Market Is on Solid Ground, Even with More Foreclosures

It’s been nearly two decades since the 2008 housing crash, but the word “foreclosure” can still make people uneasy. And if you’re planning a move, you may be wondering if more foreclosures will flood the market with homes for sale – especially if you’ve seen the headlines lately.

Buyers may be hoping for a rush of bargains. Sellers may be bracing for more competition. The latest data points to neither, and knowing why can help you plan your next move with confidence.

Completed foreclosures are up 33% from last year, according to ATTOM. That sounds like a big leap, but context helps.

Even with that increase, foreclosures are still about 26% below where they were in the first half of 2020.

Zoom out further, and today’s activity is a small fraction of what the market saw during the 2008 crash. Lenders completed about 28,000 foreclosures in the first half of 2026, according to ATTOM. Compare that to the crash years in red, when lenders often completed more than 200,000 in the span of a few months (see graph below):

Experts say today’s numbers reflect a housing market that’s still in good shape. As Rob Barber, CEO at ATTOM, explains:

“While some homeowners are still facing financial challenges, overall foreclosure volumes remain well below historical norms and the broader housing market continues to demonstrate resilience.”

And here’s why we can absorb the slight uptick in foreclosures we are seeing.

During the crash, a lot of homeowners either lost their homes to foreclosure or were forced to sell, which left the market overwhelmed with houses for sale. That isn’t happening now.

One way to see this is through months’ supply, which measures how long it would take to sell every home on the market at the current pace. Four to six months is considered balanced.

Right now, it’s about 4.8 months, according to the National Association of Realtors (NAR). That’s pretty well-balanced, and less than half of where it peaked around the last crash (see graph below):

If foreclosures were really surging, you’d see it in the number of homes for sale. As Logan Mohtashami, Lead Analyst at HousingWire, explains:

“. . . a surge of actual foreclosures in 2026 would have easily put the inventory data much higher in 2026.”

Equity is a big reason there’s no surge of distressed sales. Data from the Census Bureau and ATTOM shows nearly two in three homeowners have paid off their mortgage or have more than 50% equity. And Cotality says the average homeowner has about $310,000 in equity.

If a homeowner with equity hits a rough patch, they can usually sell their house, pay off the loan, and walk away with money in their pocket instead of facing foreclosure. That’s an option many people didn’t have during the crash. According to HousingWire, nearly one in four homes were underwater back in 2010.

Being underwater means owing more on your mortgage than your home is worth, which makes selling a lot harder. Today, just 2% of homeowners are considered seriously underwater (see graph below):

Not every homeowner has that kind of equity, but most do, and that’s what puts a ceiling on how high foreclosures can go.

If rising foreclosures have you questioning where the housing market is headed, the data says it’s in good shape. The supply of homes for sale is balanced, and most homeowners have plenty of equity.Have questions about what you’re seeing online, your local market, or about how much equity you have? Talk to a local real estate agent.

#5511. Planning To Sell in 2027? Start Prepping Now.

If selling your house is on your calendar for 2027, you may be thinking you’ve got plenty of time. Maybe you’re aiming for January. Maybe you’re waiting for spring. Either way, next year probably feels far enough away that getting ready can wait, too.

But waiting until 2027 to sell doesn’t mean waiting until 2027 to get started.

Today’s buyers have more homes to choose from than they’ve had in years. So, if you want your house to stand out when it’s time to list, a little preparation now can make a big difference later.

As a general rule of thumb, Zillow recommends giving yourself about 2-3 months to get your house ready to list. And that makes sense when you consider that the vast majority of sellers (78%) did at least one home improvement project before their house hit the market.

That gives you plenty of time to decide what to fix, find contractors, get on their schedules, actually make the updates, and get everything ready for photos and showings.

But don’t worry – that doesn’t mean every seller had some big to-do. The most common? Interior painting (see graph below):

That certainly doesn’t mean you need to tackle everything on this list. You may not need to do any of it. But odds are there’s at least one project you’ll want to do. And starting that conversation now gives you a leg up before next year.

While you might have a long list of things you think need updating, that doesn’t mean they’re all worth the time, effort, or money.

An agent will help you figure out which projects deserve a spot on your to-do list based on what buyers want most and what other sellers are doing. That way, you’re not investing in updates that won’t make much of a difference when you sell.

One thing your agent may recommend today is that you go ahead and get a pre-listing inspection. It’s basically your cheatsheet to what a buyer’s inspection may turn up later on.

And now that buyers have more options, they’re pickier – and you don’t want anything popping up in an inspection that could put them off.

For example, you know that HVAC system you’ve been hoping will make it through one more season? Now’s a good time to give it some attention – along with anything else you know needs a little TLC. That way a repair you could’ve handled months ago won’t become a surprise in the middle of your sale.

According to Angi, a pre-listing inspection typically costs $300-600 and that can be money well spent. As the National Association of Realtors (NAR) explains:

“An inspector will be able to give you a good indication of the trouble areas that will stand out to potential buyers, and you’ll be able to make repairs before open houses begin.”

The advantage isn’t just knowing what may come up, but being able to get ahead of it and space out the projects on your own schedule. So you don’t feel stressed during go-time.

But remember, not everything needs to happen right away. Some things are better saved for when you’re closer to listing.

Think deep cleaning, staging, touching up paint, and tidying up the landscaping. Those are the finishing touches that’ll help your house look its best when buyers walk through the door.

But there’s one thing you can start anytime: decluttering. Go ahead and tackle the closets, garage, or storage room you’ve been avoiding. Future you will appreciate having a few less boxes to pack.

The idea isn’t to get everything done today. It’s to spread the work out so you’re not scrambling when listing day arrives. As Redfin puts it:

“Smart preparation leads to a smoother sale, stronger offers, and fewer surprises during closing. . . Homes that are clean, well-staged, priced right, and professionally photographed tend to sell quickly.”

You don't need to spend the rest of the year renovating your house or packing up your life. But you can start making a plan.The earlier you figure out what needs to be done, the more time you'll have to do it right. #5510. EXCLUSIVE: Google Co-Founder Sergey Brin and Ex-Wife Nicole Shanahan List Malibu Home for $33 Million

The elegant Malibu estate that Google co-founder Sergey Brin purchased with his ex-wife, Nicole Shanahan, has hit the selling block for $33.5 million—months after it was listed as a rental.

Brin, 53, and Shanahan—who went on to join Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s short-lived presidential campaign—bought the "dreamy" Point Dume dwelling for $13.5 million in September 2020, just over a year before it was revealed that they had split after three years of marriage.

The details of their divorce settlement, which was finalized in 2023, were never fully revealed. However, reports suggest that Shanahan walked away with around $1 billion in assets, including shares in Alphabet, Google's parent company.

It has never been revealed how the former couple split their shared properties. Brin purchased another Malibu residence for $35 million just a few months after their separation, a move that many saw as a sign that Shanahan, 41, had kept their former marital home.

Property records viewed by Realtor.com® show that the five-bedroom, 7.5-bathroom dwelling is currently registered to a limited liability company in Nevada that is managed by Shanahan's family office. That LLC lists the same mailing address as her charitable organization, the Bia-Echo Foundation, which is named for the former couple's daughter, Echo.

While it's unclear whether Shanahan ever used the property as her primary residence, she revealed in an October 2025 interview with Frontier Magazine that she was living in a different California property: a mountaintop ranch where she was residing with her partner, Jacob Strumwasser.

Although the home was listed for rent for $175,000 a month in May, the property has now vanished from the rental market and is now available for purchase.

The listing, which is held by Michael Cunningham of Pinnacle Estate Properties, notes that it has undergone an extensive series of overhauls in recent months, describing it as a "newly completed estate."

"A long, private driveway leads to a secluded sanctuary surrounded by mature trees, lush landscaping, and beautiful ocean views, with the rare privilege of keyed access to Little Dume Beach. Meticulously designed with every detail reflects an uncompromising commitment to quality and sophistication," the listing notes.

The property comes with an array of upscale features and amenities, including "keyed access to Little Dume beach," a stunning stretch of sand that is known as one of Malibu's best areas for surfing.

The dwelling itself has plenty to offer, both inside and out. The 1.2-acre lot includes a dazzling swimming pool with a large spa and a pagoda-style area for shade.

The parcel is incredibly private, featuring a gated entrance, a long driveway, and tall trees surrounding the home.

The listing describes the home as the "epitome of 'quiet luxury,'" constructed with top-of-the-line materials and quality craftsmanship.

Upon entering the home, visitors are greeted with a spacious, airy foyer that opens to an elegant dining space and living room, where walls of windows flood the space with natural light. A curved ceiling elevates the room, while a fireplace keeps it cozy.

The dining area separates the living space from the enormous open-plan kitchen, which features a curved island and huge French doors that open to a private deck overlooking the grounds.

For those with a fondness for entertaining, a second meal prep area with its own stove and additional appliances will no doubt prove to be one of the most-used spaces in the dwelling.

Elsewhere on the main floor are a media room—which the listing notes could be turned into an office or library—as well as a generous gym and wellness suite.

"Designed with wellness and longevity in mind, the residence incorporates advanced clean-building technologies and carefully selected materials, including a state-of-the-art VRF climate system, copper and cast-iron plumbing, rigid metal HVAC ducting, sustainable denim insulation, and specialized wiring and shielding intended to reduce EMF exposure," the description adds.

Two more bedrooms can be found on this upper level, each with its own bathroom. Another bedroom is located in a separate apartment space with a private entrance, as well as an additional kitchen and living room.

In addition to Brin, the property has a history of A-list residents, having previously been owned by pop star Pink, who purchased it for $11.9 million in 2010 and used it as her primary residence until 2016, when she sold it for $12.5 million.

The property is located just a mile away from the Malibu home Brin bought for $35 million in April 2022, just a few months after it was revealed that he and Shanahan had split.

He has since expanded his Malibu holdings with another pricier property that he picked up for $49.7 million in July 2025.

However, Brin has recently joined the growing list of billionaires pulling their fortunes out of California amid the threat of Proposition 40, a one-time, 5% wealth tax on residents worth over $1 billion—a proposal that has since been rejected.

The Google co-founder has been an outspoken critic of the tax, likening California to the Soviet Union when asked why he left the state.

"I fled socialism with my family in 1979 and know the devastating, oppressive society it created in the Soviet Union. I don’t want California to end up in the same place," he told The New York Times in April.

California voters rejected Proposition 40, which would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth, with most proceeds earmarked for healthcare. Opponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, argued that the measure could drive wealthy residents out of the state and reduce future tax revenue.

Brin has, quite literally, put his money where his mouth is, snapping up several properties outside of California in anticipation of the tax, including a $42 million mansion on the Nevada shore of Lake Tahoe and a $51 million Miami Beach dwelling that he bought from LVMH CEO Michael Burke at the start of the year.

The Miami property is located on the exclusive Allison Island, a 35-acre stretch of land that sits in the Biscayne Bay, between La Gorce and Miami Beach. The 24/7 guard-gated island is home to fewer than 50 single-family homes.

It was custom-built for Burke and his wife, Brigitte Burke, in 2019, five years after they purchased the 1-acre plot of land on which the home now sits for $11.7 million.

The spectacular property spans 10,000 square feet and has seven bedrooms, 8.5 bathrooms, a waterfront pool, and a private dock. The modernist design includes two separate wings of the home connected by a central walk-through area.

It's unclear whether Brin has any plans to offload either of his Malibu homes in the wake of his move from California. Neither dwelling is currently listed on the multiple listing service.

#5508. Buyers Need Cheaper Homes. Airbnb Is Putting $1 Million Toward Finding New Solutions.

For many Americans these days, affordable housing is still out of reach.

Airbnb is stepping up to the plate to try to change that.

The company announced a $1 million annual Housing Innovation Prize to support innovators and entrepreneurs who are striving to make it faster, easier, and cheaper to buy homes. It plans to distribute one award per year over a five-year period.

The $1 million prizes are intended for U.S.-based companies and nonprofits with ideas that are already in the works but need funding to succeed. These may include factory-built homes, faster construction sides, expedited permitting, or easier financing for new homes.

“Airbnb started as a way to help my co-founders pay their rent. Today millions of people do the same. Now we are helping to finance the building of housing in communities nationwide. We want to encourage others, through this prize, to think more creatively and ambitiously about home building and delivering affordability. Necessity is the mother of invention,” said Nathan Blecharczyk, Airbnb’s co-founder and chief strategy officer, in a recent press release.

While Airbnb’s efforts are a step in the right direction, experts agree that addressing the affordability crisis as a whole requires more funding, innovation, and collaboration across the industry.

Airbnb's initiative brings renewed attention to the need for more housing in the U.S., and finding ways to build it more efficiently and affordably is becoming increasingly important.

Realtor.com® data shows how serious the housing supply gap has become.

In 2025, new-home construction fell short of household formations, pushing the U.S. housing supply gap to an estimated 4.03 million homes. This demonstrates the need for new solutions that can make it easier and more efficient to build homes.

Addressing the shortage will also require evaluating and changing policies and regulations that may slow down construction and raise costs. That’s where the Realtor.com Let America Build initiative comes in.

It strives to encourage discussions and solutions on the U.S. home inventory and affordability crisis.

Several factors are slowing down homebuilding and driving up construction costs in the U.S., and initiatives like Airbnb’s could help.

“Builders cite slow permit processes, increased material expenses, and lack of skilled labor as the main factors raising construction costs,” says Michael Pearson, senior vice president of business development at A&D Mortgage LLC in Ft. Lauderdale, FL.

Additionally, with expenses on the rise and the pressure to keep homes marketable and affordable, margins for contractors and developers are very low.

Innovations for factory-built or modular homes, for example, could improve the situation. These homes are traditionally built homes assembled off site and delivered to a plot of land.

“While modular homes are more economical, as you don’t have to ship supplies and workers to a site build and you can better control costs and material overages, they come with logistical concerns, primarily getting the modular home on site. Innovation may find a solution that so far has not shown itself,” adds Pearson.

Gay Cororaton, chief economist at MIAMI Realtors + RWorld in Miami, points out that modular homes are simply more attainable for more households.

“The average price of a new manufactured home is less than $150,000, which could go up to, say, $300,000 for a double-wide home. At today's mortgage rates, for a household with $100,000 in income, that’s more affordable than a traditional home,” Cororaton explains.

Still, while the Airbnb Housing Innovation Prize could turn promising ideas into realities, Pearson believes $1 million prizes won’t be enough and innovations must be part of a greater strategy where we highlight issues, communicate ideas, and have demonstrable progress. It’s also important for other organizations to jump on board.

“I’d like to see more companies, nonprofits, and government agencies get involved with this kind of action. Housing safety and affordability is this issue of this generation, and together we can find solutions,” says Pearson.

Robert Trent, CEO and principal at Builders Capital in Puyallup, WA, agrees with Pearson and believes the success of Airbnb’s initiative will depend on what gets built after the award.

“The best-case scenario is quality homes people can afford, delivered at a lower total cost, with results that can be replicated across different communities,” Trent adds.

#5507. Sellers Vastly Outnumber Buyers as Top Metros Shift Further: Report

Buying house, real estate deal and investment. Tiny woman carrying money in shopping cart to buy family home, agent or broker giving building model and apartment key cartoon vector illustration

Sellers have largely had the upper-hand in the housing market since the pandemic as home prices reached new peaks, giving sellers max equity to see large returns on their investments. Now, as the market is observing some shifts, a new report from Redfin found that seller’s markets are losing ground.

Homebuyers have gained more negotiating power across the country, as Redfin data estimated there were 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October. This was the biggest recorded gap seen since 2013, as well as the sixth month in a row this measure has reached a new record.

Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan said that sellers are “increasingly competing for buyers’ attention,” which has led to more “price reductions, concessions and other savings.”

“First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle—but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate,” he continued. “With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting—and can afford today’s costs—may have an opportunity to make a move.”

Looking at the 50 most populous metros in the U.S., only three were seller’s markets in October. Redfin used “proprietary” data on buyer behavior and MLS listings to estimate the balance of buyers and sellers.

Notably, all three of the seller’s markets were located in the Northeast, where home prices remain higher than other regions. These three markets saw home prices rise 3.3% year-over-year in October, compared to prices increasing only 0.3% in buyer’s markets.

The top of the three seller’s markets was Nassau County, New York, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers, a gap that actually shrank from 28.3% the month prior. The other two markets were Newark, New Jersey (14.3% fewer sellers, down from 17.6% the month prior) and Montgomery County, Pennsylvania (12.1% fewer sellers, down from 20.1% the month prior).

Another difference from September’s data was the loss of a fourth seller’s market—Milwaukee, Wisconsin, which is now balanced between buyers and sellers.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

#5506. Red Hat and Microsoft bring OpenShift virtual machines to Azure

IBM Corp. subsidiary Red Hat and Microsoft Corp. are expanding their longtime engineering partnership to enable enterprises to run virtual machines on Microsoft Azure using Red Hat’s OpenShift Virtualization platform, providing an alternative to traditional hypervisors and what Red Hat called a path to modernizing legacy applications.

The collaboration, announced today, involves changes to Azure’s underlying computing architecture to connect it natively with Linux through Microsoft direct virtualization. That’s an Azure feature that gives performance-sensitive workloads near-bare-metal access to underlying hardware components.

Red Hat said this provides a direct pipeline between key hardware such as graphics processing units and isolated workloads. The companies are also working to give Linux-based workloads more direct access to Azure’s hardware resources, including graphics processing units.

Separately, Red Hat said it’s making its Lightwell Network vulnerability remediation service available through Microsoft’s Azure Marketplace.

The virtualization initiative addresses growing enterprise concerns about hypervisor licensing costs, hardware availability and the complexity of managing virtual machines alongside newer containerized applications. Red Hat said those pressures have intensified as organizations seek to accommodate AI workloads without abandoning existing applications.

Virtualization market leader Broadcom Inc. recently took aim at the same issue by open-sourcing its software for provisioning and managing virtual machines using the same protocols that the Kubernetes container orchestrator uses. At the center of the effort is Microsoft’s direct virtualization, which lets Linux-based and cloud-native platforms running on Azure virtual machines access the same virtualization and hardware capabilities available to Azure-native services.

Red Hat said it will be the first commercial Microsoft partner to support the technology through OpenShift Virtualization on Azure Red Hat OpenShift, the jointly engineered and managed Kubernetes service offered by the two companies.

The agreement includes collaboration on several upstream open-source projects, including KubeVirt, LibVirt, QEMU and the Linux kernel. KubeVirt enables organizations to manage virtual machines and containers using Kubernetes tools.

Microsoft has extended KubeVirt beyond the Linux Kernel-based Virtual Machine hypervisor by adding support for its own hypervisor. That allows OpenShift Virtualization to run on Azure virtual machines using Microsoft’s direct virtualization technology.

The approach is designed to let organizations consolidate traditional virtual machines, containerized applications and AI workloads on a common platform. Red Hat said its migration toolkit for virtualization will help customers move workloads from existing hypervisors.

The companies said the architecture will also improve resource utilization by supporting CPU and memory overcommitment, enabling more workloads to share available infrastructure. Kernel-level isolation is intended to protect sensitive workloads without compromising performance.

“Enterprises shouldn’t have to choose between managing rising hypervisor costs and accelerating their IT roadmaps,” Chris Wright, Red Hat’s chief technology officer, said in a statement. He said the collaboration would provide a common foundation for modernizing existing virtual machines and running AI workloads.

The companies did not announce a general availability date for the new virtualization capabilities.

Red Hat also said Lightwell Network is immediately available through private offers on Azure Marketplace, allowing customers to obtain remediated versions of vulnerable open-source software dependencies.

Lightwell addresses a persistent application security problem: correcting vulnerabilities in third-party software without forcing upgrades that could disrupt production applications.

The service provides version-specific fixes through secured repositories, accompanied by signed software artifacts and supporting provenance, software bills of materials and vulnerability information where applicable.

Customers can incorporate those fixes into existing development and deployment pipelines without replacing their vulnerability scanners, artifact repositories or build systems. Findings can surface in Microsoft Defender for Cloud, while Azure Policy provides governance controls.

Customers can purchase Lightwell subscriptions through Azure Marketplace and apply eligible spending toward their Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitments.

#5504. Wisconsin Couple Seek To Enforce $1,350 Judgment Against Each of Their Neighbors in HOA Dispute

A neighborhood outside Green Bay, WI, is locked in a yearslong legal battle, as one couple is now taking legal action against their neighbors to collect a $200,000 settlement.

What began as a dispute over a backyard fence has turned into an ongoing series of lawsuits, with neighbors being forced to pay $1,350 each in a settlement—and those who haven’t are now being taken to court.

The case is centered around Michael and Lisa Newman and their five children, who reside in the Nazcr Trac neighborhood in De Pere, WI. After some of their children were diagnosed with autism, the Newmans wanted to build a fence around their backyard, as they wanted the children to be able to play outside safely.

Citing the children’s diagnoses and that two of their children “demonstrated significant risk of elopement,” according to a press release from the Metropolitan Milwaukee Fair Housing Council, the Newmans wrote to the Nazcr Trac Property Owners Association (NTPOA) to request an accommodation to the subdivision’s “no fence” rule.

Neither the initial request, sent in July 2019, nor a subsequent request in December 2020, which included information about the association’s legal obligation to consider an accommodation due to the children’s disabilities, were answered by the association.

In August 2021, the Newmans filed a lawsuit against the association in federal court, alleging that it had discriminated based on disability, a violation of the Fair Housing Amendments Act. A judge granted a preliminary injunction in May 2022 that prohibits the NTPOA from enforcing the rule, and the family built their fence in time for summer, three years after the initial request.

While the family got their wish, the battle was just beginning for other residents of Nazcr Trac.

In August 2024, a settlement was reached, requiring the NTPOA to pay the Newmans $200,000—a payment that would be passed on directly to each household in the association.

Following the settlement, each property in the neighborhood was looking at a $1,350 bill. Residents told WGBA that they were frustrated by the situation and many had been unaware of the dispute until they received the charge.

One anonymous resident told the local station that most residents would have had no issue with the fence, and a poll of members could have saved a lot of time and money.

“If the board had polled us as members, a large amount of the members would have said, 'Absolutely, let the family do what they need to do to take care of their family,’” the resident said during WGBA’s initial coverage in 2025.

At the time, Lisa Newman told the station that she felt “not great” about her neighbors being on the hook for the settlement payment.

“It's just a really unfortunate situation, I think, for everybody involved, and the board kind of made that decision for everybody,” she told WGBA.

However, in September, the Newmans filed a new lawsuit against the NTPOA and a number of homeowners who still owe on the settlement.

Sixty-nine homeowners settled following the initial lawsuit, the Newmans’ attorney, Victoria Davis Dávila, told WGBA. The rest are now facing legal troubles of their own.

“There’s an outstanding judgment," Davis Dávila told WGBA. "You had the opportunity to pay. You chose not to pay it."

In addition to the association, 33 residents are named in the new filing.

“The Newmans want just as bad as anybody else to put this behind them,” Davis Dávila said, adding that the NTPOA membership as a whole could potentially be held liable if the outstanding amount isn’t paid.

The new lawsuit is frustrating and stressful for many homeowners who thought the issue would be behind them by now.

“Why is this coming back to us? It’s so unfair,” an anonymous homeowners told WGBA.

An answer and affirmative defense was filed by the Property Owner’s Association on Nov. 16, but the contents of the document were not publicly available at the time of publication.

Realtor.com® reached out to the legal counsel of both the association and the Newmans, but received no response.
