#5503. Chainguard goes self-serve with free Starter plan and $500-a-month Team plan

Software supply chain security company Chainguard Inc. is now offering its products on a self-serve basis, with the launch today of a free plan called Chainguard Starter and a paid Team plan priced at $500 a month.

The free plan covers nearly all of Chainguard’s products, with usage limits set at a level that fits a personal project or a small team. According to Chainguard, users can sign up, pull an image, connect their package manager to its screened libraries and place coding agents in a sandbox in one sitting, with no credit card or sales call required.

The launch comes after Black October, the name given to a run of supply chain attacks and critical vulnerability disclosures in the third week of October. With incidents like those, a team may have only until the end of the day to deal with a bad dependency, according to the blog post in which Chainguard announced the plans. In such cases, the company wrote, “nobody is going to wait on a purchase order.”

Until now, access to Chainguard’s products has typically required a conversation with its sales team first. One exception was Catalog Starter, a free beta plan offered earlier this year that was limited to five container images. Chainguard says the sales-led model, designed around large companies with procurement processes, works far less well for a team that needs a hardened base image ahead of its next deployment.

In most cases, moving a service onto Chainguard requires changing only a single line in the file that defines its container image. Security engineers can also put Chainguard’s images and libraries through their own scanners before signing anything, according to the company.

Starter includes five container images from Chainguard’s catalog of more than 3,000 minimal images, which are claimed to have near-zero known vulnerabilities, with downloads of up to 100 gigabytes a month. A software bill of materials and signed build provenance are provided for every image.

Also part of the plan is Chainguard Libraries, which provides malware- and greyware-scanned dependencies for JavaScript, Python, Java, Go and .NET with a limit of 50,000 pulls a month. Under a fixed seven-day cooldown, newly published versions are held back for a week, which the company says allows a compromised release to be caught before it reaches a build.

Starter also comes with 500 hours a month of virtual CPU time on each of Chainguard Checks and Chainguard Workspaces, which launched in beta at the company’s Assemble London event in October. Checks is designed to provide hardened runners for continuous integration, with Workspaces providing hardened sandboxes for coding agents.

Other features on the free plan include hardened replacements for GitHub Actions, more than 1,000 hardened agent skills, community support and 100 gigabytes of private artifact storage. Starter users also get 1 million tokens a month for Guardener, Chainguard’s artificial intelligence agent, which inventories the GitHub Actions and container images in a customer’s repositories and opens pull requests to swap in the company’s hardened versions. Each Starter account is limited to five users.

The paid Team plan, which is billed to a credit card, includes everything in Starter with higher limits, such as unlimited users, 1 terabyte of image downloads and 1 million dependency pulls a month. Team customers also get base, application and AI images at their latest versions on top of their five chosen images, along with 1,000 hours a month each of Checks and Workspaces, 5 million Guardener tokens and 500 gigabytes of private storage.

Features reserved for Team include backported fixes for known vulnerabilities across five remediated versions, zero-day patches on the day of disclosure, ticketed support and managed policies that set rules for what is pulled and what is blocked. Chainguard says the usual reasons for upgrading include a sixth person needing access, a project outgrowing the usage limits and a team needing a patch for a version it cannot yet move off.

According to Chainguard, the upgrade takes a few seconds from the console that flags which limit a user has hit. Nothing has to be migrated, since the account, images and session all carry over. Customers can cancel at any time from the same console. Storage beyond Team’s included 500 gigabytes will be metered starting Jan. 1, 2027, according to Chainguard’s documentation.

The Enterprise offering is unchanged and still starts with a conversation with the company’s sales team. Enterprise provides companywide use of Chainguard with no usage limits, along with service-level agreements, enterprise compliance features and integrations. Starter is available now.

Chainguard says it has raised $892 million since its founding in 2021. Its most recent round, $280 million from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund, came in October 2025.

#5500. Arista takes aim at the next AI network battleground: distributed inference

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

Awareness of the network’s role in artificial intelligence has steadily increased, with much of the focus on the back end – larger clusters, faster ports and scale-across fabrics that stitch graphics processing units together across data centers. Arista Networks Inc. has seen continued, accelerated growth and has been one of the biggest winners of that buildout.

This week at SC26, Arista announced a shift in focus to the other side of the network. The company also announced a new set of Etherlink R4 routing platforms designed for what it calls distributed inferencing, along with a pluggable optical line system for data center interconnect. The lineup includes:

All are based on Broadcom’s Jericho and Qumran silicon, designed to deliver up to 60% lower power consumption than competing 7-nanometer and 16-nanometer platforms. Everything is available now, except the 7020HR4, which ships in early 2027. The speeds and feeds always make headlines, but the implications of the launch point to where AI infrastructure is heading.

During a pre-briefing, Brendan Gibbs, Arista’s assistant vice president of product line management, argued that the forces driving training across multiple sites will have the same effect on inference. Gibbs also said that roughly 30% of Arista’s AI business is now scale-across, indicating that distributed AI is rapidly becoming commonplace.

Inference will be distributed for three reinforcing reasons:

The implication is that the front-end network, long treated as plumbing, now needs back-end attributes: deep buffers, traffic engineering, multi-tenancy, and encryption, because traffic now leaves the building.

This launch is the opposite of the descriptors we typically associate with Arista. Recent announcements focused on dense 800G, 1.6T, and liquid cooling. The products launched at SC26 are smaller and less expensive. Arista dominates big iron and is now rounding out its portfolio. Arista’s customers range from hyperscalers to neoclouds to enterprises building local AI. The front end needs rich features, not massive bandwidth, and Arista hasn’t had a viable option for that tier until now.

These routers are designed as entry-level but ship with 400G uplinks, which may seem like overkill today but offer investment protection. Gibbs said the goal is a 10-year life cycle, with customers swapping optics rather than chassis. No one knows what agents will do to traffic volumes, and I suspect companies that consider this overkill today will think differently in three or four years. Headroom is cheaper than a forklift upgrade at a remote site. Also notable: Arista co-designed the 7280R4 with a hyperscaler seeking a gray-to-coherent bridge, a sign that it’s building with its biggest customers.

The most intriguing product is the hardened 7020HR4, built for 5G and AI-RAN cell sites. Telcos have largely sat out the AI buildout, yet they own the last mile and real estate near users, exactly what low-latency inference requires. This gives a carrier the backbone to offer a managed AI factory.

My view is that this performs better outside the U.S., where enterprises don’t trust carriers beyond connectivity. In Europe and Asia-Pacific, managed services are far more common, and providers such as BT, NTT and Telstra have the footprint to make it work. With sovereignty requirements, the opportunity for telcos to move up the stack has never been better. Telcos have never been a core market for Arista, so any growth from that audience is additive to its already massive market.

Since 2019, Arista has reported a far lower CVE count than competitors, even after the surge in AI-assisted discovery following Anthropic’s Mythos. I’m skeptical of CVE comparisons because counts depend on testing rigor, installed base and reporting practices, and some vendors now bundle multiple issues into a single CVE.

The more relevant benefit is operational. Customers often don’t apply patches because upgrades cause downtime and break things. If they trust the software, they patch faster, and the risk window shrinks. With Mythos accelerating the retirement of end-of-support gear, quality and longevity become buying criteria, not nice-to-haves.

On the call, Gibbs agreed it’s hard to draw conclusions from CVE counts but explained that CVE counts were a measure of Arista’s software quality. This has been Arista’s calling card since it was a startup. While CVEs provide one metric, the bigger proof point is its historical track record of quality software.

Also, wire-speed MACsec and IPsec on every port is a differentiator because AI brings different security requirements. However, integrated security does not replace firewalls. I asked Gibbs about this, and he said that Arista has no intention of replacing firewalls and expects Palo Alto Networks Inc. to continue to sit behind it in the line. I’d like to see that formalized into validated designs for distributed inference, like what Nvidia Corp.-validated designs did for the back end.

The optical line system is a similar simplification play. Arista isn’t an optical company and is reselling these products, but offering dark fiber customers a turnkey, EOS-integrated way to move 25.6 Tbps across a metro network removes a real headache.

Customers have responded positively to Arista’s entry into this market. Douglas Fast Net Chief Technology Officer Jon Vradenburg said the company needs “a compact platform that supports the services our business and carrier customers rely on.” Takayuki Sakou of Japan’s STNet cited “higher throughput and improved power efficiency while maintaining the quality of the EOS software we trust.”

The back end of AI networking is largely a solved architecture at this point. The front end is not, and that’s where the next round of competition will play out. With R4, Arista is betting that its routing credibility, built quietly within hyperscaler backbones, can make it the default there as well. Given how much traffic agentic AI is likely to generate, that’s a bet that, like most Arista bets, will likely pay off.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5498. Dell puts a single gateway between enterprise AI agents and the data they crave

Data intelligence is becoming the deciding layer of the enterprise AI factory as companies learn that racks of graphics processing units deliver little value when agents lack trusted, governed context.

Neocloud providers built the first wave of large-scale AI systems, and core enterprise customers now want the same capabilities inside their own organizations. Dell Technologies Inc. recently extended its AI Data Platform with semantic and knowledge graph features aimed at that market shift. But both the challenge and the opportunity lie in pairing structured and unstructured data so agents get full context while maintaining guardrails and human oversight, according to Srinath Alapati (pictured, right), senior director of product marketing for AI Data Platform at Dell.

“The bottom line is if you feed the wrong data, you get the wrong outcomes,” Alapati said. “What we’ve found is in our own testing — by giving the right context — you can improve the accuracy from roughly 60% to like 94%.”

Alapati, Alison Biers (center), senior director of product marketing for compute, networking and global industries at Dell, and Adam Glick (left), senior director of AI solutions product marketing for compute at Dell, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Dell is tying data, infrastructure management and validated designs together to move enterprise AI factories into production. (* Disclosure below.)

Enterprises can’t give agents unfettered access to their systems, which is where Dell’s newly announced Agentic Data Gateway fits. The gateway sits in the orchestration layer as a single point of control, backed by a Model Context Protocol server, Alapati explained. Storage intelligence tells customers what data they hold, who owns it and how large it is, while Dell’s new data intelligence capabilities track lineage and provenance. Hybrid workflows extend that model across the edge, the cloud and the data center, where companies can struggle to meet the data consolidation requirements of other data platform providers.

“They want you to bring all the data to wherever the platform is. That’s not always possible,” Alapati said. “Number one, it’s super expensive. Two is data is always being generated. It’s a never-ending game. You can’t always keep bringing in data, consolidating data. What we do is we only send metadata … That way your data stays where you want to be.”

On the infrastructure side, Dell OpenManage Rack Scale extends management beyond compute endpoints to the network fabric, power and cooling. That gives operators a single operational plane from day zero through day two, according to Biers. A rebuilt, intent-based Dell Fabric Manager replaces the company’s SmartFabric Manager, and Dell’s PowerRack systems treat the full rack as the unit of deployment.

“It is literally six hours from the time it hits your loading dock to full production,” Biers said. “Something that used to take maybe months and months [is] now cut in half, maybe even less.”

More than 6,500 customers now use the Dell AI Factory, and a growing share are core enterprises asking for help putting AI to work, Glick noted. Validated designs built with Nvidia Corp. and other partners cover both the hardware and the full software stack, and Dell is expanding its labs to keep pace with independent software companies joining the ecosystem. Compute still draws most of the attention, but that is only one part of a larger system.

“If you’ve got a factory, compute is your assembly line. It’s the important part,” Glick said. “It’s what you think of when you think of ‘factory’, but that assembly line doesn’t run if you don’t have a warehouse that’s feeding it the raw materials — that’s the data that goes into it.”

#5497. Anne Hathaway Welcomes Her Third Child With Husband Adam Shulman

Congratulations are in order for Anne Hathaway and her husband, Adam Shulman. It appears the couple have welcomed their third child, after "The Devil Wears Prada" actress was spotted with a newborn in New York City on Nov. 17.

The photos, shared first by TMZ, depict Hathaway, 44, strolling around her hometown with a friend, and an infant snuggled up into a baby carrier.

The actress first shared news of her pregnancy in June, revealing a growing baby bump in an Instagram video captioned, "Baby, I'm yours."

Hathaway and Shulman are also parents to two sons: Jonathan Rosebanks Shulman, 10, and Jack Shulman, 7.

Shortly after sharing the news, Hathaway appeared on "Late Night With Seth Meyers," and said that so far, the experience of a third pregnancy had been "amazing."

She noted that she and her jewelry designer husband were surprised to learn they had another bundle of joy on the way.

"I mean, we knew what we were doing, but we were so shocked it worked," she revealed on the talk show. "We were so shocked it went this way, so we're calling this one our buzzer-beater," she joked.

According to a People magazine source, up until the announcement, Hathaway had worked diligently to keep the news of her pregnancy a secret during "The Devil Wears Prada 2" press tour.

"She wanted to reveal the pregnancy on her own terms. The press tour was about celebrating the movie and getting fans excited to see it," shared the source.

Press tours for "Verity" and "The Odyssey" have kept Hathaway busy shortly in the time since, but according to the source, she was able to "focus on family" and soak up "a little downtime" in the time between the films.

"She's grateful for where she is in her career and for the opportunity to be part of a film that means so much to so many people. Complaining just isn't Anne. She approaches things with gratitude and professionalism, and that's exactly how she handled the press tour," the source added.

Although Hathaway is a longtime New Yorker who originally hailed from New Jersey, the family primarily resides in an Ojai, CA, home the couple purchased for $3.6 million in 2014.

The couple told Architectural Digest that it was love at first sight with the property, and they knew they had to have it from the moment they first viewed it—even if it needed a handful of updates.

"It was the ideal combination of romance and great design," Hathaway said. "Our initial instinct was that this was going to be a very important place in our lives. I could really see raising a family here."

The 3,400-square foot home has a gorgeous Swiss chalet-inspired aesthetic that's been customized after the couple spent years renovating the home.

According to a previous listing, the home had four bedrooms and four bedrooms. However, records indicate that Hathaway and Shulman also purchased a parcel of land next to the property, so there's a good chance they may have expanded the home.

Based on the baby's first public outing, it seems that they may be splitting their time between the Sunshine State and the East Coast.

The "Princess Diaries" actress has previously shared glimpses of her personal life, explaining that she really lives for simple pleasures.

"I still get the paper delivered every day, and I love sitting down with it," she told People magazine in an interview for her "World's Most Beautiful" cover story.

She explained that on a slow day, she loves cuddling with the family's new puppy and finding time to speak to loved ones.

"I'm always zipping from one thing to another," she admitted. "I'd love to have breakfast with a friend. I'd love to go for a walk, maybe do a little window shopping, maybe go to a museum. I'm very meandering on my days off."

In the interview, she also shared her appreciation for Shulman, noting that he "supports" her "completely," especially in a year as busy as the one she's having now.

"I'm so lucky that he's my partner that I spend my life with. If I didn't know that before this past year, I think I really know it now, because with absolutely everything, he's just, he's on it. He holds it down," she gushed. "I hope that doesn't sound like I'm bragging, but he's a dream partner to me."

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5496. Exec: Time for Banks to Reclaim Mortgage Biz From Non-Bank Lenders

Mortgage rates recently reached 7.51% on the 30-year fixed, almost a full percentage point higher than last year. Despite that, the CEO of Chase Home Lending plans to aggressively expand its mortgage business to reclaim market share from non-bank lenders.

In a recent report on CNBC, Sean Grzebin noted that while banks had to recover consumer confidence following the great financial crisis of 20-some years ago, he thinks that’s a done deal.

“The non-banks are all very formidable competitors, and I think they’ve had an advantage while the banks were distracted through several decades,” he said. “Now you’re starting to see the resurgence of banks. A lot of banks are actually going to grow their mortgage business through this.”

Some of the major non-bank lenders in the U.S. include Rocket Mortgage, United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM), PennyMac Loan Services, loanDepot, Better Mortgage, to name a few.

Non-banks currently dominate originations with a 66.3% share by dollar volume, up from just 27% before the 2008 financial crisis, according to CNBC. However, large banks with $50 billion or more in assets are now increasing originations by 34% annually, outperforming competitors.

“We’re going to hire a bunch of lending advisors across the United States,” said Grzebin. “We’re going to focus on areas where we haven’t had a lot of coverage, but there’s a lot of mortgage activity and transactions taking place. And it really matches the expansion that we’re having within the branch network on the consumer bank side.”

Non-banks had a 66.3% share of originations by dollar volume in the first half of this year, an increase over all of 2025, according to Inside Mortgage Finance. That compares with just a 27% share in 2000 before the financial crisis. But large banks, those with $50 billion and more in assets, are now increasing originations by 34% on an annual basis, outperforming both competing banks and non-banks.”

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5495. Microsoft rolls out new first-party models and updates to agentic AI continuous improvement

Microsoft Corp. today rolled out new generative artificial intelligence models and updates to Foundry, the company’s unified enterprise platform that helps developers and organizations ground, test and deploy AI applications and autonomous agents.

Updates to Foundry IQ, part of Microsoft IQ, now provide an enterprise knowledge graph out of the box, delivering a full estate of unstructured and application data to provide rich context for building applications and delivering on essential use cases.

Microsoft also said Foundry now uses existing transparency and observability capabilities to help customers create learning loops. Internal evaluations allow autonomous agents to establish baselines for quality, safety, latency and cost, enabling continuous behavioral improvements.

This includes human annotations, now in preview, that allow experts to rate and comment on agent traces based on business judgment. It feeds back into an improvement loop. It’s combined with optimization tests against evaluations and comparisons against real-world results. Foundry now also has new capabilities to adapt to supported models with organizational data to apply reinforcement learning while Foundry runs compute.

Each improvement becomes the next baseline and teams can continue measuring results and test changes, allowing them to improve quality.

Microsoft today announced Decision-1.1 is generally available. It’s a fast, cost-effective model designed to make reliable decisions in software at scale.

The generative AI model can make decisions dynamically at low cost, rather than relying on hard-coded rules, while offering superior decision-making capabilities compared with large language models. LLMs spend a lot of time making decisions in routing, classification, prioritization, verification and workflow control by “thinking it through,” which is unnecessary. Decision models are designed to reach answers quickly within constrained definitions and provide calibrated confidence scores, allowing applications to defer when uncertainty is high.

The new model builds on the previous generation, Microsoft-Decision-1, released in October. The new model delivers a significant improvement in intelligence and speed at a competitive price.

The company said it’s built on a new base, Google LLC’s Gemma 4 26B A4, adding multimodal support so it can analyze images in instructions.

Microsoft also extended its MAI, a Microsoft AI first-party family of models added to Foundry for enterprise trust.

These models include the new MAI-Code-2, which can handle demanding agentic coding work; MAI-Code-2-Flash supports high-volume, everyday coding, so developers can choose between performance and cost. Both are now generally available on GitHub, with Code-2-Flash in private preview in Foundry.

MAI-Image-2.7 and MAI-Image-2.7-Flash are now in preview and offer sharper editing and more consistent image generation. These will help brands maintain a consistent look across campaigns at a lower cost.

In cybersecurity, MAI-Cyber-2-Flash is a purpose-built model for cyber efforts and available in preview in Codename MDASH – the company’s agentic code security system in preview for eligible organizations.

Microsoft Foundry itself now has an expanded model pool featuring the top 50 models, supporting a model router and AI Gateway for intelligence model selection. The Foundry also offers more than 11,000 models from OpenAI Group PBC, Anthropic PBC, Meta Platforms Inc., Mistral AI SAS, the open-source community and others.

The company said supported models can be evaluated and deployed in Foundry as part of the same continuous improvement workflow used for agents.

#5494. Nvidia at SC26: Agents are the new scientists, and they need a lab

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

For most of its history, the high-performance computing market measured progress the same way: how fast a machine could solve a fixed problem. Rankings rose, a new system took the top spot, and the cycle started over. Raw performance remains the foundation of scientific computing, and Nvidia Corp. brought plenty of it to SC26.

But this week, Nvidia argued that speed at solving a single problem is no longer the right way to measure leadership. An equally important question now is how many times a researcher can go from hypothesis to result in a day, and what happens when the “researcher” is an artificial intelligence agent that never sleeps.

That idea ties together Nvidia’s bevy of announcements at the show. The company introduced open science models, a CPU-only supercomputing rack, a new HPC-specific GPU, a batch of CUDA-X libraries, quantum integration for the Slurm workload manager, a quantum co-design platform with IBM and Fermilab, and a co-packaged optics deployment at Lambda. It also marked CUDA’s 20th birthday.

Taken individually, these announcements look like a typical supercomputing show news payload. Taken together, they describe a stack built for a different user, namely the AI agent that reasons through a scientific problem, calls a simulation, reads the result and decides what to try next.

Here’s a summary of what Nvidia announced:

While each announcement is interesting, the more compelling story is what they reveal about where scientific computing is headed. I see five themes.

Ian Buck (pictured), Nvidia’s vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, summed up this thesis when introducing Rubin HPC: “For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery.” This marks an important industry shift. Simulation used to be the end product. In an agentic workflow, it’s a tool call within a much larger loop of hypothesis, simulation, and refinement.

When an agent can generate thousands of candidate molecules or material designs, the bottleneck shifts from ideas to the time required to test them. That’s why so much of the SC26 news focuses on loop speed alongside peak flops. Nvidia says cuPhoton cut the time to correlate Event Horizon Telescope black-hole data from more than a month to eight minutes.

At Pacific Fusion, a Nemotron-powered agent running on the same system can analyze plasma simulations as they run, allowing researchers to steer the simulation in real time rather than waiting for it to finish. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory is using Nvidia’s DAQIRI networking library to move electron-microscopy analysis into the experiment itself, so researchers can decide what to measure next while measurements are being taken.

All of these share the same idea: Shrink the gap between asking a question and getting enough of an answer to ask a better one. For researchers, this should change how they evaluate infrastructure. Single-job time-to-solution is an important metric, but time-to-insight per iteration is equally important and should be tracked.

The most important data point at SC26 may have come from a startup, not a supercomputer. Lila Sciences post-trained Nemotron with lab feedback, nearly doubling its accuracy on quantum-dot synthesis protocols to 61%, beating GPT-6 Astra’s 54% at what Nvidia states is 10 to 20 times lower inference cost. Therna nearly doubled accuracy over frontier models in predicting mRNA protein-expression ranges. Terray Therapeutics trained the model to extract reactants, products, and conditions from chemistry diagrams.

That’s consistent with what I’ve been hearing across my enterprise clients: frontier models are a great starting point, but domain-tuned open models often win on accuracy and economics in specialized fields. Science pushes this further than most industries for three reasons. Research data is often proprietary or regulated. Experimental feedback serves as a training signal that general-purpose models lack. Labs want models running on infrastructure they control.

That last point is why Nvidia optimized Nemotron 3.5 Super VL to run on a 128GB DGX Spark. KTH Royal Institute of Technology reports that an agent built on it fixed 81% of broken GROMACS molecular-dynamics setups in a single overnight run on a single Spark.

Nvidia releasing the dataset and the recipes, not just the weights, is important here because the model is a commodity, but the know-how to adapt it is what research teams have lacked.

Nvidia is well-known as the industry’s top GPU provider, but it also offers a CPU rack with Vera. Nvidia is now targeting the part of HPC that has never been accelerated, a market x86 has owned for decades. In Nvidia’s own testing, Vera delivered 1.9 times the performance and 2.4 times the performance per watt of x86 on an OpenFOAM airflow simulation.

DKRZ, the German Climate Computing Center, has selected Vera for its HLRE-5 system. The new Fortran compiler beta isn’t all that sexy, but it’s an important piece. Huge amounts of scientific code are written in Fortran, and nobody wants to rewrite it. Removing that friction is how a CPU challenger takes share.

Across the portfolio, Vera handles CPU-bound simulation. Rubin HPC is built for sparse, memory-bound science rather than AI training. DGX systems sit alongside IBM quantum computers. Nvidia is extending Slurm, the open-source scheduler most supercomputing centers already use, to schedule QPUs alongside CPUs and GPUs using familiar commands. Nearly 30 data centers are now deploying more than 50 quantum processors, and Alice & Bob, IBM, IQM, Pasqal and Quantinuum have adopted the expanded Slurm.

Nvidia wants to be the company that coordinates whichever processor the agent needs next. An agent doing drug discovery might call a CPU-bound molecular dynamics job, a GPU-accelerated docking run, and eventually a quantum chemistry routine. The vendor that owns the orchestration owns the workflow. Owning the hardware still matters, but less so than before.

The quantum news deserves its own mention because the tone has shifted. Two or three years ago, vendors mostly talked about qubit counts. At SC26, the focus was on error correction, decoding, and integration, which are classical computing problems. Nvidia’s new TCBP-JOBS decoder, available in CUDA-Q QEC 0.9.0, delivers up to 13,000 times faster decoding for error-correction research and reduces some design studies from 12 weeks to 45 minutes. IBM and RIKEN’s hybrid quantum-classical chemistry work, which modeled protein-ligand complexes with up to 12,635 atoms, is a Gordon Bell Prize finalist.

IBM’s Jerry Chow discussed the opportunity: “Scaling quantum and classical together will open new frontiers in high-energy and nuclear physics and beyond.” Nvidia has long embraced a systems approach spanning a broad ecosystem of partners, and IBM adds to that. IBM doesn’t need Nvidia to build qubits; it needs accelerated classical computing to make those qubits useful. That’s a typical position for Nvidia, which becomes essential to quantum, regardless of which qubit approach wins.

Energy used to be a facilities issue in HPC. Now it’s a research constraint because every watt spent on overhead is a watt not available for simulation. Nvidia’s Vera delivers twice the energy efficiency of x86 on the Weather Research and Forecasting model.

Lambda’s deployment demonstrates the same idea at the network layer. Across more than 10,000 GPUs, Lambda used co-packaged optics switches and observed network latency drop by about 4% at rack scale and up to about 10% at pod scale, with a median optics temperature of 36 degrees Celsius versus 51 degrees for pluggable optics. This approach is up to five times more power-efficient and up to 15 times more reliable than pluggables, and engineers can swap the light sources in the field.

As Nvidia’s blog notes, with agentic inference, a single network disruption can cause cascading latency across many agents. When the workload is a continuous loop rather than a batch job, uptime becomes a research metric. Lambda is also the first large-scale neocloud proof point for co-packaged optics, which I expect other GPU clouds will need to address.

It’s fitting that Nvidia marked its CUDA software’s 20th anniversary at the same show. CUDA was introduced at SC06, and Nvidia reports that more than 11 million developers now build on it, with more than 1,000 CUDA-X libraries. From AlexNet to AlphaFold, the pattern has been the same: hardware draws attention, while libraries create lock-in.

The agentic era raises the stakes for that library catalog. A human scientist might know a handful of tools well. An agent can call any of them, so the size and quality of the toolbox matter even more. Every new CUDA-X library is effectively a new skill for every science agent built on the Nvidia stack. That’s the competitive moat that AMD, Intel, and the custom-silicon players have to cross, and it deepened this week.

Most of the performance numbers at SC26 are Nvidia’s own or those of its partners. Historically, I have found Nvidia’s numbers to be accurate, but buyers should validate them against their own workloads. Several key products, including Rubin HPC and HLRE-5, won’t arrive until 2028.

Every additional layer Nvidia owns, from CPU to scheduler integration to quantum decoding, raises the familiar question of how open an end-to-end stack can be. Nvidia’s response this week was a strong emphasis on open source: open models, open datasets, open libraries, and contributions to Slurm.

The bigger takeaway is the shift in what Nvidia is selling. For 20 years, it accelerated the computations scientists ran. Now it’s building the stack for an agent to run the scientific method itself: reason, simulate, measure, refine and repeat. If that model takes hold, the winners in scientific computing won’t be the companies with the fastest single chip. They’ll be the ones that make the whole discovery loop spin fastest. Right now, no one is better positioned than Nvidia for that.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5492. Daniel Craig Stepped Away From James Bond Role To Spend More Time at Home

Daniel Craig first stepped into the role of James Bond 20 years ago, and now, he has officially passed the duties along to someone new: Robert Pattinson.

Craig made his 007 debut in the 2006 film “Casino Royale” and held the legendary gig for 15 years. He had originally planned to play the British spy for four films, but ended up having a successful five-movie run with “Quantum Solace” (2008), “Skyfall” (2012), “Spectre” (2015), and “No Time To Die” (2021).

In addition to filming one more motion picture than he had planned, Craig, 58, has spoken out about how physically demanding it is to be James Bond. In the time between the last two films, he told The Sunday Times he was “getting old.”

“I’m creaky,” he admitted in the 2019 interview. In 2024, he told The New York Times, “I find it really hard, this job, and it gets harder as I get older.”

Beyond the grueling stunts and action required for each installment, the role demanded a huge time commitment that pulled Craig away from his family.

“The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo” star married actress Rachel Weisz in June 2011 in an intimate New York ceremony. Together, they welcomed a daughter named Grace in September 2018.

Craig also has an older daughter, Ella Loudon, 34, whom he shares with his first wife, Fiona Loudon. He’s also a stepfather to Weisz’s son, Henry Aronfsky, 20, from her former relationship with filmmaker Darren Aronofsky.

Although Craig has said that he’s “not a method actor,” he described himself as a “nightmare to be with” while he’s working.

“I want to go home and forget it all and just be normal and be like, 'Hey, family,' but half my brain’s at work,” he said. But having a young daughter at home has changed his approach to his career.

“I don’t want to be away from home as much as I have in the past,” he explained.

Craig and Weisz, who both hail from England, have called New York home for quite some time.

In April of this year, they sold their Brooklyn brownstone for $11.8 million. They had picked it up for $6.75 million in 2018.

Built in 1901, the 6,600-square-foot abode spans five levels, which are accessible by elevator. It included a roof deck, a patio, and a backyard garden.

The six-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom residence was damaged by a fire in 2016, before the couple snapped it up. According to Architectural Digest, the previous owner, novelist Martin Amis, had transformed the home into a “clean, blank slate” in light of the damage, and Craig and Weisz put their own spin on it in the nearly eight years they lived there.

The off-market transaction came just a year after the couple sold an adjacent townhouse for $4.05 million.

They still hold ties to the Empire State, with an upstate retreat in Marbletown, NY, that Weisz purchased for $2.1 million in 2008. Nestled on an idyllic 124-acre parcel, the 2,500-square-foot stone home dates to 1785 and includes four bedrooms and three bathrooms.

Overseas, Craig and Weisz have a $4.2 million Victorian mansion in a conservation area in North London. It was a home the “Vladimir” actress had purchased before they were married.

According to the Daily Mail, they sought to heavily renovate the 1840 home in 2023, but had to alter their plans when an objection claimed the proposal would clash with the home’s original style. The renovation was ultimately approved in 2024.

Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5490. Idle, then spiking: Why AI agents are breaking Kubernetes resource planning

AI agents are changing the economics of cloud infrastructure, and autonomous orchestration is becoming the way platform teams keep up. Agentic workloads sit idle and then spike without warning. That pattern leaves static resource settings either wasteful or likely to fail.

Container orchestration for AI is fast becoming the backbone of production AI, and agents are adding a new layer of strain. Compute costs are climbing and reliability problems are harder to contain because everything an agent does ultimately runs on CPU and memory, according to Yodar Shafrir (pictured), founder and chief executive officer of ScaleOps Inc.

“Agents and all the agent workloads pretty much made everything way more complex when managing infrastructure,” Shafrir said. “Eventually, all the complexity that existed before just got much worse. Today, the compute cost has grown dramatically. Everything that agents execute eventually runs on compute.”

Shafrir spoke with theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how autonomous orchestration lets ScaleOps adjust resources in real time as AI agents spike, cutting both costs and crashes. (* Disclosure below.)

Agents behave differently from traditional microservices. An agent waits for a human or another agent, checks with a large language model and then runs its task in a burst. Teams must provision for the highest spike while the agent holds its memory the whole time, Shafrir explained. When resources fall short, a crashed step has to rerun and burns tokens all over again.

“We actually see that agents crash due to not having enough resources 80% more often compared with traditional microservices,” Shafrir said. “The reliability is much harder to manage.”

For ScaleOps, the answer is to make resource decisions in real time. It adjusts allocations, replicas and node placement for every application, agent and Model Context Protocol server, which the company says cuts cloud costs by 70% to 80%. Customers such as Adobe Inc. and Salesforce Inc. build trust by first running the platform in read-only mode on their hardest environments, according to Shafrir.

“We understand for every application: What is it connected to? What does it communicate with? What is the business state of every application?” Shafrir said. “We learn from historical patterns.”

ScaleOps has also added a capability that lets other workloads use an agent’s resources while it sits idle. It also uses memory swap so an agent gets memory only when it needs it. The company says this makes running agents 90% more cost-efficient without moving off Kubernetes. Given the cost of always-on agents, Shafrir sees autonomous orchestration as the only workable model.

“We are now in a phase where humans and all the traditional scaling capabilities that existed in the past are pretty much irrelevant for today’s world because they’re too static and they require a human to go and configure them,” Shafrir said. “When things are so dynamic, it no longer works the same way.”

#5489. October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices

For three years, U.S. home-sale prices rose from a year earlier every single month, even as mortgage rates climbed and would-be buyers pulled back. That streak has ended.

The median home-sale price declined 0.4% year over year to $388,634 in October. That’s  the first decline since May 2023 and a sharp slowdown from the 2.5% gain just two months earlier. With Americans’ wages growing about 4% year over year, even a slight dip in prices can improve affordability. Sale prices have risen nearly every single month for the last 13 years; the only exception was a handful of months in 2023.

With the total number of homes for sale at its highest level since early 2020 and demand cooling, homebuyers’ negotiating power keeps increasing–and that’s finally showing up in sale prices.

Home-sale prices fell nationwide, but they rose in more than half of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas. San Francisco led the nation by a wide margin, with the median sale price rising 16.8% year over year. That’s the biggest increase since 2018. Next comes New Brunswick, NJ, with a 7.7% gain. Two other NYC-area metros also had price increases ranking in the top six; the median sale price rose 4.4% in both New York City and Nassau County.

In San Francisco, AI wealth is fueling competition for scarce inventory; active listings were down 7% from a year earlier. In the New York City area, years of limited homebuilding have left buyers competing for relatively few homes in a region with a strong job market.

Home-sale prices fell most in Austin, TX, where they declined 6.5% year over year. It’s followed by Seattle (-5.1%) and Nashville, TN (-4.9%). Austin and Nashville are among the biggest buyer’s markets in the U.S., and Seattle’s shaky tech job market is curbing demand.

National sale prices are losing steam because fewer Americans can afford to buy a home. U.S. pending home sales fell 3.6% from a month earlier in October on a seasonally adjusted basis to their lowest level since 2013, with the exception of April 2020.

This is a real-time indicator of the state of the housing market; fewer homes went under contract in October largely because mortgage rates averaged 7.33%, a three-year high and up from 6.86% the month before.

All figures in this report are seasonally adjusted, with the exception of median sale price data and mortgage rate data. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

“It’s a buyer’s market, but not many people can afford to buy,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics. “That could start to shift a bit, now that sale prices are closer to reflecting the shape of the market. House hunters in most of the country should know that the price they see on a listing may very well be a starting point; they should try offering below the asking price, and negotiating for closing costs, repairs and maybe even mortgage-rate buydowns. If you can’t get the price or monthly payment you want on one house, move on to the next one–with a big pool of inventory sitting on the market, buyers can afford to be picky.”

Pending home sales declined in all of the most populous U.S. metros. That’s the second month in a row that has happened; before September, the last time was three years earlier.

The biggest declines were in Seattle and San Diego, both places where pending sales fell more than 20% year over year. Those West Coast metros are some of the priciest in the U.S., so 7%-plus mortgages hit house hunters’ monthly payments there hard. In Seattle, an uncertain local job market is also curbing demand.

Closed home sales fell to their lowest level in nearly 3 years. They declined 2.1% month over month in October to their lowest level since December 2023; before that, the last time sales dropped that low was 2014. Many of the deals that closed last month went under contract in August and September, when rates were already climbing and economic uncertainty was deterring a lot of house hunters.

With homebuying demand falling, supply is building. The total number of homes for sale rose 0.9% from September to its highest level since early 2020; that’s the biggest monthly gain since May 2025.

More supply gives buyers more homes to choose from and more leverage:

“Buyers are nervous about rates, the economy, and everything they’re seeing in the news– so they need the house and the price to line up perfectly before they’ll make an offer,” said Callie Kimmel, a Redfin Premier agent in Philadelphia. “I’m advising sellers to price just below current market value from day one–and not comps from six months ago, but homes that are listed right now. Otherwise, the home is likely to end up sitting on the market for a bit and selling for less than they hoped. There are a few exceptions: Move-in ready homes in the most desirable neighborhoods are still competitive; in those cases, sellers have the upper hand.”

While total housing supply is growing, fewer sellers are adding new inventory to the pool. New listings of homes for sale fell 1% month over month to the lowest level in more than two years. Would-be sellers are pulling back as homebuying demand slows and sale prices lose steam.

The figures below are based on a list of the 50 most populous U.S. metropolitan areas. Some metros may be removed from time to time to ensure data accuracy. Refer to our metrics definition page for explanations of metrics used in this report. All changes below represent year-over-year changes.

#5488. Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze

Just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller’s markets in October. That’s tied for the fewest in records dating back to 2016, matching April 2020, when the pandemic froze the housing market.

Nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%).

All three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers.

The seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater New York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers.

Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013.

That marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas.

When sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market.

We estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

It’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today.

“A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn’t solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan said. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers’ attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate.  With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.”

The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace.

There were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers.

On the flip side, there were an estimated 1,526,984 home sellers in the market, the most since March 2020. That’s up 0.9% month over month.

The number of homes on the market is piling up because many homes are lingering on the market for months without going under contract. Each month, more new listings are adding to the big pool of supply.

Some homeowners keep listing their houses despite falling demand because many have given up on waiting for lower rates. They may want to sell now because they’re worried prices could decline, and some need to move for a new job, a growing family, or another life change. But many homeowners who don’t need to move have substantial equity and little pressure to sell, so they may hold off on listing.

Over 80% of U.S. metro areas, 41 of the 50 Redfin analyzed, are buyer’s markets. That matches September’s record.

For the third month in a row, Miami and Nashville have the biggest surpluses of sellers over buyers. Miami had 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, and Nashville had 159.5% more. Las Vegas (149.9%) was third on the list. In the top 13 buyer’s markets, there were more than twice as many sellers as buyers in October. Nearly all are in the Sun Belt; four are in Texas and four are in Florida.

The Sun Belt, particularly Texas and Florida, is home to some of the nation’s biggest buyer’s markets, partly because of robust homebuilding. Builders are continuing to add new homes even as demand cools, swelling inventory and giving buyers more options and negotiating power.

Demand has cooled largely because rising mortgage rates and stubbornly high home prices are pricing buyers out. In Florida, rising HOA and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating the affordability squeeze.

Six metros were “balanced” in October, neither buyer’s nor seller’s markets: Chicago (8.1% more sellers than buyers), Boston (7.5%), Providence, RI (7.5%), New Brunswick, NJ (5.6%), Milwaukee (0.6% fewer sellers than buyers) and San Francisco (6.9% fewer).

The surplus of home sellers over buyers grew month over month in 34 of the 41 buyer’s markets in October.

The surplus increased most in Miami, which also has the biggest surplus of sellers over buyers; there were 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, up from 160.5% the month before. The next-biggest monthly increases were in Las Vegas, where there were 149.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 122.8%, and Nashville (159.5%, up from 134.3%).

House hunters lost negotiating power in seven buyer’s markets. The surplus of sellers over buyers fell from September to October in Fort Worth, TX (91.6%, down from 100%), St. Louis (23.1%, down from 27.1%), Austin (124.8%, down from 128.2%), Dallas (118.6%, down from 120.5%), Jacksonville, FL, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. All of them remain buyer’s markets.

#5487. Hammerspace enters the hardware market with new storage and intelligence capabilities

Hammerspace Inc., which provides high-speed access to distributed data, is expanding beyond its traditional role as a software provider to offer complete, integrated data systems for artificial intelligence workloads, adding its own high-performance flash storage hardware and new data intelligence capabilities to its existing data orchestration platform.

The company said the Hammerspace Data System combines data discovery, management, orchestration and storage into a single offering designed to simplify the infrastructure needed to support AI training and inference. Customers can purchase fully configured systems with hardware, software and support or continue deploying Hammerspace software on existing infrastructure.

The announcement marks a significant expansion of Hammerspace’s business model as enterprises increasingly seek turnkey infrastructure for AI applications rather than assembling systems from multiple vendors.

“We also see plenty of opportunities, particularly in the AI space, where they just want one [stock-keeping unit],” said Floyd Christofferson, vice president of product marketing at Hammerspace. “They want a system, end-to-end, hardware, software, fully integrated and supported.”

While software companies have historically had limited success expanding into hardware, Hammerspace’s approach is more than just a bundled, said Mark Nossokoff, research directory at Hyperior Research Holdings LLC.

“Hammerspace is working with distribution partners to develop and fulfill a branded system optimized for their software stack, maintaining their software business model,” he said in e-mailed comments. “This can be advantageous when the hardware is based on an emerging standards-based platform, such as the Open Flash Platform, until the hardware platform becomes a standard offering from multiple suppliers.”

Hammerspace has traditionally specialized in providing unified access to data distributed across different storage systems, data centers and clouds. Its software creates a global namespace that allows applications to locate and access files regardless of their physical location, eliminating the need for large-scale data migrations.

In March, the company introduced an AI-focused data platform that automates the discovery and delivery of enterprise data directly to graphics processing units. The technology builds on Hammerspace’s parallel Network File System, which uses enhancements to Linux to accelerate data access without requiring proprietary client software.

The new offering extends those capabilities with integrated hardware and data intelligence.

A major addition is the Hammerspace Open Flash Platform, a high-density storage system built around data processing units rather than conventional storage servers. The architecture integrates processing, networking and solid-state drives into compact hardware designed to reduce power consumption, cooling requirements and rack space.

Hammerspace said the platform achieves throughput of 350 gigabytes per second per rack unit. Broader performance testing is still underway.

The storage complements the company’s existing Tier 0 technology, which aggregates local Non-Volatile Memory Express storage across GPU servers into a shared resource. That capacity can be used to store key-value caches for AI inference, allowing applications to reuse previously computed context rather than repeatedly processing the same information.

“The flash subsystem employs a unique design and touts some impressive performance and storage density metrics,” said Hyperion’s Nossokoff. “More compelling will be results based on end user workloads, including relative improvements and comparisons with respect to performance, performance/power, and cost/performance metrics, among others.”

The company said customers can combine tier 0 storage, the new flash platform and lower-cost disk or object storage within a single namespace. The new hardware is optional. Customers can continue using third-party storage systems, with Hammerspace handling data access and orchestration across the infrastructure.

Another addition is a data intelligence module that extends Hammerspace’s existing metadata management capabilities.

The software can catalog distributed files, index detailed metadata and scan content to identify sensitive information, including personally identifiable information and regulated data. Users can search the catalog using natural language and translate requests into automated data management policies.

For example, an administrator could identify files containing personal information and establish policies preventing that material from entering an AI training pipeline.

Christofferson said the new capabilities extend beyond the file attributes traditionally used to manage storage.

The module also supports integration with existing enterprise catalogs and governance tools through application programming interfaces, avoiding the need to replace established systems.

For current Hammerspace customers, the intelligence capabilities will be added through a software upgrade. The company said existing deployments won’t need to change their underlying architecture.

Hammerspace will assemble, install and support systems using configurable server hardware, metadata nodes and storage components based on customer requirements. The company will continue basing software pricing on the capacity of data under management. Hardware configurations will be priced individually, with no standardized public price list.

Senior Product Marketing Director Eric Bassier said the company doesn’t intend to collect hardware revenue or impose a hardware markup. Instead, components will flow through suppliers and distribution partners, while Hammerspace provides integrated deployment and support.

The strategy addresses the struggles customers often encounter with the logistics of acquiring servers, storage and other components, said Molly Presley, senior vice president of global marketing.

“They’re looking to their vendors to simplify getting things deployed to start with,” he said. “As long as Hammerspace doesn’t dilute their resources and continues to prioritize their investments on addressing the needs of the growing scientific and engineering communities adopting AI into their advanced technical workflows, they appear well poised for continued momentum.”

Nossokoff said Hammerspace’s distributed data architecture using a global namespace is well suited to emerging AI workload requirements. “Hammerspace has been building out their Data Intelligence software stack to address the requirements of the AI pipeline,” he said. The expansion follows a $100 million funding round in April 2025 that supported Hammerspace’s international expansion. The company says its customers include Meta Platforms Inc. and the U.S. Department of Defense.

#5486. Study Finds a Nearly 50% Drop in Renters Becoming Homeowners Since 2009

As economic pressures continue to rise, a shocking new study has found that the share of renters who convert to homeownership has fallen 46% since 2009.

TransUnion, a leader in global information and insights, released its 2027 Personal and Commercial Lines Annual Insurance Outlook on Tuesday, which focuses on what the insurance industry needs to stay profitable in a changing market.

The report states that personal line underwriting has been strong throughout this year, but companies need to assess their strategies going forward as fewer people buy cars and homes, therefore reducing the pool of potential policyholders.

According to the report, the share of renters who convert to homeownership was 3.9% in 2025, a sharp decline from 7.2% in 2009.

This represents a shocking 46% decrease in the share of renters transitioning to homeownership in just 14 years.

Combined with a 2025 report from the National Association of Realtors®, which stated that the median age of first-time buyers climbed from 33 to 40 in just five years, TransUnion concluded that the pool of potential policyholders is shrinking.

The decrease in renters buying homes goes back to affordability and economic pressure, according to Ryan Thomson of The Assumable Guy.

“Renters didn't stop wanting to own. Rates tripled and prices kept climbing, so the monthly number stopped working,” Thomson tells Realtor.com®. “In Colorado Springs, where I sell, 71% of households could afford a median-priced home in 2019. By 2023, it was 25.3%. So renters stay put. Or they move wherever the payment still works.”

TransUnion also found that Florida, Texas, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Tennessee had the greatest influx of new residents between July 2025 and June 2026, with Florida gaining nearly 87,000 net-new residents.

The most significant outbound migration was seen in Massachusetts, New Jersey, Illinois, New York, and California, with the Golden State alone with a net loss of 146,000 residents.

This migration pattern is likely taking place as people chase affordability, looking for places that offer more space for lower costs.

“A household may want a certain lifestyle, but not be able to afford it given the high costs of housing and of living in general in the area. State and local taxes may also play a role,” Cameron Walker, a real estate expert at Clever Real Estate, tells Realtor.com. “Texas, Florida, and the Carolinas may be more affordable and have lower state and local taxes.”

The TransUnion report notes that the growing states all have an elevated exposure to hurricanes, severe convective storms, and other catastrophic weather compared to the states people are leaving.

While the growing states are all located near the Sun Belt and generally considered more affordable than coastal states such as New York and California, the increased risks elevate costs beyond purchase price.

“People may be assuming the Sun Belt states are generally affordable, and that isn't always the case,” Walker adds. “Property values are increasing in Sun Belt states because of in-migration, which increases property taxes and insurance costs, and inflates housing costs.”

For insurance companies, TransUnion recommends strategies like focusing on retaining and creating more value from current customer, winning policies from competition, and combining risk mitigating and marketing efforts when discussing migration.

For the housing market, improving outlooks and rebuilding the renter-to-homeowner path comes down to affordability and opportunity.

“We need to increase the supply of entry-level, affordable housing. This includes promoting the construction of new housing in high-demand, high-growth communities. The industry needs to offer new financing options and improve responsibility to help new homebuyers qualify to enter the housing market,” says Walker.

“People aren’t giving up their dreams of homeownership. They’re postponing them because the housing market has changed and the financial requirements to homeownership are out of the reach of many. The markets that can provide jobs and affordable housing will thrive, and gain the most, from future homeowners.”

#5485. Zillow Launches Four Tools to Narrow Down Homes, Agents and Affordability

To help renters and homebuyers answer questions, Zillow has announced the release of four new tools to help users rent or buy with more confidence.

According to a release, Zillow’s Home Loans’ BuyAbility℠ tool allows users to answer the question: How much can I afford? The Home Loans’ BuyAbility tool can help keep a buyer’s home budget more current and accurate.

Buyers can link to Experian—the credit reporting company—once to verify their credit and debt, and their target home price will update automatically each month based on any changes. BuyAbility is also refreshed daily with updated interest rates from Zillow Home Loans, Zillow notes.

Because the Experian integration is built on a verified credit score, the release notes that Zillow Home Loans can estimate what buyers can afford more accurately, so they can search with more confidence from the start.

Buyers can also plan for and track their progress toward homeownership as they pay down debt and improve their credit. The BuyAbility tool is free, has no impact on credit scores and doesn’t obligate buyers to use Zillow Home Loans.

“Moving is a series of important decisions, and each one gets easier when you have clear information in front of you,” said Cynthia Taylor, Zillow’s senior vice president of product. “These tools give both buyers and renters clarity at every step, and connect homeowners with local experts if they’re ready to sell.”

Zillow’s Regional Insights page addresses the questions of: Where should I live? The release says that it can also describe what it’s like to live in cities and neighborhoods across the U.S., so renters and buyers can weigh neighborhood tradeoffs and compare prices early in their search.

The “compare homes” module further narrows down lists of homes for buyers. Now, buyers and renters can view their top homes side by side, with photos, financial information and key details in one place. They can start a comparison from search results, listing or their “favorites,” and stop toggling between multiple tabs.

For the final new tool available, the release states that for off-market homes, Zillow now displays a curated list of Zillow Preferred℠ agent partners who recently sold similar homes nearby, allowing homeowners to compare and contact local listing agents who may be a good match.

All four tools are live on Zillow, with availability that varies according to the tool and the user’s platform, such as the web, iOS or Android.

For more information, visit https://www.zillow.com/product-releases/fall-2026/.

#5483. Jensen Huang says he’s willing to return to Nvidia, in first statement since resignation

Former Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang today said he’s open to returning to his old post.

Huang expressed his willingness to be reinstated in a post on X. It marks his first public statement since his ouster from Nvidia last week. He resigned following revelations that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former cloud executive suspected to be a Chinese spy.

Huang apologized for his conduct in today’s X post. He went on to cite recent calls for him to return as a factor behind his willingness to resume his work at Nvidia.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang wrote. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

Huang’s statement isn’t a complete surprise. On Sunday, the Financial Times reported that he had discussed a comeback with confidants. The paper said that a member of Huang’s circle was working to assemble a group of tech executives to support the effort.

Last Thursday, an anonymous user launched an online petition to reinstate Huang. It drew the support of several prominent tech executives including Elon Musk, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Epic Games Inc. CEO Tim Sweeney. The petition also garnered 180,000 other signatures, although it appears that not all of them are genuine. One entry spotted by Business Insider read “Tim Cruise, Hollywood actor.”

It’s unclear whether the efforts to reinstate Huang are realistic. On Monday, CNBC reported that Nvidia’s board is not considering bringing him back. And today, on Nvidia’s earnings call, Chair Harvey Jones repeated that the board doesn’t intend to reinstate him. Earlier, sources had told Reuters that he had misled the chipmaker’s general counsel and chief marketing officer about his relationship with Alice Huang.

While some U.S. officials believe Alice Huang was part of an espionage operation, others see the evidence as inconclusive. On Thursday, sources told CNN that the intelligence collected on her doesn’t prove she’s a spy. The same day, the Justice Department stated it had not yet concluded Alice Huang is a Chinese asset.

Huang is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud provider that has ordered billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips. The Justice Department is investigating the company over alleged export control violations. As early as 2024, officials identified “suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential ​sensitive semiconductor diversion.”

The Wall Street Journal today reported that Nvidia has hired a prominent executive search firm to find a new CEO. According to the paper, it plans to evaluate both internal and external candidates. Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress currently leads the company as interim CEO.

Kress also supervises a new national security and export control oversight committee that Nvidia formed today. It will be responsible for the company’s national security policies, adherence to export control rules and global trade risk management.

The committee comprises three Nvidia directors on launch. It will carry out its work in collaboration with the chipmaker’s executives and external experts in fields such as law, national security and global trade compliance. Nvidia says that the committee will meet at least once per quarter.

#5482. Engel & Völkers sets sights on Aruba as brokerages add agents

Engel & Völkers announced an Aruba shop, Realty of America entered San Diego, and eXp Realty added a Tampa Bay brokerage and an Ohio team.

Brokerage expansion stretched from the Caribbean to the West Coast in recent days, as firms moved into new markets and picked up agents and teams from other companies. Engel & Völkers is headed to Aruba, where it plans to open a shop in April 2027, and Realty of America reached California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 of her Team Z Realty agents in San Diego.

eXp Realty picked up a Tampa Bay brokerage and a Cincinnati-area team that spent 20 years with REMAX. Baird & Warner brought on Oak Park, Illinois, boutique Beyond Properties, and Dane Briggs teamed up with Phil Sexton at HomeSmart’s NEXT team. IRES MLS welcomed back a former staffer to run operations, and Howard Hanna Portside added an agent in Massachusetts.

Engel & Völkers expanded into Aruba with license partners Zobaida Akkari and Richard Franken, Aruba-based entrepreneurs with backgrounds in real estate, luxury sales, hospitality and tourism. The shop is projected to open in April 2027 at L.G. Smith Blvd. 330 in Palm Beach and will serve clients across the island, according to the company.

“Aruba is a compelling addition to the network’s growing presence in the Caribbean,” Stuart Siegel, president and CEO of Engel & Völkers Americas, said in a statement.

Realty of America entered California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 Team Z Realty agent partners in San Diego. Ulloa has generated more than $4.2 billion in sales volume over her 13-year career, and Team Z peaked at 72 agents and $589 million in annual volume, according to the company. Agent-owned ROA, founded in September 2024, says it has more than 3,900 agents across 26 markets.

“People around me may see what I am giving up, but I see what I am making room for,” Ulloa said in a statement.

Rene Carpena and Dana Carpena moved Florida’s 1st Choice Realty, their independent Greater Tampa Bay brokerage, to eXp Realty, where it now operates as 1st Choice Collective. The group brings more than 70 agents and support staff and recorded more than 325 transactions and $60 million in sales volume in 2025, according to the company.

Jon Bowling also brought his 17-person team in Mason, Ohio, to eXp after 20 years with RE/MAX. eXp Realty is the core subsidiary of AGNT Inc.

Baird & Warner added Beyond Properties, a boutique brokerage in Oak Park, Illinois, whose dozen agents will operate as Beyond Properties Group. Owner and designated managing broker Erica Cuneen, who founded the firm almost 20 years ago, will co-lead the group with team leader Cynthia Howe Gajewski. The group joins Baird & Warner’s Oak Park office and keeps its Marion Street location.

“This partnership will allow me to simplify the operational side of the business and spend more time doing what I love, which is focusing on our agents and clients,” Cuneen said in a statement.

Dane Briggs, an Arizona real estate veteran, partnered with Phil Sexton, founder of HomeSmart’s NEXT team, in a leadership role focused on agent workflows and AI integrations. Briggs has worked as a designated broker and title executive, founded referral brokerage Roosted and led expansion initiatives at Homie. He has also served as an Inman Ambassador.

“Before long, we weren’t just talking about what Phil was building. We were talking about what we could build together,” Briggs said in a statement.

IRES MLS, which serves Northern Colorado and parts of the Front Range, rehired Samantha Ewing as director of operations. Ewing spent 13 years at IRES as a projects manager and quality assurance tester before leaving in 2018, and she has more than 20 years of experience in MLS operations and real estate technology.

“Having Samantha return to IRES is an exciting opportunity for our team and the local industry we serve,” CEO Julie Dahl said in a statement.

Howard Hanna Portside Real Estate Group added Melissa Winter, an agent with nearly 15 years of experience who focuses on first-time homebuyers, to its Massachusetts team in Amesbury. Portside, which has more than 200 agents, entered a strategic partnership with Howard Hanna in 2026, according to the company.

“What drew me to Portside was the energy, the people, and the opportunity for growth,” Winter said in a statement.
