#5433. Homebuilder confidence sinks to a 14-year low as buyers hibernate

NAHB’s HMI fell 4 points to 25 in November, the lowest since 2012. Builders reported heavier concessions, with 46% cutting prices and 68% offering incentives as rates above 7% weighed on demand.  AI Summary

Homebuilder confidence fell in November to its lowest point since the latter days of the Global Financial Crisis, as elevated mortgage rates, persistent inflation and buyer hesitancy continue to weigh on demand.

The National Association of Home Builders (NAHB)/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) fell four points to 25 in November, representing the weakest homebuilder confidence reading since April 2012.

Builders have relied ever more heavily on discounts and mortgage buydown tactics to move inventory, with NAHB reporting that 46% of builders cut prices during the month, the highest share since the onset of the Covid-19 pandemic. Typical discounts ran flat at 6% for the eighth straight month, and 68% of builders used sales incentives, another post-Covid high. It was the 20th consecutive month that at least 60% of builders had featured margin-eroding price-cut promotions.

Further, in November, all three of the key HMI components sank. The index of current sales conditions declined six points to 28, while the measure of sales expectations over the next six months slipped two points to 30, signaling a prolonged pessimistic outlook. Meanwhile, the gauge of prospective buyer traffic dropped two points to 16, the lowest level in 15 years outside of the early months of the pandemic in 2020.

“Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today’s economy,” NAHB Chairman Bill Owens, a home builder and remodeler from Worthington, Ohio, said in a statement. “Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction.”

NAHB Chief Economist Robert Dietz said in a statement that a combination of policy and macroeconomic pressures is straining both supply and demand.

“The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges, including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability,” Dietz said. “Mortgage rates above 7%, softer consumer confidence and an uncertain economic outlook are holding buyers back.”

Public homebuilders echoed that picture on recent earnings calls, citing hesitant buyers, heavier discounting and thinner margins.

Century Communities Executive Chairman Dale Francescon, during an earnings call on October 28, noted that high mortgage rates, continued inflation and macroeconomic uncertainty weighed heavily on consumer confidence, particularly among first-time buyers.

“As we moved through the quarter, our buyers became more cautious, did not feel an urgency to transact and felt more comfortable moving to the sidelines,” Francescon said during the call.

It’s not that buyers have abandoned the market. Rather, they are waiting out volatility and elongating decision-making timelines. At the same time, the number of households that can qualify for a mortgage at today’s borrowing costs and sales prices continues to shrink.

LGI Homes chairman and CEO Eric Lipar noted the increasingly challenging market conditions during an earnings call on November 3.

“As expected, the market became more challenging as the quarter progressed,” Lipar said. “Affordability remained the defining story of the quarter.”

The homebuilder, which primarily serves rate- and payment-sensitive entry-level buyers, reported a cancellation rate of 53.8%, compared with 33.6% a year earlier and 26.2% two years ago. While this trend was an outlier among most of its public homebuilding peers, it underscores how strained entry-level buyers are right now.

During PulteGroup’s earnings call on October 22, the builder’s president and CEO Ryan Marshall agreed that market conditions have become more challenging in recent months, leading many buyers to put their homebuying process on the back burner.

“What changed in the quarter…is that the big move higher in interest rates, along with inflation, global tensions, and waning confidence, reached the point where more consumers simply put their search on pause,” he said during the call.

Traffic to PulteGroup communities fell 14% year over year and 11% sequentially in the third quarter, with first-time buyers making up most of the missing traffic.

Marshall also noted that, with 30-year mortgage rates still sitting at around 7.5%, move-up buyers are increasingly having a difficult time selling their current home, further dragging on homebuying demand.

“One of the biggest impediments that we’re seeing right now is that our move-up and active-adult buyers need to sell their existing home, and that is tough,” Marshall noted.

With homeownership increasingly out of reach for the average working American, renting has become the more affordable option. Zillow research found that renting a home costs more than $1,000 less per month than buying one, a gap that draws many would-be buyers away from for-sale homebuilders and toward the rental market.

For many homebuilders, winning over cautious buyers now means resorting to more and more incentives, in effect paying for sales. Concessions are climbing, and total sales prices are coming down with them. The median new-home sales price in September was about $400,000, down nearly 4.0% from a year ago.

Builders continue to use mortgage rate buydowns as a sales tool, and the numbers show it. A recent Realtor.com report found that the average new-home buyer had a starting mortgage rate of 5.01% during the third quarter, compared with 6.15% for existing-home buyers.

Century Communities is among the builders leaning hard on incentives to facilitate sales. The company reported that, during Q3, incentives averaged about 13.0% of the total sales price, up from 12% in Q2 and 11.0%. The builder’s CFO Scott Dixon noted on an October earnings call that incentives will likely rise in the fourth quarter as Century pushes to meet its year-end goals.

“We expect incentives on closed homes in the fourth quarter of 2026 to be 200-250 basis points higher than third quarter levels as we navigate a higher rate environment, muted consumer confidence and compete with other builders for year-end closings,” he said during the call.

Meritage Homes Executive Vice President and CFO Hilla Sferruzza concurred that the incentive environment is likely to stay elevated for some time, as she addressed analysts on an October 29 earnings call. The builder continues to use incentives and price discounts, with its average closing price down 4% year over year to $365,000.

“Absent a sustained market-driven catalyst that provides meaningful mortgage rate relief, we expect incentives to remain at this elevated level for the near term,” Sferruzza said.

On the other hand, during a session at the HousingWire Homebuilder Summit last month, Taylor Morrison CEO Sheryl Palmer warned that homebuilders have trained today’s buyers to expect more and more concessions.

“We, as builders, created this environment,” Palmer said during the session. “We created this place where the longer the house has been sitting there, the more we’re going to give you.”

For builders, the question is how much profit they are willing to trade for sales. Those who protect margins risk losing volume, while those who chase volume are watching margins thin.

Most public homebuilders reported lower gross profit margins in the third quarter than a year earlier, including:

Beyond the immediate sales and margin challenges, many homebuilders are struggling to determine how much inventory to carry and what their 2027 production plans should look like.

Meritage Homes, for example, declined to give formal Q3 guidance, arguing that volatile market conditions limit their visibility.

PulteGroup’s President and CEO Ryan Marshall agreed that “the current environment has made it a more difficult planning time.”

And D.R. Horton Executive Vice President Jessica Hansen echoed this sentiment during an October 29 earnings call.

“Given the uncertainty in these conditions and the broader economy, our initial fiscal 2027 guidance reflects wider ranges than usual,” Hansen explained.

Builders have navigated this challenging market by cutting cycle times, extracting costs, improving floor plans and leveraging AI to improve operational efficiency. What’s out of their control is whether buyers feel ready to commit, or when that will change.

#5431. From store outlets to methane leaks, every scrap of power is now fair game for AI compute

AI factories are outgrowing the traditional data center as models get bigger and distributed inference moves from concept to deployment. The infrastructure behind those models now has to span racks, sites and even scattered pockets of power.

Dell Technologies Inc. is betting that the answer lies in building complete systems rather than components, from rack-scale management to fully liquid-cooled designs. The size of modern AI clusters dwarfs anything high-performance computing has handled before, according to Ihab Tarazi (pictured), senior vice president and chief technology officer for AI, compute and networking of Dell.

“The difference with AI is the scale is massive. Tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of GPUs that are all on a single fabric. It may be multiple clusters, but they end up being a single fabric at the end of the day,” Tarazi said.

Tarazi spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed Dell’s 100% liquid-cooled networking system, distributed inference and turning stranded energy into AI capacity. (* Disclosure below.)

Dell’s latest move takes liquid cooling beyond the GPU. The company is shipping what it calls the first 100% liquid-cooled networking system, with switches, optics and cabling pretested in its factory and delivered as a single rack, Tarazi explained.

“The fact that it’s pretested as a single-rack system means, instead of having to assemble hundreds of pieces on-site and take maybe two weeks or three weeks to find the bugs, it all comes in, you install it [and] we turn it up in hours,” Tarazi said.

The networking launch follows Dell’s debut of liquid-cooled storage for AI racks. Compute, networking and storage now share the same cooling and power specs. That matters as operators design new facilities around water cooling, according to Tarazi.

“Instead of building two data centers — one for GPU, one network — being able to do one is a massive reduction in time and cost for us,” Tarazi said.

Software is the next lever for distributed inference. Customers want a single control plane that can work across different GPUs and CPUs and link as many as 1,000 small sites that each have some spare power, Tarazi noted. That approach turns stranded energy into AI capacity for companies that can’t build a massive data center quickly.

“You’ll be surprised what power availability means,” Tarazi said. “It doesn’t mean just that you have power in your store. It could also mean methane coming out — every source of power possible. People are going backwards to say, ‘How do I leverage that power for compute and enable inferencing in a distributed manner?'”

#5430. Fitch warns of growing balance-sheet strain at top nonbank mortgage firms

Fitch Ratings affirmed long-term issuer default ratings for nine nonbank mortgage lenders but revised outlooks on Pennymac, Planet and Freedom to negative, citing elevated leverage, concentrated MSR exposure and profitability constraints expected in 2027.   AI Summary

Fitch Ratings revised its outlooks on three major nonbank mortgage companies to negative and warned that elevated leverage and growing mortgage servicing rights (MSR) exposure are weighing on credit profiles in a higher-for-longer rate environment.

In a periodic review of nine publicly rated nonbank mortgage firms released Monday, Fitch affirmed all long-term issuer default ratings but shifted the outlooks for Pennymac Financial Services, Planet Financial Group and Freedom Mortgage Holdings to negative from stable.

Fitch maintained the following long-term issuer default ratings: Onity Group at B-, UWM Holdings Corp. at B+, Pennymac at BB, Planet at B, CrossCountry Mortgage at BB-, Rocket Companies at BBB-, Freedom at BB-, Finance of America at CCC and Provident Funding Associates at B.

Fitch said profitability for several lenders is likely to be constrained in 2027, given a challenging rate backdrop that limits refinance volume and makes it harder for companies to retain earnings and pay down debt. That dynamic is expected to pressure leverage ratios across the sector.

At Pennymac, corporate leverage has exceeded Fitch’s 1.5x downgrade trigger since the first quarter of 2026. And a failure to make meaningful progress toward reducing corporate leverage to 1.5x or less over the outlook horizon could lead to a downgrade to BB-, Fitch said.

“Fitch expects profitability to be constrained in 2027 by a challenging rate environment and the lag in realizing the full impact of recent expense reduction initiatives,” Fitch stated.

For Planet, the agency pointed to a significant increase in MSR exposure since 2021, as the company retained servicing from its own originations and acquired bulk portfolios. MSRs represented about 363% of company equity in the second quarter of 2026, up from 293% a year earlier and above the level of higher-rated peers, Fitch said.

Planet’s corporate leverage also rose to 5.5x, up from 4.3x during the same period. Fitch considers that level high and a key constraint on the rating. The agency said it could downgrade Planet if leverage rises above its 7.0x trigger.

At Freedom, corporate leverage — measured as gross nonfunding debt to tangible equity — reached Fitch’s 2.0x downgrade trigger in the second quarter, up from 1.9x at the end of 2025. Shareholder distributions exceeded earnings in the first half of the year, contributing to the increase.

Fitch expects Freedom’s leverage to rise further as it grows its servicing portfolio and uses available borrowing capacity to meet potential margin calls under its hedging program.

At UWM, Fitch cited high leverage, MSR valuation risk and reliance on short-term, largely uncommitted secured funding as constraints on its rating. Corporate leverage, excluding origination funding, climbed to 5.3x in the third quarter of 2026, nearly double the 2.7x figure at the end of 2025.

MSR mark-to-market volatility and a $603 million hedge loss in the second quarter have weighed on profitability. Still, Fitch pointed to a 30% adjusted EBITDA margin for the trailing 12 months through the third quarter as evidence of solid core earnings.

“Fitch expects leverage to decline over time, supported by planned MSR sales and earnings above the expected $165 million annual preferred dividend. Common dividends are suspended. Even so, Fitch expects corporate leverage to remain above 2.0x over the Outlook horizon.”

Regarding CCM, its acquisition of Two Harbors Investment Corp. brought $156 billion in unpaid principal balance to its servicing portfolio, along with the RoundPoint Mortgage Servicing platform’s in-house capabilities. Fitch expects the added scale and greater retention of servicing economics to improve profitability, although it does not anticipate the full integration benefits until the end of 2028.

The acquisitions also drove up leverage. Corporate leverage rose to 2.9x, up from 1.2x and above Fitch’s 2.0x rating sensitivity. Fitch expects CCM to reduce leverage toward its 1.0x corporate target. Failure to bring leverage below downgrade triggers within 12 to 24 months could result in a negative rating action.

At Rocket, corporate leverage stood at 1.1x in the third quarter, down from 1.4x at the end of 2025 but above the 0.5x recorded at the end of 2024, before its acquisitions of Redfin and Mr. Cooper Group.

Although Rocket remains above Fitch’s 1.0x downgrade trigger, the agency expects leverage to fall below that level over the next 12 months through repayment of secured borrowings and moderate earnings retention. The pace will depend on market conditions and whether the company realizes the expected acquisition synergies, Fitch said.

#5429. NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO says

License under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license.

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents said.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint said he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”

White also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton said it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or plan.”

Pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also said the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

“NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears said the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

“John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” said David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”

“Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”

#5427. Fitch affirms Finance of America’s CCC rating as key risks, leverage persist

Fitch Ratings affirmed Finance of America Companies' long-term issuer default rating at CCC with a positive outlook, citing improved liquidity and better underlying profitability as the company addresses near-term debt maturities. The agency maintained Finance of America Funding’s senior secured rating at CCC- with an RR5 recovery rating. Despite FOA’s leading position in reverse mortgages, Fitch highlighted weak liquidity, very high leverage of 33.7x, a largely secured and short-term funding structure, and earnings pressure from interest rate volatility.   AI Summary

Finance of America Companies’ long-term credit ratings remain deep in speculative-grade territory, even as the company reduces near-term risk and improves underlying profitability, according to a review published Monday by Fitch Ratings.

Fitch this week affirmed the long-term issuer default ratings of Finance of America Companies and its subsidiaries, Finance of America Equity Capital LLC and Finance of America Funding LLC, with a CCC rating and a positive outlook. Fitch also affirmed Finance of America Funding’s senior secured debt rating at CCC- with a recovery rating of RR5.

Fitch defines CCC ratings as having a very low margin for safety, with default considered a real possibility. But the ratings agency also explained that it maintains a positive outlook for Finance of America (FOA) due to its “established market position within the reverse mortgage sector,” along with experience senior management and support from Brian Libman, who chairs its board of directors.

The action is part of Fitch’s periodic peer review of nine publicly rated nonbank mortgage companies. Like other lenders, FOA has been contending with volatile interest rates, high leverage and constrained liquidity as the broader mortgage market remains cyclical and capital intensive.

Earlier this month, FOA reported a net loss of $110 million in the third quarter of 2026 as noncash fair value adjustments offset growth in its home equity lending business. The company reported funded loan volume of $748 million from July through September, up 24% from the same period in 2025, while its year-to-date volume of $2.07 billion was up 17% year over year.

The company also said during its Q3 earnings call that it expects to complete a $60 million paydown of senior secured notes in November. In June 2024, FOA announced a restructuring of unsecured debt into secure notes while extending the original 2025 maturity date. That debt was restructured into two tranches, with $200 million in secured first-lien notes due in 2026 (along with an option to extend to 2027) and $150 million in exchangeable senior first-lien notes due in 2029.

In its report, Fitch said the positive outlook reflects FOA’s work over the past year to address material near-term obligations and its improved profitability when excluding fair value marks.

The agency indicated it could raise FOA’s issuer default rating to B- if the company builds a “substantial” liquidity cushion beyond remaining repayment obligations and continues to de-lever through retained earnings.

The ratings remain constrained by relatively weak liquidity and high leverage, a short-term and largely secured funding profile, and elevated key person risk tied to Libman. Additionally, the review factored in the highly cyclical nature of mortgage originations, as well as the volatility tied to mortgage servicing rights valuations and securitization residuals.

The announcement illustrates that while FOA has taken steps to stabilize its balance sheet, its capital structure and earnings volatility still present elevated credit risk for mortgage and capital markets participants — including warehouse lenders and secondary market investors.

Fitch noted that its positive outlook could be revised to stable, or the CCC rating could be cut, if Finance of America fails to bolster its liquidity before upcoming maturities.

Other factors that could drive a downgrade include deteriorating profitability and sustained leverage above 15s. The ratings agency said that FOA’s ratio of total debt to tangible equity — excluding obligations tied to HECM Mortgage-Backed Securities (HMBS) and nonrecourse debt — was 33.7x at the end of September, up from 14.0x at the end of 2025. Fitch said it believes leverage will stay sensitive to interest rate movements.

In December 2025, FOA issued $50 million of preferred stock to funds managed by Blue Owl Capital. Fitch treats these preferred shares as debt, since change-of-control provisions mandate redemption of the preferred shares in cash. But the agency said it does not believe the preferred shares will be a permanent part of FOA’s capital structure as scheduled increases in coupons, starting with a 300-bps increase at the seventh anniversary date, provide an incentive to redeem and create an effective maturity.

“We think it speaks a lot to the interest in the reverse segment, the fact that they’re willing to make an equity commitment to us and acquire the product that we’re generating,” FOA CEO Graham Fleming told HousingWire‘s Reverse Mortgage Daily earlier this year about the transaction.

Fitch also noted potential upsides for FOA’s ratings. These include sustained improvement in liquidity after near-term obligations are repaid, return on average assets being maintained above 1% with positive cash generation, and gross leverage staying below 10x.

The agency also cited better funding flexibility through long-term and more committed facilities, growth that strengthens the FOA franchise brand, and deeper management expertise and clear succession planning as potential reasons to bolster the company’s ratings down the road.

#5426. Stalled data center buildouts send inference chips hunting for space in telco and colo sites

Demand for inference is outrunning the construction of new AI data centers, as power, capital and permitting delays push fresh capacity further out. That gap is sending chipmakers to hunt for room in existing facilities.

Many older telco and colocation sites have the space and power. But most can’t take today’s dense, liquid-cooled GPU racks without costly retrofits, which opens the door for air-cooled inference systems, according to Anton McGonnell (pictured), vice president of core product at SambaNova Systems Inc.

“We as an industry are just encumbered by the velocity of data center buildouts, and that’s been slowed down by just the physics of how long this takes, by the access to capital, and more and more by legislative hurdles — particularly in the U.S.,” McGonnell said.

McGonnell spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed AI data centers and the demand for air-cooled inference racks. (* Disclosure below.)

SambaNova’s fifth-generation chip, the SN50, targets the decode phase of inference, where output tokens are generated and data movement becomes the bottleneck. Its racks stay air-cooled and light enough to fit existing facilities, McGonnell explained. Newer GPU racks, by contrast, can demand reinforced flooring and 120 to 250 kilowatts of power per rack, he noted.

“On all of this stuff — the power and the cooling gear — there’s 18- to 24-month lead times to get this equipment into the data centers. Never mind all of the construction costs,” McGonnell said.

SambaNova, which investors valued at $11 billion in July, pairs its decode chips with partners that handle prefill, the compute-heavy first phase of inference. At SC26, it is demonstrating Intel’s D-Series GPUs for prefill alongside its SambaRack SN50 for decode in an air-cooled heterogeneous setup.

“They have developed a chip that has much, much better cost performance for the prefill phase of inference,” McGonnell said. “They’ve sacrificed HBM, which isn’t needed for prefill because it’s a compute-bound problem.”

#5425. AI Inspo Unveils an All-in-One AI Social Media Agent That Bridges Strategy and Execution

AI Inspo's AI agent unites personalized social media strategy, content creation, publishing, and performance analysis in one platform for creators, marketers, and businesses.

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AI Inspo today announced the official launch of its AI-powered social media agent, a connected platform that brings strategy, content creation, publishing, and performance review into a single workflow. Designed for creators, marketers, and businesses, the agent combines two core capabilities: social media strategy and creative content creation. Together, they help users set priorities, turn plans into content, and use performance insights to shape what comes next.

Managing multiple social platforms and accounts often requires moving among planning tools, creative software, publishing schedulers, and analytics dashboards. That fragmented process adds repetitive work and can make it difficult to turn insights into action. AI Inspo brings these activities into one workflow, allowing users to carry a strategy through publication and apply what they learn to the next round of content.

"AI Inspo was built around the real-world needs of creators and marketers managing multiple accounts across social media platforms," said Dong Lin, CEO of QuVideo and Project Lead for AI Inspo. "By bringing research, data analysis, and content creation together, we aim to reduce repetitive tasks and give users more time to focus on strategy, informed decision-making, and creativity."

Two Core Capabilities Link Strategy to Creative Execution

The agent combines account analysis with trend discovery and content creation, helping users decide what to publish and develop ideas suited to their audience.

Its social media strategy capability assesses account performance and recommends next steps based on each user's goals and stage of account development. AI Inspo also finds trending topics relevant to the account and helps turn them into content ideas. This gives users a way to identify trends their audience may care about and connect those opportunities with their publishing plans.

Its creative capability helps users make trending ideas their own. Users choose a viral reference and add their topic; AI Inspo adapts the reference's format into ready-to-publish content built around that topic. By giving a new idea the structure of a high-performing post, the agent provides a concrete starting point for creation while keeping the user's subject at the center.

Users can take an idea from trend discovery through creation and publishing, then review how it performs. Those insights inform the next content brief and help users refine their choice of topics and formats over time.

Personalized Guidance That Evolves with Each Account

An account's needs change as it develops. For a creator launching a new account, early priorities may include choosing a content direction and establishing a consistent production routine. As the account matures, attention may shift to refining formats or improving an existing strategy.

The agent remembers how users manage their accounts and create content, then tailors recommendations to their changing goals and workflows. That continuity lets users build on earlier work and receive guidance aligned with their current priorities.

Account context and performance insights help users judge which trends and formats deserve further creative effort.

Ongoing Support for Consistent Content Production

Consistent social media activity calls for sustained planning, production, and review. Alongside its AI agent, AI Inspo provides ongoing user support and a Discord community where creators, marketers, and businesses can exchange ideas, seek guidance, and refine their social media workflows.

This combination supports AI Inspo's mission to make high-quality content easier and more affordable to produce. The workflow is designed to reduce routine work, leaving users more time for creative decisions and planning.

#5424. Done right, verification gives loan officers their time back

When verification is fragmented, loan officers absorb delays and manual follow-up. A connected workflow pulls income, employment and asset data early in the application, syncs to the LOS and reduces rekeying and repeated document requests.   AI Summary

Verification has a way of becoming the loan officer’s problem.

A missing pay stub turns into an email. An employer that doesn’t respond turns into a phone call. A borrower who missed a verification request needs another reminder. And bank statements tend to be the biggest headache of all: pages go missing, borrowers send photos instead of PDFs or the statements don’t cover enough months, so the request goes out again.

If income, employment and asset verification are handled through separate systems or at different stages of the loan, someone has to keep track of what was completed, what was not and what still needs to happen. Even when the underlying problem sits with an employer, vendor or data source, the loan officer is often the one who has to absorb the delay and explain it to the borrower.

As more lenders move verification earlier in the workflow, often into the point of sale, it is easy to see why LOs might worry that more of that work is being pushed onto them. But moving verification earlier does not have to mean moving more work onto the LO. Done right, it can do the opposite: give loan officers reliable information sooner, reduce manual follow-up and preserve more of the time they need for borrowers, referral partners and new business.

Loan officers know how quickly administrative work can take over a day. Individual verification tasks may be small, but together they eat into the hours an LO could spend advising borrowers, structuring deals, developing referral relationships and bringing in new business. That is the “green time” loan officers need to protect.

For lenders still relying heavily on manual verification, reducing document collection is one of the clearest places to reclaim time. When borrowers can connect directly to their payroll provider, employer or financial institution, the lender can receive income, employment and asset data without asking the LO to collect every piece manually. That means fewer pay stubs to chase, fewer employer responses to track down and fewer borrower reminders to send.

A direct connection to the borrower’s financial institution also solves much of the pain with bank statements because far less time is spent on things like combing through to identify and source deposits. But automation is only part of the equation. Timing matters, too.

Traditionally, verifications happened after application, once a file reached processing or underwriting. More lenders are now moving those steps to the point of sale, while the borrower is already completing the application. From the LO’s perspective, that can look like more work moving closer to the borrower relationship they manage.

A well-designed workflow does the opposite. When verification is built into the application experience, the borrower can complete it while already engaged in the process by connecting directly to their accounts instead of manually entering income, employment and asset information in the form fields.

That gives borrowers a faster, simpler application, which makes for happier borrowers, and it gives the LO reliable information sooner without creating another request to initiate or chase later. That earlier visibility also gives the LO more time to address missing information or a financial scenario that needs a closer look before it becomes a downstream surprise.

Moving verification earlier does not help much if the workflow surrounding it is fragmented. When income, employment and assets live with different providers, the resulting data can land in disconnected systems. Loan officers and operations teams may have to toggle between platforms to confirm what’s been completed and rekey information into the loan file.

This fragmentation also creates friction for borrowers, who may not know verifications are the cause, but who will certainly notice they are waiting or being asked for another document. In the worst case, that frustration costs the lender the loan. Even when borrowers stay, verification delays stretch application-to-close timelines, negatively affecting performance metrics that may factor into LO compensation and creating additional costs for the lender.

A connected verification experience brings income, employment and assets into one borrower flow and syncs the resulting data back to the LOS in real time. That means fewer systems for lending teams to manage, less information to rekey and fewer separate requests for borrowers to complete, helping keep the file moving without adding more work for the LO. Direct-source data can also be refreshed when reverification is needed later in the loan cycle, without sending the borrower back through another round of document collection.

Done right, verification takes administrative work out of the loan officer’s day instead of simply moving it from one stage of the process to another. It gives LOs better information earlier, keeps borrowers moving and protects more of the green time loan officers need to serve customers and grow their businesses.

Loan officers notice which lenders give them verification technology that protects their selling time and which ones expect them to work around operational friction.

Daniel Esquibel is the Vice President of Mortgage at Argyle.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

#5423. Homeward cash-offer product launches nationwide for agents

Homeward expanded its agent-only cash-offer program from 13 states to all 48 contiguous states. The company says sellers can close in as little as 14 days and receive any resale upside back, while agents gain more certainty and timeline control.  AI Summary

Homeward has expanded its cash-offer product from 13 states to all 48 contiguous states, giving real estate agents nationwide a way to offer sellers a cash sale, the company announced on Wednesday.

The Austin-based company, which works only through real estate agents, said agents in every contiguous state can now bring a Homeward cash offer to their listings. The product is designed to reduce the risk of failed transactions tied to buyer financing or last-minute cancellations.

The move comes as contract fallout remains a concern. In a low-inventory, high-mortgage rate market, a canceled contract often means agents must re-market the property while managing client frustration and timing pressures around the seller’s next move.

“Agents are doing everything right and still watching deals fall apart at the finish line,” Tim Heyl, founder and CEO of the HousingWire Tech100 firm, said in the announcement. “A cash offer fixes that, but most cash buyers make their money by underpaying the seller. We don’t. Now agents everywhere can give their clients a sale they can count on, without asking them to leave money on the table.”

Through the cash-offer program, homeowners can sell to Homeward for cash in as little as 14 days and skip traditional showings, according to the company. Unlike many investor or iBuyer models, Homeward said any upside when the home is later resold is passed back to the seller rather than retained by the buyer.

For listing agents, the pitch centers on certainty of close and timeline control. A cash buyer eliminates the need to navigate financing contingencies, re-negotiations after appraisal issues and the risk of a buyer walking away late in the process. That stability can be critical for sellers who must coordinate a purchase on their next home or who need proceeds on a specific schedule.

For housing professionals, products that convert financed buyers into effective cash buyers or that provide institutional cash to sellers have become more prominent as higher mortgage rates, tighter credit conditions and affordability constraints increase fallout risk. Homeward’s nationwide expansion gives brokerages and teams in smaller and midsize markets access to a tool that had been limited to 13 states.

Alongside the nationwide cash-offer launch, Homeward said its Buy Before You Sell program is on track to be available in most states by the first quarter of 2027.

The program is designed for move-up or move-down buyers who need to tap their existing equity but want to avoid a home sale contingency. Homeward pairs short-term bridge financing with a guaranteed backup offer on the customer’s existing home, allowing agents’ clients to write offers on a new property without first selling their current one.

Buy Before You Sell is currently available in 16 states: Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Iowa, Maryland, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Washington.

Bridge-style and buy-before-sell products have gained traction over the past several years as a way to unlock trapped equity for existing homeowners. For agents, they can shorten transaction timelines, reduce dependence on contingent offers and help keep purchase deals intact if the client’s sale is delayed.

#5421. Humyn Labs raises $47M to bridge the gap between AI training and real-world robotics

Humyn Labs, a company turning human experience into training for robots and artificial intelligence, today announced it has raised $47 million in early-stage funding to accelerate intelligent robotic deployment readiness in real-world environments across Brazil, South Korea and India.

Accel led the $26 million equity portion of the round, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Finserv Intelligence through Bajaj Finance, Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton and Jump Trading LLC. Lighthouse Canton led the remaining $21 million in venture debt, with participation from Trifecta Capital.

Founded in early 2026, Humyn’s proposal is that AI models for humanoid robots don’t learn dexterity from staged demonstrations; they must learn by observing how humans move in real environments. This provides actual behaviors showing how hands work on objects, reach, touch, handle and recover without explicit instructions.

Unlike generative AI models that learn from vast amounts of text, images and video, physical AI models must learn how to interact with the world around them. That means understanding not only what objects look like and where they are, but also how to manipulate them, how much force to apply and how to respond when something goes wrong.

“The results can be very, very, very dramatic and catastrophic,” co-founder and Chief Executive Manish Agarwal (pictured) told SiliconANGLE in an interview.

Agarwal pointed out how mistakes that might be inconsequential for a chatbot can have serious consequences for a robot operating alongside people. That makes access to diverse, high-quality data about how humans physically interact with their environments critical for training robots to work safely and reliably in the real world.

To address this, the company built a video corpus captured from head-mounted cameras as participants performed everyday household tasks, comprising up to 200,000 hours of intentional human motion. The company also shipped a dataset of 120,000 faces across five regions for facial recognition, including adjustments in lighting, pose, expression, glasses, hairstyle, facial hair, accessories, age and locale.

That’s combined with more than 50,000 hours of representative speech data for underserved language markets, including Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Odia, Assamese, Korean, Tagalog, Arabic, Vietnamese and Portuguese. Voice AI models that understand natural language already have vast amounts of data for widely spoken languages such as English, Mandarin or Spanish, but real-world customer support within South and Southeast Asian markets lacks routine coverage.

Humyn’s engine uses sound, sight, motion and touch as data inputs, which it curates, normalizes and labels so that AI models can understand the kinematics of motion, force and environmental factors. Together, this provides training patterns for physical AI models, world models, general foundation models, and audio and voice AI.

Geographic diversity is also important because robots must understand the environments and cultural practices where they will operate. “Diversity gets you in the room. The quality ensures that you stay in the room,” Agarwal said.

To make this point, Agarwal emphasized the importance of geographic and cultural diversity in collecting training data. A household robot trained in the United States may struggle with tasks in an Indian home, where everything from cooking utensils and kitchen appliances to laundry practices and room layouts can differ. These regional differences mean that robots need experience with the specific environments and practices of the people they will eventually serve.

By collecting data across more than 20 countries, Humyn can train models on data that more closely resembles their intended deployments, potentially accelerating readiness for real-world work.

Agarwal added that the company is seeing interest from customers building household robots for domestic tasks and elder care, alongside industrial applications involving object manipulation and movement through factories, warehouses and commercial environments.

“The next phase in the deployment cycle is about how well these models perform in the wild,” Agarwal said.

In the end, data is only the beginning. Humyn wants to measure where robots fail in real-world conditions and use that to feed the AI flywheel and build better models. That means using virtual simulations, physical replicas and partnering with the enterprise and researchers to have field deployment labs to identify the differences between expected and actual performance.

The company said it intends to use the new funding to build deployment-readiness infrastructure in Brazil, South Korea and India, develop its hardware and enrichment engine, and expand its on-the-ground presence in San Francisco, London and Seoul. Agarwal said this will also involve testing robots in real-world environments to identify gaps between their expected performance and actual behavior, feeding those results back into model development.

#5420. Medicare’s Part B premium keeps climbing past $200, and CMS blames health care spending

Free daily briefing on global business news.

CMS set the 2027 Part B deductible at $292, up from $283, and the Part A hospital deductible at $1,776, up $40

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services set the standard monthly Medicare Part B premium at $209.40 for 2027 on Tuesday, up $6.50 from $202.90 in 2026. The agency linked the higher premium and deductible to expected increases in health care spending.

The annual Part B deductible for all beneficiaries will be $292 in 2027, up $9 from $283 in 2026, CMS said. Part B covers physicians' services, outpatient hospital services, certain home health services and durable medical equipment.

The inpatient hospital deductible under Part A will climb $40 to $1,776, from $1,736. Daily coinsurance for the 61st through 90th day of a hospital stay will be $444, up from $434. Skilled nursing facility coinsurance for days 21 through 100 will be $222, up from $217.

Most Part A enrollees pay no premium. Those who buy in after earning 30 or more quarters of coverage, either on their own or through a spouse, will pay $328 a month, up from $311. Enrollees who must pay the full Part A premium will pay $597 a month, up from $565.

Higher-income beneficiaries pay more for Part B. Total monthly premiums for people with full Part B coverage range from $293.10 for individual filers with modified adjusted gross income above $112,000 up to $711.80 for those at $500,000 or more. Joint filers face the same range at income thresholds of $224,000 and $750,000. The standard premium for the immunosuppressive drug coverage available after a kidney transplant will be $125.70.

The $6.50 increase works out to 3.2%, according to Money. Money also reported that the increase falls short of last year's $17.90 jump, the program's second-steepest on record. The Social Security Act requires the premium to cover roughly a quarter of the projected costs of serving beneficiaries age 65 and older.

The 2027 premium would total $2,512.80 over a year, according to MarketWatch. MarketWatch said the figure was close to expectations the Social Security and Medicare Board of Trustees set in June, and that the 2026 premium was the first to top $200 a month.

The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 on Oct. 14, which lifts the typical retiree's monthly check by $75 beginning in January. Part B and Part D costs are often withheld directly from monthly Social Security checks. The standard Part B premium had been projected at $209.50 for 2027 in a report from Medicare trustees.

Medicare enrollees can see their 2027 premium amount in their my Social Security Message Center starting in late November, the Social Security Administration said. Information on Medicare changes for 2027 will be available at www.medicare.gov.

Weichert, Realtors has joined HouseCanary’s Google Listings Program, making active listings from the brokerage’s company-owned offices visible in a dedicated carousel within Google mobile search results across selected markets, according to an announcement on Wednesday.

#5418. Maia and Karen Zupko and Associates, Inc. Partner to Bring Independent Coding Expertise to AI-Generated Orthopaedic Coding

Four plus decades of orthopaedic coding authority meets EHR-integrated AI-native coding support technology. KZA will conduct ongoing independent audits of Maia's coding output.

ROSEMONT, Ill., Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Maia, an AI-powered medical coding and revenue cycle platform built exclusively for orthopaedic practices, and Karen Zupko & Associates, Inc. (KZA), the healthcare consulting and coding education firm that has advised surgical specialists since 1985, today announced a partnership pairing independent coding and audit expertise with AI-generated coding at the point of care.

Under the partnership, KZA will conduct ongoing independent audits of Maia's AI-generated coding output across both evaluation and management (E/M) and surgical cases. Each review is performed by KZA's certified consultants against AMA CPT guidelines, ICD-10-CM guidelines, CMS National Correct Coding Initiative edits, and AAOS Global Service Data. KZA provides its findings to Maia's engineering and machine learning teams, which use the feedback to guide improvements to the platform's coding models, rules, and review workflows.

In addition to the ongoing audits, KZA and Maia will explore how specialty-focused education and expert review could support oversight of Maia's coding output.

"AI will play an increasingly important role in how medical practices approach coding. "What impressed us about Maia was their proactive commitment to independent auditing before anyone required it. Free daily briefing on global business news.

Pony AI reported third-quarter revenue of $44.6 million on Wednesday, up 75.2% from $25.4 million a year earlier, as its robotaxi business grew.

That topped the $37.5 million analyst estimate, according to Bloomberg. Bloomberg also said robotaxi revenue growth was the slowest of the year for the business.

Robotaxi services revenue rose 165.4% to $17.8 million and made up about 40% of the total, the company said. Fare-charging revenue increased by close to 400%. The robotaxi fleet reached 2,768 vehicles as of Sept. 30. The company is working toward a year-end target of 3,500 vehicles.

Gross profit rose 69.5% to $7.9 million. Loss from operations narrowed to $68.7 million from $69.7 million a year earlier.

The net loss widened to $136.3 million from $61.6 million, a swing the company attributed chiefly to declines in the fair value of its trading securities. Net loss attributable to Pony AI was $105.6 million, compared with $61.3 million a year earlier.

In China, the company said its previously separate operating areas in downtown Guangzhou and Nansha District now form a single contiguous area of more than 1,000 square kilometers (386 square miles). Overseas, Pony AI began what it described as Europe's first fully driverless test rides with invited passengers in Zagreb, Croatia, in September. The company is advancing deployments in London and Manchester, with road testing under way in Manchester.

Pony AI's U.S.-listed stock is down 72% year to date.

However, the market is not quite ready for a bullish victory lap. Open interest is falling, long positions have already suffered heavy liquidations, and XRP still needs to reclaim important resistance levels.

XRP traded around $0.95, following another difficult session for the crypto market. Meanwhile, its futures market is flashing a rate that dropped in aggregated funding to -0.0068% every eight hours, equivalent to roughly -7.4% annually.

Negative funding means short sellers pay long traders to maintain their perpetual futures positions. In other words, bears are effectively paying a premium to maintain their bearish exposure.

Hyperliquid showed an even more pronounced imbalance, with XRP funding reaching approximately -10.2% annually. The figures suggest bearish positioning has become increasingly expensive across several derivatives markets.

The immediate question is whether bearish positioning has become sufficiently expensive to trigger an unexpected reversal. A negative funding rate alone cannot confirm a short squeeze. XRP needs to attract fresh spot buyers, recover momentum, and force short sellers to close their positions.

The first important hurdle remains $1.00. Reclaiming this psychological level could encourage sidelined buyers to return and create additional pressure on leveraged shorts.

A sustained move above $1.00 would put $1.10 within reach, followed by a potential test of $1.20 if short liquidations accelerate.

However, the bearish scenario remains firmly in play. Losing the recent $0.89 low could expose XRP to another decline toward $0.80, particularly if Bitcoin continues weakening.

For now, the XRP price prediction hinges on whether negative funding translates into actual buying pressure. Bears are paying longs, but bulls still need to deliver the rally. If they do, the same traders betting against XRP could become the fuel behind its next recovery.

#5415. YIMBY groups bare claws in lawsuit over LA bid to stop housing project

YIMBY Law and allied housing groups filed a petition in Los Angeles County Superior Court seeking approval of 398 homes under AB 2011. The case challenges the city’s mountain lion habitat finding and cites the Housing Accountability Act.  AI Summary

A mountain lion that may never have set a paw on a golf course is now at the center of a lawsuit against Los Angeles over a proposed housing development.

As expected, housing groups sued the city this week to force approval of 398 homes at Woodland Hills Country Club. The developers invoked Assembly Bill 2011, which allows ministerial approval of housing in commercially zoned areas if the project includes affordable units. City planners blocked it by declaring the course a puma habitat.

Yes In My Back Yard, Sonja Trauss, the California Housing Defense Fund and Californians for Homeownership filed the petition in Los Angeles County Superior Court. Trauss is founder and executive director of YIMBY Law.

They asked a judge to set aside the city’s Aug. 20 determination and order the project approved under AB 2011 and the Housing Accountability Act.

The petition argues the city applied the wrong evidentiary standard to deny the project. It highlights the city’s own habitat report, which shows no documented GPS locations of mountain lions on the property. The petition notes that the city’s ecologist dated the report one day before the denial and the developer never saw it.

“This insanity of mountain lion habitat in an urban area on an active golf course would be the single biggest abuse of state housing law in the history of California,” developer’s attorney Dave Rand wrote on social media. “It won’t stand.”

Rand’s client isn’t part of the lawsuit other than being identified as a real party in interest.

While petitioners seek a court order, Rand has threatened the city with a lawsuit to recover damages. Rand sent the city a letter with a deadline to reverse course or face a lawsuit seeking at least $20 million in fines, attorney’s fees, costs and compensatory damages.

The base fine is $10,000 per unit. AB 712, signed into law last year, raises it to an automatic $50,000 per unit if the city has lost in court at least once in the same housing element cycle.

Rand’s letter also cites an Oct. 23 ruling from the Second Appellate District that a homeowner could seek damages when a city misses a mandatory permit deadline. That case involved an accessory dwelling unit, not AB 2011.

Plaintiffs note that Councilmember and district representative Bob Blumenfield wrote to constituents Dec. 9, 2025, saying that he would pursue public input and environmental review. That was less than three weeks after the application was filed.

The petition alleges he then introduced motions, wrote to state legislators and the governor, and published op-eds, all seeking a way to stop the project. Planning staff, meanwhile, sent letter after letter demanding more studies, producing a prolonged 9-month back-and-forth.

On Aug. 20, the city declared that an operating golf course, in regular use by golfers and staff, is mountain lion habitat. Blumenfield called the determination “Great news!” on the Council District 3 website.

But the state Department of Housing and Community Development countered with a notification that the city is violating state law. The petition says the city has not reversed it.

The department set a Nov. 25 deadline for the city to respond to its letter. It said it could refer the matter to the state attorney general.

#5414. Starburst adds context support to give AI agents consistent access to business data definitions

Starburst Data Inc. is expanding its data federation platform into business context management with the introduction of Context Studio, a new capability designed to help artificial intelligence agents produce more accurate and trustworthy answers from information distributed across enterprise systems.

Context Studio collects business definitions from existing data catalogs, business intelligence tools, metric stores and documents, making them available alongside data when AI agents respond to prompts. The system is intended to eliminate conflicting definitions that can cause AI agents to produce incorrect results.

The new capability addresses a problem the company encountered as customers began deploying its Aida natural-language data assistant in production environments, said Starburst co-founder and Chief Executive Justin Borgman.

“We’ve found that as you get into production, the biggest issue is context because you need to trust the answers the agent gives back,” he said.

The challenge is particularly acute in large organizations where different departments may use different definitions of common business metrics, such as revenue or active customers. Without a consistent understanding of those terms, AI models can produce plausible but inaccurate answers.

“When those definitions conflict, the [large language model] doesn’t know any better; it’s just going to guess,” Borgman said. “That’s what leads to bad answers and an erosion of trust.”

Context Studio builds on Starburst’s existing data products architecture, which allows organizations to create curated views spanning multiple data sources. Those products incorporate business definitions, metadata and access controls that can be applied consistently when agents retrieve information.

Unlike conventional semantic layers that require organizations to consolidate definitions within a single platform, Context Studio federates existing definitions without requiring customers to move or rebuild their underlying data.

Built-in approval workflows resolve conflicting definitions, and a feedback mechanism is provided through which agents can propose improvements. Human reviewers approve changes before regression testing checks their impact on other queries.

Borgman characterized the expansion as an evolution of Starburst’s longstanding strategy of querying distributed data without centralizing it.

“We think context is going to live everywhere, just like we think data will live in multiple places,” he said. “Our approach treats [context] as a first-class principle in our design.”

Starburst hasn’t yet disclosed quantitative evidence of Context Studio’s impact on AI accuracy or productivity. The company said it is collecting benchmark data from private preview customers.

The company is also emphasizing traceability to increase confidence in AI-generated answers. Context Studio records which data sources agents access, the SQL queries they generate and the information used to produce responses. Access controls remain attached to underlying data products.

“Context is going to increase the probability of a good answer, but there’s also a need to trace how it got to that answer,” Borgman said.

An agent can interview domain experts to capture business knowledge and convert it into draft data products. Starburst is also extending its Aida data assistant to answer questions across multiple data products and introducing an agent that automatically generates dashboards.

Other platform enhancements include Mission Control for monitoring usage and costs, automated Apache Iceberg maintenance, a bring-your-own-cloud deployment option and graphics processing unit-accelerated querying. Starburst claims its recently introduced Torin query engine delivers up to sevenfold performance improvements in company benchmarks.

Context Studio is available in private preview for Starburst Galaxy and Starburst Enterprise. A public preview is planned for January, with general availability expected in the first quarter of 2027. Pricing hasn’t been finalized.

#5413. Road to Esports Nations Cup 2027 Gives National Teams More Chances to Compete and Fans More Matches to Follow

All countries and territories that qualified in 2026 retain their places, following a first qualification season involving nearly 200,000 players.

RIYADH, Saudi Arabia, Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Esports Foundation (EF) today announced the Esports Nations Cup's expanded Road to ENC 2027, with events run by National Team Partners (NTPs), new qualification tournaments, larger national rosters, and the ENC Ranking.

The Road to ENC 2027 gives players more chances to represent their countries and territories. National teams will have more opportunities to compete, creating new rivalries for fans throughout the season, while building momentum toward the inaugural Esports Nations Cup Finals in November 2027.

Nearly 200,000 players competed in 210 regional qualifiers during the first ENC qualification season, with 2,000 players from 123 countries and territories helping secure places at the Esports Nations Cup. Every place earned by a national team in 2026 will be protected, with players who represented those countries and territories included in ENC's expanded national rosters, from which coaches will select their Finals squads.

Countries and territories yet to qualify will also have another route through new regional online tournaments leading into a final LAN qualifier. Regional online qualifiers will kick off February 26, 2027, and run over five weeks across multiple game titles. The game-specific dates and final LAN qualifier details will be announced at a later date.

"Representing your nation is one of the proudest moments in any athlete's career. For fans, supporting their country or territory can be their first connection to a sport and the beginning of a lasting passion," said Ralf Reichert, CEO of the Esports Foundation. "As we build towards the first Esports Nations Cup, we want to help national teams grow together and give fans a team to believe in. Road to ENC creates more opportunities for those teams to compete and for fans to get to know the players, follow emerging rivalries, and become a part of their team's journey. When those teams arrive at ENC 2027, we want fans to have been part of how they got there."

Four elements will support national teams on the Road to the Finals:

National Team Partner-led events will give fans more opportunities to watch and support their national team before the Finals. National Team Partners can organize local activations, friendly matches, and multi-nation invitationals, creating more competitions while giving coaches opportunities to test new players. Supported through the ENC Development Fund, these events are designed to build national fandom and a stronger local esports ecosystem. National Team Partners can submit proposals for 2027 events until the end of December 2026.

New qualification tournaments will give countries and territories that missed out in 2026 another route to ENC. Teams will face off in regional online qualifiers, with seven regional winners and one invited nation from the ENC Solidarity program advancing to a final LAN qualifier to compete for the remaining places.

Expanded national rosters give coaches more flexibility to develop their teams. National team coaches can add eligible players to the squads that qualified in 2026, allowing them to test different combinations in national team matches before selecting their Finals lineups by May 31, 2027. Updated expanded rosters are due by January 15, 2027. For solo titles, the earned slot remains with the player who qualified for their country or territory.

The ENC Ranking will create year-round competitive stakes and give fans a live view of where their country or territory stands throughout the season. Players will earn points for their national teams through results in international Club leagues and tournaments, as well as national team competitions. The standings will evolve as players compete throughout the season, helping determine seeding for the ENC's group stage draw and informing direct invitations to future editions of ENC.

More details about the ENC Ranking, the schedule for the new qualifiers, and NTP-led events will be announced in the coming weeks.

To learn more about the Esports Nations Cup, visit the ENC website or follow the Esports Foundation on LinkedIn.

About the Esports Nations CupThe Esports Nations Cup (ENC) is a global international esports competition for nations and territories. Bringing together leading players to represent their countries across multiple game titles, ENC is designed to create a new platform for national pride, elite competition and long-term ecosystem development.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Purchase applications fell 3% and refinance requests fell 2% as the average 30-year rate rose to 7.35% from 7.21%

The Mortgage Bankers Association said total mortgage application volume fell 2.3% last week from the prior week on a seasonally adjusted basis as the average 30-year fixed rate rose to its highest level in three weeks, according to CNBC.

The average contract rate climbed to 7.35% from 7.21% for 30-year fixed mortgages up to the $832,750 conforming limit. Points, which include the origination fee, edged up to 0.79 from 0.75 on loans requiring a 20% down payment.

"Treasury yields rose last week amid data showing inflation accelerated in October and Fed officials acknowledging that additional rate hikes may be needed in the coming months," said Joel Kan, vice president and deputy chief economist at the association, according to CNBC.

Refinance applications declined 2% over the week, leaving them 54% under their year-ago level. Federal Housing Administration refinance applications rose close to 7%. "The FHA rate was roughly 30 basis points below the conforming rate, which supported refinance opportunities for some homeowners," Kan said, according to CNBC.

Applications to buy a home slipped 3% over the week and sat 18% under their year-ago pace. Buyers are struggling with affordability and feel less confident about the economy because inflation persists, according to CNBC.

A separate rate tracker showed a larger average. HousingWire's Mortgage Rates Center showed conforming 30-year loans averaging 7.58% on Tuesday, an increase of 0.23 percentage point over the prior week, according to HousingWire. The same outlet said more than 93% of traders expect a 25-basis-point Fed rate increase at next month's meeting, up from 76% a month ago.

Rates have been flat so far this week, according to a Mortgage News Daily survey cited by CNBC. The Census Bureau is set to release housing starts and building permits this week, and the National Association of Realtors is set to publish its pending home sales index.

The latest reading follows a run of declines. Mortgage applications had fallen for a third straight week through Oct. 30, even as the 30-year contract rate eased to 7.30% from 7.37%. The purchase index was then near its weakest reading since January 2025.

The rate had reached 7.50% in the week ended Oct. 9, the highest since November 2023.

The integration will enable BetaNXT's broker-dealer, custodian, asset manager, and wealth management clients to introduce digital asset services alongside traditional securities, using their established technology and operational processes.

U.S. financial institutions rely on established systems to process transactions, maintain client records, and manage securities operations. Over the last several months, BetaNXT joined more than 30 firms completing production transactions using DTC-tokenized assets across workflows including collateral, securities lending, Treasury repo, equity delivery-versus-payment and margin. In October 2026, DTCC named Taurus an ecosystem collaborator and integrated wallet provider for its Tokenization Service.

The service enables eligible securities held at The Depository Trust Company (DTC) to be represented on blockchain networks. Taurus has integrated with DTCC's APIs and nodes to provide wallet infrastructure and connectivity for participating institutions.

Building on these developments, Taurus and BetaNXT aim to help eligible clients incorporate tokenized securities into their existing custody and securities processing workflows, subject to applicable participation requirements. "Financial institutions want to expand their digital asset offerings while maintaining control over their operations," said Lamine Brahimi, Co-Founder and Managing Partner at Taurus. "Integrating Taurus-PROTECT with BetaNXT will give U.S. financial institutions access to secure custody and blockchain infrastructure through their existing technology, helping them introduce new services without duplicating their operational systems."

Christopher Waller, governor of the US Federal Reserve, speaks during the C. Peter McColough Series on International Economics at the Council on Foreign Relations in New York, US, on Thursday, Oct. 16, 2025. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller pushed Wednesday for forceful measures to combat inflation as Fed officials voiced differing views on how fast to raise interest rates.

Waller told CNBC that the Fed will probably have to lift its benchmark rate by 50 basis points when the Federal Open Market Committee meets Dec. 8-9. He said the central bank has to unwind the trio of quarter-point cuts it made last year, and possibly go beyond that.

"You might need to, like, shock people," Waller told CNBC's Steve Liesman. "I'm very, very concerned about inflation. It's kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it's spreading out."

St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem outlined his views on Tuesday in a speech at the Central Bank of Argentina's Money and Banking Conference in Buenos Aires. He said the economy "will likely require several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027 to achieve price stability in a timely manner."

Musalem said he expects the economy to need a real policy rate between 2% and 2.5% before spring 2027, and he estimated the current real rate at the lower end of a 1% to 1.5% range. He said the nominal policy rate "may need to do most of the work." He described a scenario in which no further increases are needed as unlikely but plausible.

That path points to increases at the December, January, March and April meetings, according to CNBC.

Other officials have urged a slower approach. “I don’t think the situation calls for dramatic action,” New York Fed President John Williams said Tuesday, according to CNBC. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack has endorsed more gradual tightening.

Waller said last week that a half-point increase should be considered at the December meeting if October consumer price data resembled the two prior months. He said then that he was leaning toward a quarter-point increase if monthly inflation improved. Musalem said October headline and core consumer price inflation rose more than expected.

The Fed raised rates by a quarter point in September, its first increase since July 2023, and held the target range at 3.75% to 4% in October. Governor Lisa Cook and Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase at that meeting. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, who votes on the December decision, has said the committee needs at least two more quarter-point increases.

Futures prices reflect a quarter-point increase at the December meeting and another in January, according to CNBC.

#5408. AI and supercomputing merge as universities build GPU clusters at cloud-provider scale

Universities racing to build AI infrastructure are learning that raw compute changes the pace of science itself, from molecular discovery to materials engineering.

AI and high-performance computing are converging, and campus technology leaders are now building like cloud operators. The Texas A&M University System is standing up two major clusters for researchers across its 12 universities and eight state agencies, according to Vince Kellen (pictured), chief information officer of The Texas A&M University System.

“A lot of it is going to be related to molecules, molecular discovery, and the size of these computers lets researchers go through their research program in a fraction of the time. What would normally take five months now gets done in a week,” Kellen said. “That’s a big deal for the scientists. It lets them do more exploration more frequently.”

Kellen spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how the system’s supercomputing clusters are speeding up molecular discovery, the security and operational demands of running them, and the convergence of AI and supercomputing. (* Disclosure below.)

The system’s VISION supercomputer, an Nvidia Corp. DGX H200 SuperPOD, ranked No. 66 on the June 2026 Top500 list, making it the most powerful university supercomputer in the U.S. — with a second cluster on the way, according to Kellen. The Texas A&M Engineering Experiment Station selected Dell Technologies Inc. to build IGNITE, a platform running Advanced Micro Devices Inc. GPUs in an Equinix Inc. data center in Dallas. With some research tied to highly secure federal contracts, protection tops the policy agenda.

“On the policy side, our main concern is security. Are we doing this in a secure way?” Kellen said. “Are we vetting the employees who are coming into the platform to make sure that they’re properly credentialed to come in?”

Texas A&M is working through those access questions as it brings more computing power to researchers across the system, but faster molecular discovery is only the first payoff. Materials engineering, fluid dynamics and other engineering disciplines are next in line, and the system has no plans to slow its buildout, according to Kellen.

“We already know that AI and supercomputing are one and the same,” he said. “That trajectory is going to continue in Texas for some time.”
