#5382. 12 terms that show how the inflation rate is built and what it leaves out

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Baskets, price indexes, core measures and more: 12 terms from the Cleveland Fed explain how the inflation rate is built.

Most people look up the inflation rate and accept it as a plain fact about the economy. That habit matters more now that price growth has picked up. Consumer prices rose 2.9% from December 2023 to December 2024, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and BLS reports that the 12-month increase reached 3.8% by April 2026. Faster price growth takes more out of household budgets. When a number has that much effect on people's money, how it is made becomes the reader's business. Each term in the vocabulary of inflation marks a point where someone chose what to count, what to compare or what to ignore.

Nobody observes the inflation rate directly. It is the change between price readings taken at two points in time, such as a month, a quarter or a year apart, and without both readings there is no rate. A lapse in federal appropriations left October 2025 without survey data, and BLS reports that 12-month changes for most series went unpublished in October 2026. The need for a second reading applies to every other choice behind the number. A different mix of goods, a different span of time or a different set of excluded items can change the headline even when no price has changed. A reader who knows where those choices sit can tell a real shift in the cost of living from a result of the method.

The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland set out to explain how inflation is gauged and to define the terms related to it, from the basket of goods behind every price index to median CPI, deflation and stagflation. Those terms fall into three groups. Some describe how the inflation number is built, and some describe how economists separate a lasting trend from a passing jolt. Others name extreme conditions, such as prices that rise out of control or fall for a long stretch. The value for a reader lies in knowing which question each term answers. With that knowledge, the next inflation headline can be read for what it actually says and for what it leaves out.

Inflation is measured from a chosen shopping list rather than from every price in the economy, so every reading carries the judgments built into that list. Measurement begins with a representative set of household purchases whose prices statisticians collect, and statisticians rebuild that set as spending habits change. The basket tries to capture what a typical household buys and also how much of each item it buys, and that quantity is an estimate. "The basket does not contain every good or service but is meant to be a good representation of both the types of items and the quantities of items that households typically consume," the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland said. When statisticians update that estimate of typical spending, the inflation reading can change even if no price tag does.

The weights shape the answer as well as the prices do, though in January 2026 the effect on the headline was small. Each item counts in the basket at its quantity times its price, and statisticians add those values across all items. BLS reports that the monthly increase in consumer prices for January 2026 was 0.37% under the new weights and 0.40% under the weights from 2023, using the same prices. Anyone who follows the headline can take some comfort from that, because refreshing the basket left the overall picture of the month intact. That total is an average across categories with very different results, and some of those categories shifted far more.

Under the newer weights, the increase for the groceries families buy every week was much sharper. The increase for fruits and vegetables in January 2026 was 1.01% under the new weights and 0.73% under the 2023 weights, according to BLS. The basket is a sample of typical consumption and not a full list of what anyone buys, so a household that spends heavily on produce faces a different inflation rate from the basket's average.

Reweighting changes only how much each price counts toward the total, never what a single price did. Gasoline was 2.52% cheaper that month under either set of weights, according to BLS. When a headline shifts after a basket update, the mix has changed, not the price at the pump.

A reader whose costs seem to outrun the official rate should look first at what they buy, because the official rate can describe the basket accurately and still not match that reader's spending.

Thousands of separate price tags say nothing about inflation until statisticians combine them into one figure that people can compare over time. A price index sets what the whole basket costs today against what it cost in a base period, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, and every inflation figure starts from that comparison. The result depends on a choice about whose purchases count. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports that its headline consumer price index follows how much prices move for shoppers in urban areas, averaged across all of them. The figure is precise about that average urban shopper and uncertain about any one family's costs.

Averaging is the purpose of an index, and it is also the reason large price shocks can sit unnoticed inside a calm headline. Across all items, the index rose 3.7% over the 12 months through September 2026, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, a moderate pace for a full year. Over the same year, gasoline cost 34.2% more. The headline blends gasoline with everything else households buy, so one steep increase moved the total far less than it moved the cost of filling a tank. A gap between the headline and particular purchases is therefore built into how an index works. A household that drives a lot faced a much steeper increase than the one reported in the news.

The price index gives a fair reading of the average household and a poor one for any single budget.

"Prices are high" and "inflation is high" sound like the same complaint, but they answer different questions. The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland explains that inflation measures how fast an index climbs in percentage terms, and that the index on its own reflects what living costs. In October 2026, the index that tracks prices paid by city shoppers stood at 337.511, according to BLS. That figure tells readers how costly everyday life has become, not the speed at which costs are rising. A household that feels squeezed at the store is reacting to the level. A calmer pace of inflation does not bring that level down; only an actual drop in prices would.

The big index number is a record of the past, measured from a starting line that someone chose. Every index level compares today's overall prices with a base year, and for the consumer price index that base is the period from 1982 to 1984, according to BLS. The October 2026 reading is therefore a running total of price increases since the early 1980s, not a gauge of how fast prices are moving today. Its size means something only next to that chosen base, and the current direction of prices is visible only in how much the level grows from one period to the next.

Anyone measuring inflation first has to decide how far back to compare, and the same prices give a different rate depending on that decision. Year to year is one common span, and inflation can also be measured over others such as quarter to quarter or month to month, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland. No single span is the correct one, so a headline that reports "the" inflation rate gives readers one window among several. The yearly rate compares each month with the same month a year earlier. It shows how far prices moved over a full year but not the path they took in between, and a headline can mislead in that gap.

A violent swing in a single category can account for much of a sharp move in the yearly rate, because the overall rate blends every category in the basket. In July 2008, energy cost 29.3% more than a year earlier, according to BLS. Anyone checking the headline that month saw all items 5.6% pricier than a year before, which looked like a serious squeeze on household budgets. By December 2008, the same yearly comparison showed energy 21.3% cheaper than a year earlier. In about one season, a steep annual rise in energy had turned into a steep annual fall. When the yearly rate jumps or plunges, a reader should ask whether one volatile category accounts for the move before concluding that prices across the board have changed course.

A large price move stays in the yearly rate for a full 12 months, and after that it becomes the starting point for the next comparison. In July 2009, all items cost 2.1% less than a year earlier, according to BLS, and that comparison reached back to the month of the 2008 energy surge. Part of the drop came from measuring current prices against an unusually high starting point. A negative yearly rate therefore does not prove that prices are sliding now, since it can mean that last year's spike has become the point of comparison.

Before trusting what a yearly rate says about today, a reader should check what prices were doing a year earlier.

There is no single inflation rate, and a report about "inflation" rests on one index chosen from several. The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland explains that different indexes weight different products, so they show price changes for households, for producers or for the whole economy. These indexes are not rival estimates of one true number. Each one gives its own answer to the question of whose prices count. Two indexes that the public treats as interchangeable can therefore report different results from the same price changes, and that gap comes from their design, not from an error.

In March 2026, software and computer accessories held a weight of 0.035% in core CPI, while the category's share of core PCE was 1.2%, according to the Federal Reserve Board. That category barely counts in one index and is a real input in the other. The two federal agencies build their weights from different kinds of data. The Bureau of Labor Statistics relies on what households report buying in its Consumer Expenditure Survey, while the Bureau of Economic Analysis relies on what companies tell the Census they shipped. One source tracks what people say they bought and the other tracks what businesses sent out, and the two do not agree. A jump in software prices therefore barely registers in the CPI but counts noticeably in PCE.

The overall inflation rate cannot tell a short-lived increase in prices from one that will last, and underlying inflation is the measure built to separate the two. Policymakers use it to set aside temporary noise and see the price growth that persists. The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland defines it as the price growth that would be left if brief jolts in the data could be stripped away. That condition makes underlying inflation an estimate rather than a direct reading. It also makes it another choice in how the number is built, because someone has to decide which price effects are short-lived and which will last.

Underlying inflation tracks a trend over the medium run, a span of several years, and not the bill a shopper pays this month. A household can pay far more for a single item this month while underlying inflation barely changes, and both readings are accurate because each answers a different question. When something a household buys becomes sharply more expensive, the useful question is whether the increase is temporary or part of a lasting trend. Only the lasting kind is meant to appear in the underlying rate.

Policymakers can respond differently depending on how they classify a rise. A rise they judge persistent may lead them to recommend raising interest rates, which makes borrowing more expensive for households and businesses. One they judge temporary may leave rates where they were.

For households, that classification matters because a rise that policymakers read as lasting can lead to higher borrowing costs.

The full consumer price index counts every sharp price swing, so a single month's reading can mislead anyone trying to judge where prices are heading. The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland describes median CPI and core measures as practical ways to estimate underlying inflation, either by keeping only the middle price change or by dropping food and energy. Both approaches set aside real price changes on purpose. Readers should treat these measures as deliberate edits of the data, made by people who decided which prices to leave out.

The two measures define noise in opposite ways. Median CPI judges a price change by its size rather than by what was bought, and it excludes every change except the middle one. Whatever moved most sharply in a given month is set aside, whether it was gasoline or haircuts. Core measures make the reverse choice and decide in advance which items to ignore. Food and energy stay out even in a month when their prices hold steady, while a wild swing in some other item stays in. Each method aims at the same trend and misses different price changes, and each reflects a judgment about which prices deserve trust.

Once the inflation number has been built and cleaned up, people want to know where it is headed, and the most familiar answer comes from the job market rather than from prices. The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland explains that the Phillips curve links inflation and unemployment inversely, though other drivers can loosen the connection. In plain terms, price growth tends to be weaker when more people are out of work, and the idea carries that caveat from the start. It is named for the economist A. W. Phillips, which makes it an established economic concept that a reader can look up, not a market slogan. The relationship Phillips first described concerned wages, and later work extended it to price inflation. That means the jobs-to-prices link people cite today goes one step beyond what was first observed.

The trade is easiest to see in a hypothetical slowdown. Suppose unemployment stands at 4% at the start and 7% at the end, a shift that would put many more people out of work and dominate the news. In the curve's logic, inflation over the same stretch is 5% at the start and 2% at the end. Price growth would go from a pace that strains household budgets to a much gentler one. Those figures illustrate what the idea predicts and are not drawn from any real episode. They show the curve's ideal shape, not evidence that the economy behaves this way. Even in that tidy form the bargain is grim, because calmer prices come at the cost of lost jobs.

The job market is only one influence on prices, and that is why the tidy trade often fails to appear. "However, economic conditions are only one of the factors that determine inflation," the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland said. One of those other factors is what people expect inflation to be, and no jobs report measures that. Changes in exchange rates are another, and they have nothing to do with how many people are working.

Readers should treat a weak jobs report as a reason prices may rise more slowly, not as a forecast that prices will fall.

Every measure of inflation in this guide assumes that prices change slowly enough for a comparison with last year to tell people something useful. Hyperinflation is the case where that assumption fails. It is extreme, accelerating inflation, commonly defined as above 50% per month, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland. That definition counts inflation in months instead of years, so a shopper would face a sharply higher grocery bill before the next paycheck arrived. The word "accelerating" matters as much as the number, because in hyperinflation the pace of price increases typically keeps rising instead of holding steady at one high level. The term describes a breakdown in how prices behave, not just an unusually bad year for the cost of living.

In some of the most extreme cases, prices can double within days. At that speed, even a monthly inflation figure describes the past. By the time statisticians publish it, shoppers are already paying far more than it shows. For people living through hyperinflation, the inflation rate no longer helps them plan. It records how much buying power they have already lost.

Falling prices look like good news to a shopper, but a lasting drop in prices is a warning about the economy. A price level that falls for a long stretch can lead people to cut back on what they buy, and that pullback can set off a cycle in which conditions keep getting worse, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland. Consumer spending supports businesses and the jobs they provide. A broad, sustained slide in prices therefore points to an economy in trouble rather than a season of bargains.

The danger of deflation is that it builds on itself instead of arriving as a single shock. Economists call this process a "deflationary spiral." Once prices start to fall, the decline can continue instead of settling at a new, lower level. The risk for a household lies in where that pattern leads over months and years, not in any single price tag that has dropped.

No single reading can show deflation, because it requires a fall in the overall price level that lasts. A one-month dip in an index does not qualify. A slowdown in inflation does not qualify either, because economists treat it as a separate condition with its own name, disinflation. The price level as a whole has to fall and keep falling.

Before calling a headline deflation, a reader should ask whether the overall price level has fallen and stayed lower over a long stretch.

When a news report says inflation is coming down, many people hear that prices are coming down, and disinflation is the term for the gap between those two ideas. Disinflation means the inflation rate slows, say from 6% to 4%, while prices still rise, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland. An inflation rate of 4% is still a positive rate. A household paying for groceries, rent and fuel still spends more than it did a year earlier, only by a smaller margin than it would at 6%. The improvement is in the pace of increases, not in what anything costs. A reader who hears only that the rate is falling can easily come away believing that the household budget is getting easier when it is only getting harder more slowly.

Disinflation offers narrow relief because it slows the rise in the overall price level without reversing it. The price level keeps going up for as long as disinflation lasts. The increases a household has already absorbed stay in place, and new ones keep arriving on top of them, only smaller. A family whose budget was stretched by last year's prices gets no money back when the rate cools. It simply faces smaller additions to costs that remain high. When a headline says inflation is easing, the useful question is which number is easing: the rate of increase or the prices themselves.

Stagflation is the extreme in which households face fast-rising prices, a weak economy and scarce work at the same time. It is high inflation alongside a weak economy and rising unemployment, the combination that the Phillips curve leads people to expect will not occur. Americans have lived through a severe version of it. Consumer price inflation was above 10% during the recessions of 1973–1975 and 1980, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland. At that pace, the everyday purchases in a household's basket became sharply more expensive within a single year. Those double-digit increases took place during recessions, not booms, and that timing is what separates stagflation from ordinary overheating.

The usual trade-off suggests that households hit by a weak job market would at least find some relief at the checkout as price growth slowed. Under stagflation, households lose that relief, and people lose income just as everything costs more. In both U.S. episodes, the unemployment rate was rising rapidly while prices were rising at double-digit rates. Stagflation is defined by two readings at once, and no inflation figure, however carefully built, can identify it alone. A reader can recognize it only by setting the price figures beside the jobs figures.

A high inflation reading alongside rising layoffs is the one pairing the usual rules say should not happen, and Americans have paid for it twice.

Index points are a poor guide to how fast prices are rising. In a worked example, two items each had an index 18.0 points higher than before, according to BLS. For one item, that was an 8.0% increase, and for the other it was a 16.4% increase, because the two started from different levels. The same visible jump can hide very different speeds of price growth.

For any index, the question that reveals inflation is how much it changed in percentage terms, not how many points it moved.

The two indexes also do not serve as independent checks on each other, because PCE takes its software prices from the CPI. The PCE price index for that category is derived from the CPI series for computer software and accessories, the Federal Reserve Board reports, so a problem in the CPI series passes into PCE without being caught. The CPI item behind that series, Computer Software and Blank Media, includes blank media, while the PCE category gives blank media no weight at all. A rise in memory product prices may therefore show up in a PCE category that contains no memory products. Correcting for that mismatch would lower the category's measured contribution to core goods inflation, but that correction is an estimate by Federal Reserve Board researchers Barbarino, Diercks and Miran, not an official revision by the Bureau of Economic Analysis or the Bureau of Labor Statistics, so the official numbers stand.

Whether goods inflation signals broad price pressure can depend on this single small category. Core goods PCE rose at a 5.5% annualized pace over the four months to March 2026 and at 2.7% without software, according to the Federal Reserve Board. Including software makes goods inflation look like a serious surge, while leaving it out shows a modest pace. Much of the alarm comes from a category whose measurement researchers question.

The number is not fake, but before reading a surge as economy-wide, a reader should ask which index produced it and what the category driving it contains.

Leaving prices out is a choice, not a requirement. Some gauges of the underlying trend keep every item in the basket. Deciding what counts as noise is therefore a method someone picked, and the measurement itself does not demand it. When a report says underlying inflation is cooling or heating, the useful question is which method produced that reading and what it left out. A gap between a core reading and a median reading is not a contradiction to explain away. It shows that two reasonable definitions of noise caught different price changes.

Hyperinflation can sound like a problem from old economics textbooks, but its cases are recent. People in Yugoslavia lived through it in the 1990s, within living memory in Europe, and Venezuelans began living with it in 2017. Modern economies are not protected from it.

Baskets, weights and core measures help people understand prices only while prices change at a pace statisticians can measure, and hyperinflation is the point where that stops.

Disinflation describes a cost of living that is still going up, only more slowly.

#5381. AI’s hidden energy tax: More than 80% of scale-up traffic is just memory moving around

Memory bottlenecks are emerging as one of the costliest problems in AI infrastructure as inference overtakes training. GPUs sit idle waiting on data, while high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, stays bolted to processors that cannot share it.

Photonics is shaping up as one way out. Marvell Technology Inc. has been pairing optics with photonic memory to stretch memory beyond the edge of a chip. The payoff is better efficiency in data centers enterprises have already paid for, according to Preet Virk (pictured, left), senior vice president and general manager of the Photonic Fabric Business Unit at Marvell.

“In the data center today, we have a lot of room for improvement of efficiency,” Virk said. “And when I say efficiency, I’m alluding to the wasted flops because we have GPU utilization that’s very low.”

Virk and Andy Mills (right), vice president of advanced product development at Penguin Solutions Inc., spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Amit Eyal Govrin at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how photonics and shared memory pools can ease memory bottlenecks in AI infrastructure. (* Disclosure below.)

Penguin’s MemoryAI Photonic Appliance moves HBM into a separate box tens of meters from the GPU, linked by Marvell’s Photonic Fabric. Each appliance holds 16 terabytes of HBM and DDR5 memory that servers across multiple racks can share, Mills explained.

“The challenge there is making sure your LLM doesn’t forget what you started talking to it about 10 minutes ago,” Mills said. “To do that, you need a large amount of memory, large token lengths.”

Optics also changes the energy math. Copper still works inside a rack, but crossing a pod of thousands of GPUs requires optics, according to Virk. More than 80 percent of scale-up network traffic is memory transactions, and a shared pool means much of that data never moves at all, he noted.

“Within data movement, the memory transactions are a place to focus on,” Virk said. “So with this solution versus a copper-based data movement, we could immediately get to a quarter of the energy, picojoules per bit, of data movement.”

Agents raise the stakes, generating far more token requests than human users ever did. As inference spreads across more racks and sites, Mills sees shared pools as the practical answer to memory bottlenecks.

“If anything, distributed encourages shared because you don’t want to recompute,” Mills said. “The whole thing about KV cache was a huge success because it stops recomputation of the same data. And when you can share that data on a broader base and wider across more racks, your efficiencies go up as well.”

#5377. Jensen Huang and Howard Lutnick agreed to testify before Senate Banking Committee

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott hopes to finish before Christmas; Huang also reached an agreement for a Dec. 1 House interview

Former Nvidia $NVDA CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have both consented to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, Chair Tim Scott, a South Carolina Republican, told CNBC on Wednesday. No hearing date has been announced.

"They both have agreed," Scott said on "Squawk Box." "We will hopefully have this done before Christmas." He said the appearances will give the committee "more information about what they knew, when they knew it and why they didn't do something about it."

Commerce Department spokesperson Kristen Eichamer said Lutnick agreed to a voluntary appearance to address the committee's questions, according to ABC News. ABC News said it is not clear when Lutnick will appear.

Scott had sent letters to both men asking them to testify in public, according to ABC News. The committee asked Jensen Huang to appear on Dec. 3 and Scott said he would subpoena him if he declined.

Jensen Huang struck a deal on Tuesday with the leaders of three House committees to sit for a closed-door, transcribed interview with all three panels on Dec. 1, according to CNBC. The pressure on Capitol Hill stems from his affair with someone suspected of spying for China.

Lutnick faces accusations that he held off on adding Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer, to a government list of firms seen as national security risks, according to ABC News. ABC News said that came despite U.S. intelligence suggesting Megaspeed may have been funneling Nvidia chips to China. ABC News also said lawmakers want to know if the Commerce Department violated its own procedures while supervising shipments of Nvidia's chips to China.

Sen. John Curtis, a Utah Republican, said in a social media post that Jensen Huang’s “gross negligence exposed cracks in our national security,” according to ABC News. Curtis added that Lutnick's reported delays on export controls cast doubt on the Commerce Department's commitment to serving Americans' best interests.

Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on Nov. 12 after reports of affairs with at least two women. U.S. officials suspect one of them, Alice Huang, who is not related to him, of relaying information to China's intelligence services. Jensen Huang said on Tuesday he would be honored to return as CEO if Nvidia's board decides it serves shareholders, employees, the company and America.

#5376. SAS spotlights the 5 most urgent fraud challenges facing governments in 2027

For Fraud Week, expert predictions focus on protecting public revenue, essential benefits and citizens as fraud tactics evolve

CARY, N.C., Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Protecting public money means protecting the people who depend on it. For International Fraud Awareness Week, data and AI leader SAS is putting five government fraud challenges in focus: tax fraud and compliance, social benefits payment integrity, procurement fraud, ID theft and elder fraud.

The outlook below centers on a common priority: identifying risk earlier while protecting legitimate taxpayers, beneficiaries, suppliers and people targeted by scams.

"We should not expect someone facing an apparent family emergency to become a deepfake expert." - Carl Hammersburg, SAS

Tax agencies getting better at parsing the fraudsters from the friendlies

Tax agencies are grappling with rising identity and refund fraud, workforce strain and service pressures, and modernization challenges tied to legacy IT. Additionally, value-added tax fraud, a form of tax evasion in which individuals or businesses deliberately underreport or falsely reclaim value-added tax, is on the rise.

As AI becomes embedded in everyday digital services, the biggest shift won't be "more automation." It'll be a new operating model where agencies guide taxpayers in real time, target enforcement with precision and explainability, and prove fairness and accountability at every step. Rather than a distant or speculative vision, this shift is already taking shape through practical, incremental changes agencies can begin today.

Expert prediction: "In 2027, tax agencies will increasingly bring fraud checks and taxpayer guidance closer to the point of filing. As AI makes false submissions more convincing, agencies will look beyond whether a return appears complete to whether its claims align with reliable, lawfully available information. For businesses and individual taxpayers, the goal will be earlier help correcting mistakes and more targeted checks on suspected fraud, not more hurdles for everyone seeking a legitimate refund."

-     Teya Dyan, Principal Tax and Revenue Compliance Consultant, SAS

Bonus prediction: "In 2027, VAT fraud will be fought on the invoice, not after the refund. As organized networks use AI to fabricate invoices and shell companies, tax agencies will connect invoice, registration and payment data to spot suspicious transaction chains before a refund is paid. The aim is to hold back the risky claims while legitimate businesses keep their refunds flowing."

-     Alexandre Negadi, Public Sector EMEA Director, SAS Fraud & Security Intelligence

Social benefits payment integrity: Accuracy must protect access

Social benefits agencies face a difficult balancing act: delivering timely, accurate benefits to eligible recipients while protecting public funds from errors and fraud. Rising caseloads, workforce shortages, changing regulations and increasingly sophisticated fraud schemes are straining already limited resources. Fragmented data, legacy systems and manual processes further complicate eligibility determination, ongoing verification and payment accuracy, obscure risks across programs and create processing bottlenecks. The challenge is to identify potential fraud and payment errors without slowing essential assistance or making it harder for eligible people to receive support.

Agencies such as the Nevada Department of Social Services and India's Government of Kerala are using AI and analytics to reduce errors, strengthen governance, service delivery and accountability across social benefits programs. In fact, Nevada estimates savings of more than $1.2M since putting SAS findings to work in March.

Expert prediction: "Benefits agencies will face pressure to move from measuring errors after payment to preventing them during case processing. The strongest approach will be continuous monitoring solutions that detect and help prevent errors, identify changing circumstances or potential fraud, and enable front-end AI use cases to minimize errors. Success will be measured in both accuracy and timely access."

-     John Maynard, principal solutions architect, SAS

Procurement fraud: The suspicious invoice is only part of the story

In August, the US General Services Administration announced it had uncovered $13 billion dollars in procurement fraud, making it the largest suspected fraud bust in GSA history by both number of contractors involved and total dollar amount. Additionally, according to research by the Association of Certified Fraud Examiners (ACFE) and SAS, public sector respondents named procurement fraud the top area they are currently deploying data analytics or automated monitoring tools to identify red flags of potential fraud.

Common procurement fraud schemes include bid-rigging, kickbacks and bribery, duplicate or inflated invoices, false invoices for fictitious vendors, conflicts of interest, product substitution and collusion between employees and suppliers. The public sector competitive bidding process can be complex, and current fraud detection methods may not be able to keep up with evolving threats. To protect against errors and abuse related to invoices, purchases and contract discrepancies, organizations must implement appropriate controls such as continuous monitoring and analytics techniques that can find anomalies that human investigators could easily overlook.

Expert prediction: "In 2027, government agencies will increasingly monitor procurement risk activity, supplier behavior, invoices, contracts, and payments in near real time rather than with random audits. Additionally, procurement spending risk alerts will be accompanied by an AI-generated narrative explaining, what happened, why it matters, and recommended next actions."

-     John Stultz, Government Fraud Solutions Specialist for the Security Intelligence practice at SAS

AI-powered identity fraud: Fake identities, real risks for governments

A convincing identity is no longer proof of a real person or the right person. Criminals are using AI to produce realistic identification documents, cloned voices and deepfake videos, making impersonation schemes more believable and easier to scale. Synthetic identities add another layer of deception by combining real personal information with fabricated details to create someone who does not exist. For public agencies administering benefits, tax refunds and digital services, the stakes extend beyond stolen identities: fraudulent claims and diverted payments put taxpayer dollars and people's essential support at risk. These attacks result in financial loss and damage to the reputation of government agencies. The challenge is to distinguish legitimate applicants from convincing impostors without making government services harder to access.

Expert prediction: "In 2027, identity checks cannot stop at the front door. Agencies will need to ask whether a sensitive account change, such as changes to contact information or payment destination, fits the person's wider activity, not just whether a document looks authentic. Stronger protection must also give legitimate users a practical way to prove who they are and regain access."

-     Shaun Barry, Global Director, Risk, Fraud and Compliance, SAS

Elder fraud: Protect people before a scam becomes a loss

According to the US Federal Bureau of Investigation's Crime Complaint Center, US citizens over the age of 60 have lost more than $7 billion annually to fraud targeting the elderly. AI-enabled impersonation can turn a familiar voice or an apparent authority figure into a tool of deception. Criminals pose as government employees and threaten to arrest or prosecute victims unless they agree to provide funds or other payments, even targeting people who have already lost money to scams. For governments, this makes citizen protection a priority alongside protecting agency budgets.

Expert prediction: "In 2027, telling older adults to be more careful will not be an adequate fraud prevention strategy. We should not expect someone facing an apparent family emergency to become a deepfake expert. Elder fraud prevention will demand closer coordination among governments, financial institutions and community organizations to make it easier to verify a request and interrupt a scam before money is lost."

-     Carl Hammersburg, Senior Manager, Global Civilian Government, Procurement and Healthcare Fraud & Compliance, SAS

A shared priority: Earlier action, accountable decisionsAcross these five challenges, the proposed 2027 call to action is the same: connect relevant information lawfully, prioritize meaningful risk and keep people accountable for consequential decisions. Fraud prevention should protect public resources without making essential services harder to access.

Expert prediction: "In 2027, government agencies will move beyond isolated AI experiments and start redesigning fraud operations around them. AI is already helping detect manipulated evidence, uncover connections and explain why activity is suspicious; the next step is to bring these capabilities into everyday decisions so investigators can intervene earlier. The agencies that make the most progress will combine AI with connected data, clear processes and human accountability, rather than treating it as a separate technology initiative."

-     Ensley Tan, Lead for Public Sector Consulting, SAS Asia Pacific

For International Fraud Awareness Week, learn more about fraud awareness and prevention.

#5375. 4 AI flashpoints from TwitchCon 2026 that left streamers uneasy

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Streamers at TwitchCon 2026 mocked OpenAI's hackathon, fought Twitch's opt-out AI training and split over which AI tools help creators.

Creators who argue about artificial intelligence now spend less time on what the technology can do and more on who controls the material it learns from. That question follows them from one service to the next, because Twitch is not the only company that hosts creators and uses AI. YouTube Live, Netflix $NFLX and Roblox $RBLX use it too, according to CBC. For people who stream on Twitch, the company training AI on their channels is their own platform's parent, Amazon $AMZN. A live streamer's material is their face, their voice and the audience they gather in real time. For them, the dispute centers less on the technology itself than on whether they ever agreed to hand those things over.

Streamers' frustration lasted for months. Twitch announced its AI training policy in August and explained it on a livestream that same week, according to CBC. Streamers were still angry in mid-November, when they gathered in San Diego for TwitchCon, the platform's biggest event of the year. Anger that lasts that long reflects more than one unwelcome setting. Many streamers feel that companies are putting AI into their work without consulting them. That doesn't make them opponents of AI. Many of them separate AI that helps a streamer from AI that takes a streamer's work. That distinction explains their anger as much as the technology does.

Yahoo set out to sum up how AI controversies shaped the way streamers reacted at TwitchCon 2026. Its account runs from the fight over Amazon training AI on streamers' channels unless they opt out to the attendees who mocked OpenAI's presence on the convention floor. It also covers the answers Twitch's leaders gave and the AI tools some streamers were glad to use. Each controversy came down to whether streamers get a real say over how AI uses their work. Each also raised the question of whether the companies' answers give them that say.

The most visible AI flashpoint at TwitchCon came from OpenAI, a company from outside the streaming world, rather than from Twitch's own policies. Attendees mocked OpenAI's Codex hackathon, which offered $25,000 in prizes, according to Yahoo. OpenAI meant the contest as an invitation for streamers to build with its technology. The people it hoped to court answered with ridicule instead of signing up. A cash prize is a sales offer, and this crowd treated it as a joke.

OpenAI could not win streamers over with prize money, a sign that cash alone would not ease their concerns about AI. These streamers' own platform had already enrolled their channels in AI training without asking. To them, a company arriving at their own gathering with money to spend could look like more of the same. The hackathon also gave them something they could see and laugh at in person. A default setting tucked inside their own accounts offered no such target, even though it touched their work far more directly. That makes OpenAI the most visible object of the anger rather than the whole story. Streamers' harder fight was with their own platform, where opting out took more than walking past a contest on the convention floor.

Twitch picked that default knowing that few streamers would turn the setting on by themselves. "If it was opt-in, nobody would opt-in ... that’s honestly the answer. So it’s going to be on by default," Mike Minton, Twitch's chief product officer, told CBC. His answer shows the opt-out is not a courtesy to creators. Twitch designed it on the expectation that most people would leave it alone. Streamers therefore don't see the default as a neutral design choice.

A streamer's own switch also doesn't cover everything that streamer says on Twitch. Messages a streamer posts in another channel's chat follow that channel's settings, and every channel starts out enrolled. A streamer who opted out can still have those words used for training wherever the host hasn't turned the setting off. Each visitor's protection then depends on every host finding and flipping a switch that starts in the on position. On a platform where streamers and viewers move constantly between each other's chats, no one can fully opt out alone, and the grievance is about lost control rather than a forgotten setting.

Twitch has answered streamers' anger by reassuring them about what has already happened, not by pulling back from the policy. Twitch CEO Dan Clancy has argued that a channel sitting in the program by default has not necessarily had its data collected yet, and that a streamer who switches the setting off stops that collection, according to Yahoo. The person who runs the platform is defending the default itself. His case rests on the harm still being avoidable. Under his explanation, every channel stays enrolled unless its owner does something about it, and the opt-out design that set off the backlash remains in place.

Clancy's reassurance addresses a different question from the one streamers were mainly asking. Their complaint is that they were signed up without a say. His answer is about timing, and it tells them that nothing has been taken yet. That answer puts the work of staying out of AI training on each streamer, one account at a time. A streamer who wants out has to find the setting called "Training for Generative AI" and switch it off, and a streamer who never gets around to it stays in. Clancy's explanation may ease the fear that a channel's data is already gone, but it does little for the resentment. Telling streamers they can still stop the training is not the same as asking them first, and that difference keeps the issue alive.

Streamers at TwitchCon did not object to every kind of AI. Some attendees value AI helpers that caption streams, clip highlights and assist with moderation, Yahoo reports, while they oppose generative AI that would replace what creators make. After the scorn for OpenAI's hackathon and the anger over training data, it would be easy to assume the convention was full of people who want AI gone, but their objection is selective. They separate tools that relieve a streamer of chores from tools that would make the streamer unnecessary.

The tools that attendees support handle the work around a live performance, not the performance itself. With automatic captions, viewers who watch with the sound off, or who can't hear it, can still follow a stream, so the streamer reaches more people without anyone else speaking for them. Twitch's AI clip tools help a streamer package highlights as vertical video for phone screens, which takes the editing off the streamer's hands while the moments stay the streamer's own. Moderation tools help a streamer keep order in a live chat, a job that is hard to manage while also performing, and they protect the community the streamer built instead of drawing on it. In each case the streamer stays on camera and stays in charge of the work.

Seen this way, the backlash at TwitchCon looks less like fear of the technology and more like a demand to keep control of it. Streamers welcome AI that serves their work. They resent AI that takes their work to build something that could compete with them.

Any platform's AI plans will have to pass the same test as the tools attendees praised: the streamer stays in control.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Apollo's Diego De Giorgi links the increase from €800 billion in the Draghi report to spending on defense, power and AI

Diego De Giorgi, head of Europe at Apollo Global Management, said the continent now requires roughly €1.4 trillion ($1.5 trillion) in investment each year, compared with the €800 billion figure former Italian Prime Minister Mario Draghi put forward in his report, according to Bloomberg.

De Giorgi spoke at Bloomberg's Global Credit Forum in London. He linked the higher estimate to Europe's need to catch up on defense, power and AI spending, and said little headway has been made in making the region's capital markets deeper or more integrated, according to Bloomberg. He became Apollo's head of Europe earlier this year and previously served as chief financial officer of Standard Chartered.

"Finding ways of financing, not just the big corporates of Europe, but the supply chains that enable those big corporates to deliver to us more tech sovereignty, more defense capabilities, more next gen manufacturing ability is one of the most important challenges for Europe," De Giorgi told Bloomberg. He said Apollo is "very, very focused on defense."

Apollo has become one of the largest financiers of the global AI build-out, through shorter-term, investment-grade credit, according to Bloomberg. De Giorgi said Apollo generated over $300 billion in new assets last year, with as much as 85% in credit and roughly 80% rated investment grade.

He said higher-for-longer interest rates, together with what he called the most massive capital-spending wave ever seen in AI, are likely to create more openings next year.

A tech sell-off in October and the exit of Nvidia $NVDA boss Jensen Huang have prompted doubts over whether the AI boom can last, according to Bloomberg. De Giorgi said the turmoil reinforces the "need to put layers of safety" in investments, and that the healthy cash generation of the biggest tech firms provides some reassurance.

Apollo's AI financing includes a proposed deal in which it is expected to lead a $40 billion financing for SpaceX's purchase of Nvidia AI chips, which was in preliminary talks as of early October. Apollo has also struck a $7 billion financing arrangement with Elon Musk's xAI for Nvidia chips earmarked for the Colossus 2 data center in Memphis.

Earlier this month, Apollo rolled out a European private-credit platform worth €10 billion, named European Credit Co., whose backers include the Abu Dhabi Investment Council, according to Bloomberg. #5373. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

#5372. Amazon tops Forbes’ list of America’s best companies, edging out Apple for No. 1

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 12, 2026 at 1:16 pmNovember 12, 2026 at 1:16 pm

Amazon is the best company in America, according to Forbes.

The Seattle tech giant took the No. 1 spot on the publication’s 2027 “America’s Best Companies” list, moving up from No. 2 last year and edging out Apple.

Three other Washington state companies landed in the top 50: Microsoft at No. 6, Costco at No. 13 and Alaska Air Group at No. 39.

Last year’s No. 1, Berkshire Hathaway, slipped to No. 4. Nvidia ranked No. 3 on the same day CEO Jensen Huang resigned, following his admission of an extramarital affair. JPMorganChase, Alphabet, Royal Caribbean Group, Walmart and Marriott International round out the top 10.

Now in its third year, the ranking scores thousands of the largest public and private U.S. companies on factors including customer and employee sentiment, financial performance, creditworthiness, cybersecurity and innovation. Forbes said it worked with 12 data organizations to build the index.

Forbes said Amazon’s financial strength and size, its standing in news and social media, and the range of voices across the company and its leadership lifted it to No. 1. Apple scored especially well on employee satisfaction, customer loyalty, financial strength and innovation.

Forbes also pointed to Amazon’s speed, citing a feature that lets customers shop by text message. An employee suggested it in October and it launched Nov. 6.

“Innovating for customers, doing it fast, working backwards from their needs, that’s really at our core,” Beth Galetti, Amazon’s senior vice president of people, experience and technology, told Forbes.

In its own blog post Thursday, Amazon highlighted everything from faster delivery and custom AI chips to warehouse robotics and higher pay for frontline workers.

The ranking comes after a year of workforce cuts at Amazon. The company eliminated about 30,000 corporate jobs in rounds announced in October 2025 and January 2026, including more than 4,500 in Washington state. Smaller cuts followed throughout the year, including layoffs of fewer than 1,000 corporate employees in October, mainly in its Stores unit.

#5371. AI found a critical flaw in Java that could let hackers hijack enterprise servers

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Oracle included a fix in its November update on Tuesday, and CISA urged organizations to patch immediately; Calif rated the flaw 9.2 out of 10

Security firm Calif disclosed a critical flaw in OpenJDK, the most popular Java runtime, that it says lets an attacker with no credentials overwrite memory and run code on a server. Oracle $ORCL included a fix for the flaw in its November Critical Security Patch Update, which it released Tuesday.

The flaw carries the identifier CVE-2026-114938 and the nickname Java4Shell. It sits in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder, which Calif said uses specialized x86-64 processor instructions to decode data faster. Calif said researcher Quang Luong found the bug in an hour using the AI tool Codex and built the first working exploit in two more hours. The total token cost was less than $200, the firm said.

Java4Shell affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer, Calif said. Distributions built from OpenJDK are also vulnerable, including Amazon $AMZN Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft $MSFT Build of OpenJDK and Oracle Java SE. The bug requires an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI support. ARM64 chips are not affected.

Calif said it demonstrated remote code execution without authentication in Keycloak, Atlassian $TEAM Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate. It showed execution that requires a login in Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. The firm said no single exploit works everywhere, and every target demands its own custom approach.

Calif published a proof of concept that triggers the memory corruption. It is not yet releasing product-specific exploits, in order to give users a window to upgrade.

Calif scored the flaw 9.2 on a 10-point scale under CVSS 4.0, calling it critical. Oracle's advisory scores it 8.1 under CVSS 3.1 and lists the attack complexity as high.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency urged organizations to patch immediately, starting with internet-facing systems. For those that cannot, the agency recommended restricting and validating Base64 input, enforcing input-size limits and limiting unauthenticated access. Calif recommends launching OpenJDK with the -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics option as a temporary measure, according to BleepingComputer.

There were no reports of the flaw being exploited in the wild by Tuesday evening, according to CyberScoop.

The Java disclosure follows an AI-assisted discovery of two bugs in PHP, software that runs an estimated 70% of all websites. Sites including 4chan, DeviantArt and the Internet Archive went offline for hours or days after a fix was released. Hackers made millions of attempts in the first day but largely failed because the flaws were difficult to exploit.

Calif said in its write-up that it also used AI to find and weaponize a flaw it calls PHP2Shell.

#5370. ‘The Romans are laughing at us’: physical AI founder raises $97 million in quest to stop wasting time with archaic infrastructure maintenance

Alex Hawkinson keeps a collection of Roman artifacts at BrightAI’s robot demo center, and he has a saying to go with them: “The Romans are laughing at us.”

Think of the way the Romans inspected their roads, Hawkinson told Fortune: “They sent teams of technicians out periodically on schedule” to check on their infrastructure. Two thousand years later, power companies, water utilities, and pipeline operators still do. In his telling, two out of three of those trips turn up nothing to fix, and the failures that matter happen in between visits anyway.

Hawkinson is convinced this can change, and investors are paying for the idea. BrightAI said Wednesday it has raised $97 million in a round led by Smith Point Capital, the growth-stage firm started by former Salesforce co-CEO Keith Block. GE Vernova, already a BrightAI customer, also invested, along with Cobalt Capital, Marlinspike Partners, Zero Infinity Partners as well as existing backers Khosla Ventures, Inspired Capital, and Upfront Ventures. The round brings total funding to $184 million and values BrightAI at $750 million, according to a person familiar with the matter. Hawkinson insisted he “doesn’t care” about so-called unicorn status: The point is bring infrastructure out of the ancient Roman era.

His pitch has three parts. Replace scheduled human inspections with sensors and AI that watch infrastructure all the time. Go after what BrightAI estimates is more than $7 trillion a year in waste worldwide. And along the way, create a kind of data that has never existed: a continuous record of how pipes, poles, and pumps actually wear out. If it works, the companies running the world’s power and water get to stop paying for trips that find nothing.

The Romans knew the problem well. Frontinus, who was named Rome’s water commissioner by the emperor Nerva in the late first century A.D., wrote a treatise on running the city’s aqueducts. He worried about leaks in underground channels that were hard to find and fix, about people tapping the lines without permission, and about trees whose roots could damage the masonry.

BrightAI’s release says the systems that power modern life “still operate on a centuries-old model: inspect, detect, and react.” Hawkinson is a believer from personal experience. In 2011, the power went out at his family’s cabin in Leadville, Colo., a remote mountain town, and nobody knew until the pipes had frozen and burst and water had run through the walls. He built a connected sensor hub in his garage, launched it on Kickstarter as SmartThings, and sold the company to Samsung in 2014. He has cofounded eight companies and run four as CEO, all of which exited. He bootstrapped BrightAI, founded in 2019, for its first four years.

He spent the first half of his career in software as a service, and his SmartThings put sensors in people’s homes, not substations or sewers.

“I wasn’t from infrastructure,” he said. When he started going out in the field, at one point in a hard hat in a sewer, he was “shocked” by how the systems everyone depends on are actually monitored and break down. In industry after industry, he asked frontline technicians how often they get sent out and find nothing to fix. The answer kept coming back at 50% to 70% of the time. BrightAI’s release puts it more conservatively, at more than half of scheduled inspections.

He assumed at first the operators were doing it wrong. He came to see it as an equilibrium. Send crews less often, and something breaks catastrophically, so you send them more often. Send them more often, and the labor, which is expensive and often dangerous, becomes unaffordable. Operators settle where “two out of every three times they send somebody out, even the most talented operators, it’s unnecessary,” he said, and failures still slip through between visits.

The wooden power pole is his favorite example. By his count, the U.S. has about 150 million of them, “little matchsticks sticking up,” and each one sees a human inspector roughly every eight to 10 years. The 2018 Camp Fire—California’s deadliest wildfire—killed 85 people after a worn hook on an aging PG&E transmission tower gave way. Cal Fire determined the utility’s lines caused it. Hawkinson’s point is that the hook was “completely invisible in the world” until it failed.

The $7 trillion figure is BrightAI’s own. The company says it surveyed 12,158 operators across 16 industries and put the addressable annual impact at more than $7.5 trillion. It also found 98% of those operators lack adequate visibility into their assets. It tallies the wasted trips, the labor, and the cost of letting things break, which he said is far more expensive to fix than to maintain. The outside research the release cites—from the Energy Department, the EPA, Swiss Re and the National Safety Council—puts the cost of infrastructure failure alone at $2.5 trillion a year.

The examples Hawkinson gives are mundane, which is part of his point. He cited one customer, a UK water utility that has about a thousand pumps and can’t tell which ones will be the next to fail. Its limited staff runs around “like chickens with their heads cut off” trying to catch them. When heavy rain hits, failed pumps send raw sewage into rivers.

Hawkinson said he’s a Lord of the Rings fan, and this breaks his heart, to see raw sewage being pumped into a landscape that looks “just like the Shire.” (This Fortune interviewer agreed, saying Hawkinson’s physical AI descriptions sound a bit like something Gandalf would get up to; Hawkinson laughed, but didn’t quite agree.)

Closer to home, a break in the Potomac Interceptor sewer line in January released an estimated 243 million gallons of untreated wastewater into the Potomac River, according to the Maryland Department of the Environment.

There’s also copious waste in replacing parts that are fine. Hawkinson described a customer COO who suspected his company was swapping out spark plugs in its machines too early, at a cost of tens of millions of dollars a year. Once BrightAI’s models had the sensor data, Hawkinson said, they found about half of the replacements were premature. The call depended on some 30 variables no technician would track.

BrightAI’s platform, Stateful, pairs edge sensors on poles, pipelines, compressors, and tanks with autonomous robots, drones and wearable AI copilots for field crews. The company says it runs at more than 50,000 locations and processes tens of trillions of sensor readings. Customers include GE Vernova, Reworld, Osmose Utilities Services, Azuria Water Solutions, Kodiak Gas Services, and Diamondback Energy. On average, Hawkinson said, customers see trouble coming 51 days before what would have been a catastrophic failure.

GE Vernova, whose equipment helps generate about one-quarter of the world’s electricity, wanted in. Hawkinson said BrightAI hadn’t planned to take money from strategic investors this round, but GE Vernova insisted. The release says it will use BrightAI across its Power, Wind, and Electrification businesses.

Most of the new money goes to taking the platform global. BrightAI says nearly 60% of its addressable market is outside North America, and it’s opening offices abroad after doubling its headcount in 2025. Hawkinson said bringing on a new customer used to take two to three years, and now takes less than six months.

The coming year, he said, is about going from “proven concept” to deployments at scale with the biggest utilities. Until then, most of America’s 150 million wooden poles will keep getting checked the Roman way, about once a decade.

Nick Lichtenberg is business editor and was formerly Fortune's executive editor of global news.

#5369. OfferUp co-founder sees ‘mini power plants’ in buildings full of EVs

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 2:41 pmNovember 12, 2026 at 2:41 pm

Nick Huzar co-founded Juicer Energy in 2023 to make electric vehicle charging more widespread and reliable. Now the Seattle-area startup is pursuing a broader goal: helping buildings manage rising electricity demand and costs.

Juicer installs and operates EV charging systems at apartment buildings, hotels and other properties. It is also developing battery systems to store electricity on-site and help manage the power needed for charging and other building uses.

The push comes as data centers and the growing use of electricity for transportation, heating and other needs put more pressure on the grid. Batteries can help balance supply and demand by storing energy when electricity is plentiful and releasing it when demand peaks. In some cases, they can reduce the need for costly grid upgrades or new power plants built to meet peak demand.

“We think there’s a big opportunity there,” Huzar said. He spoke at an event this week hosted by GeekWire and Bank of America at the Bellevue showroom of Ferrari of Seattle.

Other companies are similarly pairing EV charging with battery storage. Fellow Seattle startup Electric Era has deployed battery-backed fast chargers at retailers including Costco and convenience stores. ADS-TEC Energy and XCharge also sell fast-charging systems with integrated batteries.

Huzar, OfferUp’s co-founder and former CEO, sees an opportunity to make buildings more self-sufficient by combining hardware and energy-management software. He said Juicer has a project scheduled to come online in 2027 with 70 chargers in one building.

His longer-term vision also includes tapping the energy stored in vehicles connected to those buildings.

“Imagine you’re an apartment owner and you have 20 EVs, 40 EVs plugged in,” Huzar said. “That is a huge amount of power. Like you’re a mini power plant at that point.”

He described feeding excess electricity back to the grid as a possibility that remains years away. He also predicted that most businesses, apartments and homes would have on-site batteries within the next decade, in part because battery costs continue to fall.

Juicer started with EV charging, Huzar said, “but the more we’ve gotten into this, the more we realize that we actually can build an asset for buildings versus relying on the grid.”

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5368. Bitcoin Price Holds $64K Ahead of Nvidia Earnings: AI Bubble Finally Pops?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin price is struggling to find direction just below $65,000 as we brace for Nvidia earnings report. BTC USD has recovered from its weekend low near $62,000, but remains down 13% over seven days. Its modest rebound comes as technology stocks face yet another selling pressure.

This timing puts the Bitcoin price in an uncomfortable position. Nvidia’s results could determine if investors return to risk assets or abandon another crowded trade. With market sentiment still deep in extreme fear, we still have little conviction that the worst is over.

Meanwhile, Michael Burry is increasing his bearish bets against technology stocks. The investor made famous by The Big Short is targeting the Nasdaq-100 and semiconductor sector. His positioning raises an ugly question: Is the AI boom approaching its own dot-com moment?

Burry doubled his Nasdaq-100 put position on November 12, targeting early 2027 options 20% below the index’s market level. He also bought back part of his previously reduced bearish position in the VanEck Semiconductor ETF.

His argument goes beyond stretched stock valuations. Burry believes conventional accounting earnings can exaggerate technology companies’ underlying profitability. Depreciation schedules, particularly across expensive data-center infrastructure, sit at the center of his concerns.

Consider a hyperscaler investing billions in GPUs and AI infrastructure. Those purchases become capital assets rather than immediate operating expenses. Companies subsequently recognize depreciation across their estimated useful lives.

This accounting treatment can make current earnings look stronger than the underlying cash economics. If hardware becomes obsolete faster than expected, reported profitability could overstate actual investment returns.

The concern becomes significant when companies must continuously replace expensive accelerators. Their infrastructure spending needs to generate sufficient revenue before the equipment loses economic value.

Burry isn’t alone in questioning the investment cycle. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman previously acknowledged excessive enthusiasm surrounding artificial intelligence.

“Are we in a phase where investors as a whole are overexcited about AI? My opinion is yes,” Altman said.

Jeff Bezos offered another interpretation, describing the spending cycle as an “industrial bubble.” He argued that excessive investment could still produce valuable infrastructure, even when individual investors lose money.

Nvidia’s own Jensen Huang previously defended the industry’s economics. According to him, the AI infrastructure was already generating productive revenue, rather than merely attracting speculative capital.

The disagreement exposes the central tension surrounding the AI bubble. Demand can be genuine while valuations and infrastructure commitments become unsustainable.

The dot-com crash offers an important historical comparison. The Nasdaq Composite lost 78% between March 2000 and October 2002. Internet technology survived, but countless businesses and investors did not.

Today’s AI infrastructure market has similarities, particularly aggressive capital expenditure and expectations of exponential demand. However, established hyperscalers now finance much of the expansion through enormous operating businesses.

Now, can future AI revenue justify today’s investment?

Bitcoin once traded with relatively little correlation to traditional equities. That relationship changed dramatically as institutional participation expanded.

CME Group’s historical correlation research illustrates the shift. Between 2014 and 2016, Bitcoin’s correlation with the S&P 500 stood near -0.01. Its correlation with the Nasdaq-100 was effectively zero. Between 2020 and 2022, those correlations climbed to 0.40 and 0.42, respectively. They remained positive through April 2025, reaching 0.30 against both indices.

The shift matters because institutional investors increasingly treat Bitcoin as another liquid risk asset. Portfolio rebalancing, leveraged positions, and macroeconomic conditions can influence its price alongside technology stocks.

An AI sell-off could create another liquidity shock across crypto. Investors facing losses elsewhere might sell Bitcoin to raise cash or reduce overall exposure. But an AI correction doesn’t automatically invalidate Bitcoin’s monetary thesis. A technology valuation reset could eventually redirect capital toward alternative assets.

The gap lies between an isolated technology correction and a financial liquidity crisis. Bitcoin could eventually decouple from semiconductor stocks under the first scenario. The second could pressure both markets simultaneously. For now, Bitcoin price remains exposed to the same risk appetite driving technology shares.

Nvidia’s third-quarter fiscal 2027 results arrive at a particularly sensitive moment. Wall Street expects $109 billion in revenue and $2.47 in adjusted earnings per share.

Investors will focus heavily on Data Center revenue, gross margins, and forward guidance. The company’s Vera Rubin platform also faces scrutiny as customers expand their AI infrastructure commitments.

A headline earnings beat might not satisfy investors demanding another acceleration in growth. Strong revenue accompanied by cautious guidance could trigger another sell-the-news reaction.

The opposite scenario could restore confidence across technology stocks. Strong guidance would reinforce expectations that hyperscaler spending remains sustainable. Bitcoin could benefit if investors regain their appetite for speculative assets.

Technically, Bitcoin needs to stabilize above its recent $62,000 weekend low. A break below that level would expose the psychologically important $60,000 threshold.

A stronger recovery would put $68,000 back into view as an important technical resistance area. Reclaiming that level could help establish if buyers are returning.

Bitcoin price now faces a test extending beyond crypto markets. Nvidia must demonstrate that AI infrastructure spending can translate into durable earnings growth.

Burry is betting that expectations have run too far ahead. Huang’s former company built the infrastructure powering the AI revolution, but investors now need proof of its economic returns.

If the AI bubble starts deflating, Bitcoin must answer another question: Can it survive without Wall Street’s appetite for technology risk?
