#5367. Apple's outage hit 5 areas, from iCloud and Apple Pay to AppleCare and stores

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Apple blamed an internal update for its Nov. 17 outage. Here are 5 aspects, from cause and status to stores.

Most people expect a bank transfer, a flight check-in or a work email to go through without a second thought, and few notice how small a group of systems all of that depends on. That expectation kept breaking this month, when a major system somewhere ran into serious trouble every business day for four days running, according to CNBC, including the Thursday outage that cut Microsoft $MSFT Outlook users off from their mail. The trouble reached industries with little in common. The Associated Press reports that a technical problem at JPMorgan $JPM Chase spread to Zelle and to customers at several other banks, and that United Airlines' outage ran more than 90 minutes. When so much ordinary activity depends on so few systems, one breakdown can stop work that people never thought was connected to it.

A run of failures this close together makes it easy to assume someone is attacking these systems, but officials and companies keep finding no attacker. "This is not cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation state," Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC. Microsoft ruled out a cyberattack or AI agents as the cause of its own outage, according to The Associated Press. Clayton ties the wider run of outages to upgrades, with some upgraded systems and some handoffs between systems not working as expected afterward, ABC News reports, though the root cause of the FAA's router failure has not yet been determined. In Clayton's account, the trouble comes from upgrade work, which is supposed to improve systems. Naming a general trigger has not settled why one change can do so much damage, and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has asked for a congressional briefing, according to CNBC. For now, the explanation covers the run of outages in broad terms, while individual failures still lack one.

TIME set out to summarize the cause, the timeline and the affected services of Apple $AAPL's outage, which joined this run of failures. Apple's case is worth following because the trouble reached both Apple Pay and in-store purchases at Apple's own stores. The questions to carry through are what Apple's own change broke, how much of it is truly back and what remains unexplained.

Apple $AAPL blames its outage on a change it made to its own systems. Losing payments and cloud storage at the same moment can look like the work of an intruder, but the company says the trouble began with an internal update, according to TIME. ABC News reports that Apple gave the same explanation, which puts the start of the failure inside the company in Apple's own account. That account comes only from Apple, and the company has offered no detail on what the update changed or which part of its systems failed. A reader therefore knows where Apple says the trouble began, but not what went wrong. "Internal update" names a type of mistake. It does not diagnose this one.

An update by itself does not explain why so many Apple services failed at once. Liz Fong-Jones, a tech labour organiser, offers one place to look. "Part of the resilience of a system comes from people who are experienced with a system," Fong-Jones told ABC News. Her remark concerns systems in general, but it raises a fair question for Apple: how much experience did the people who made this change have with the systems they changed? Nothing on record connects Apple's failure to its staffing, so that question is a lead to pursue and not a finding about the company.

Until Apple says what its update changed, the cause of the outage remains a label rather than an explanation.

Apple $AAPL's outage counts as fixed only for the day as a whole, so a reader should treat the recovery as partial. TIME reports that the outage occurred on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, and was resolved by that evening. That resolution applies to the outage in general. The trouble began in the morning and ended by evening, but no exact times are on record, and nothing shows when any single service, such as a payment or a sign-in, came back. After an outage, most people need to know whether the thing they rely on works again. A reader whose payment still fails gains little from an all-clear for the day.

Apple itself claimed less than a full recovery. "Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning," Apple said in an emailed statement, as reported by the Associated Press. "Many" is not "all," and the company's own wording leaves the evening all-clear an open question. The rest of Apple's systems were still being brought online, with no timeline given. Apple offered no date for those services, and the evening resolution names none of them, so a reader cannot plan around the return of any specific one. The accurate label is "partly restored." A reader who still sees errors after Tuesday should not assume Apple's fix has reached every service.

Apple has said what set off the outage, but it has not said when each of its services came back.

On an iPhone, paying, emailing and saving a file feel like separate tasks, but this outage reached all of them. Apple $AAPL Pay was among the services affected, according to TIME. Email and stored files were hit too. iCloud went down along with iCloud Mail, which affected mail kept on an Apple account as well as the photos and files people store there. Moving to a laptop browser offered no way around the problem, because iCloud's web apps were down as well. The App Store was also among the affected services, so getting a new app or an update was not a reliable option either. Payments, mail, files and apps that people treat as separate tools all appeared on the same list of services the outage touched.

At least one security researcher sees disruptions such as this one as a sign that the technology industry has not yet grown up. "We're in the weird teenage phase of technology not quite maturing enough to know how to do this without disrupting services and so forth," Tom Hegel, research head at SentinelOne, told CNBC. Until companies can change their systems without disrupting services, people who run payments, mail and files through one account are accepting that all of them can fail on the same day. The practical step is modest. A physical card and a way to reach important email outside an Apple account let people pay and stay in touch when the phone's services are down.

The more of the day people run through a single account, the more of the day they lose when one update fails.

Apple $AAPL's own support service was caught up in the outage along with the products it exists to help fix. When an iPhone payment or an iCloud sign-in stops working, most customers turn to Apple for help. This time AppleCare, the company's support service, was among the services affected, according to TIME. The support channel that customers would normally rely on during a breakdown was itself part of the breakdown. A customer with a stalled device could not count on the usual first step to work normally on Tuesday. Apple has not said how badly AppleCare was affected or which parts of it failed, so the size of the gap in support remains unclear.

The failure also reached organizations, not only individual customers. Apple Business, a service named for companies, was among the affected services. The outage therefore became a problem for employers and the staff who use Apple's tools at work, not only for people trying to pay for coffee or open their email. Schools were caught in it too. Apple School Manager and SchoolWork, two tools named for schools, both appear among the affected services. Schools that use them depended on systems that failed alongside the consumer apps. Because the fault came from an update inside Apple, nothing a school's staff did on their own side could restore those tools.

Businesses and schools depend on Apple's systems but control no part of them, and a single change inside Apple reached them all the same.

During the outage, staff at some Apple $AAPL stores could not sell anything at the counter. In-store purchases were among the affected retail functions, according to TIME. NBC10 Philadelphia reports that store employees could not complete purchases after the internal software they use stopped working. The problem was not on a shopper's phone or in a customer app. It was in the tools Apple's own workers use to ring up a sale. Appointment scheduling failed too, and employees could not book customers for help, so the store could not serve as a place to get an iPhone or Mac looked at in person. Both of those failures happened behind the counter, on the staff side. Apple's internal systems, the ones its own employees work on, appear to have failed along with its public services, though no account confirms exactly which internal systems broke.

How widely the store trouble spread is unclear. Only some locations were affected, and nobody has given a count of the stores involved. The staff accounts came from employees who spoke to NBC News, according to NBC10 Philadelphia, and nothing on record shows that the same problems reached every store. The store problems show that the failure went deep into Apple's systems. They do not show that Apple's whole retail operation shut down.

During an outage like this one, a trip to an Apple store is not a reliable workaround, because the store counter runs on Apple's internal systems too.

#5366. ‘A huge pain in the ass’: Microsoft 365 starts to recover after a day of global email turmoil

by Todd Bishop on Nov 13, 2026 at 7:24 amNovember 13, 2026 at 4:23 pm

Updated at 4 p.m. PT Nov. 13 with additional Microsoft statements.

If emails sent by Outlook users on Thursday are just now landing in your inbox, no, you haven’t gone back to the days of the Pony Express. Microsoft is still digging out from a nearly daylong outage that cut off email for businesses, schools and governments around the world.

As of early Friday, the company reported that email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels,” though some users could still have trouble getting in or see delayed messages.

In a post on X Friday morning, Microsoft said it was “deeply sorry” for the disruption to customers and partners. The company said the outage was a technical issue, not related to a cyberattack or AI agents.

The problem was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade and surfaced after a more recent network change, the company said, adding that it has addressed the underlying issue and is still restoring service to remaining customers and regions.

We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services.This was a technical issue…

In an update on its status page at 5 a.m. Pacific, Microsoft said it was seeing “broader improvements now observed in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe,” along with early signs of recovery in Asia Pacific.

The problems started Thursday morning with Exchange Online, the Microsoft service that runs Outlook email for businesses, and spread to other Microsoft 365 services that depend on it, including Teams calendars, Copilot and SharePoint.

Microsoft said servers were failing automated health checks and dropping out of service, which overloaded the ones that were left. The company paused all deployments while it worked on a fix, and some of its repairs Thursday evening were “not taking as expected.” Microsoft said it restored service gradually, checking stability at each stage, which took longer but helped ensure a stable restoration.

Earlier, The Verge’s Tom Warren reported on X that his sources linked the outage to configuration changes in Azure Virtual Network, Microsoft’s cloud networking service.

Australia’s Home Affairs Minister, Tony Burke, told reporters in Sydney that Microsoft believes it is dealing with something similar in some ways to the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, “where there is an update that has gone awry,” the Associated Press reported.

“We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us,” said Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, in a statement provided to GeekWire. He said Microsoft’s teams are reviewing what happened and how to prevent similar problems.

In a post on X Friday afternoon, Lamanna said the investigation points to “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter,” which made recovery harder than normal. A thundering herd happens when large numbers of clients try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online.

He said Microsoft will publish a post-mortem “shortly” with a step-by-step timeline and the repairs it plans to make to avoid similar outages.

The outage reached well beyond email. Government offices in Japan, Singapore and the Philippines reported disruptions, according to the AP. Workhorse Group delayed its quarterly earnings call, and OpenAI and Anthropic both reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools.

Credit rating agency Morningstar DBRS estimated insured losses of $300 million to $500 million, well below estimates for CrowdStrike, which ranged from $400 million to $1.5 billion. Some cyber insurance policies cover only malicious attacks, the firm noted, though it said the toll could grow if the outage drags on for several days.

The disruption hit close to Microsoft’s home. Ansel Herz, a spokesperson for the Seattle mayor’s office, told the Seattle Times that the outage didn’t bring city government to a halt but knocked out the systems that move documents and messages around City Hall.

The newspaper quoted Herz calling the outage “a huge pain.” In a post on X, he chided the paper for not using his whole quote, which we presume was “a huge pain in the ass.”

We’ve followed up with him to confirm this important detail. Here’s hoping he gets the email.

Update, 10 a.m.: Herz did receive GeekWire’s message and responded, confirming the quote and saying that, to his knowledge, nothing public-facing was affected at the city. Email appears to be back and working properly as of Friday morning, he said.

#5365. 14 key facts about the DEFIANCE Act and Paris Hilton's push for it

Free daily briefing on global business news.

14 facts on the DEFIANCE Act, from the right to sue and damages to Paris Hilton's push and the House vote that has not happened.

Sexual deepfakes have stopped being an occasional celebrity scandal and become something people produce in bulk. The number of nonconsensual deepfake porn videos online has grown ninefold since 2019, according to one researcher's count reported by the Senate Judiciary Committee. The volume has since moved well past the figures in the policy debate. At least 1.8 million explicit images were shared through the Grok chatbot in just nine days, according to a New York Times analysis reported by ABC News. For a victim, the problem is no longer a single image to report and remove but an unknown number of copies spread across the internet. Few people defend the practice. In a poll published in 2024, 84% of respondents told the Artificial Intelligence Policy Institute that deepfake porn should be illegal, according to TIME. The harm itself is not in dispute.

That broad agreement has not given victims a federal way to go after the person behind an image themselves. The argument in Washington is over which tool fits the harm. Prosecutors could bring criminal charges, platforms could be forced to take images down, or victims could file lawsuits that they control. The DEFIANCE Act would supply the third option, and even it would have a hard edge. The bill would apply in the United States only, according to ABC News. A creator working from another country would fall outside its remedy. Because of that limit, the real test of each provision is what it can do for a victim and what it cannot.

Congress.gov set out to outline what the DEFIANCE Act does and why Paris Hilton backs it, weighing the bill's mechanics alongside its most visible champion, from suing under a pseudonym to the time victims would have to bring a case and the end of the "it's only a fake" defense. Every one of those protections is conditional. The bill has passed the Senate, but the House has not voted, so none of these rights exists yet for anyone harmed by a sexual deepfake. Two questions remain for each provision: whether it fills a gap that existing law leaves open, and whether a lawsuit would work against creators who are anonymous or hard to find.

The DEFIANCE Act would let the person shown in a sexual deepfake decide whether a case goes forward. Under the bill, someone depicted in such an image could file a civil suit in federal court against whoever made or spread it, according to Congress.gov. Rep. Joe Morelle's separate federal proposal, the Preventing Deepfakes of Intimate Images Act, was a criminal bill, according to TIME. Under a criminal law, prosecutors decide which cases to bring. Under DEFIANCE, a victim would not have to wait for her case to become a prosecutor's priority before someone answers for the harm. The bill would also cover more people than the one who made the image. A person who shares or publishes a deepfake made by someone else could be sued, and passing an image along would carry its own legal risk. Anyone who solicits a deepfake could be sued as well, which reaches the person who commissions an image before it exists. A threat to distribute one would be grounds for a suit on its own. A victim facing blackmail could go to court before the image ever spreads.

A victim who wins a DEFIANCE Act case could leave court with more than a check, because a judge could also order the images taken offline and make the defendant cover her legal costs, according to CNBC. Those two remedies address a victim's most practical needs: getting the image down and not paying for the fight herself. The bill would also let a victim seek punitive damages, an award that goes beyond repaying what she lost. Those damages penalize the person who made or spread the image. For the bill's best-known advocate, that penalty is the point. "People need to know that there's going to be consequences for their actions," said Paris Hilton, chief advocacy officer at Loti AI. Backers want the money to deter the next creator as well as to compensate the person depicted.

The DEFIANCE Act cleared the Senate without a single dissent, and the House has yet to vote on it. The Senate passed the bill unanimously on Jan. 13, 2026, according to Congress.gov, with no senator willing to stand against it. The bill has stalled in the House since then. "For 10 months, this critical legislation has sat untouched in the House, just waiting to be put on the floor," Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a Democrat from New York, said, as reported by Parade. Until the House acts, none of the new protections in the bill is available to victims.

Congress has stalled on this bill before, and earlier versions of it never got through the House. The Senate passed one of those versions unanimously in 2024, according to , and senators passed the bill again in 2026. Each new round of Senate support shows the same agreement again without bringing the bill any closer to law.

For Paris Hilton, the bill's best-known champion, sexual deepfakes are a flood of images rather than a single fake to report and remove. Loti AI has removed more than 60,000 deepfakes of her, according to Hilton's figures reported by Congress.gov. Removals on that scale are far beyond what any one person could manage alone. No one has said how many remain online, so even a cleanup effort that large has no clear finish line. The removal count deserves some caution, because Hilton is chief advocacy officer at Loti AI and has a stake in how the company's work is seen. Takedowns deal with the images, not with the people who make them. A right to sue is meant to reach those people.

Sexual deepfakes also target women who hold public power, including women in Congress. Research by Hilton's team, as she described it, counted 83 women with sexual deepfakes of themselves online among the 156 women serving in the 119th Congress. No independent count has confirmed that finding. If it holds, a majority of the women in Congress have been targeted by the same kind of image the bill addresses. The harm would then reach inside the institution weighing the bill, not only celebrities and private citizens.

If the DEFIANCE Act becomes law, the Senate's version is the likeliest text to carry it, because it has already passed one chamber. The Senate passed S. 1837 on Jan. 13, 2026, and the House has yet to act on it, according to Congress.gov. Its sponsor is Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., who serves as Senate Democratic Whip and Judiciary Committee Ranking Member, according to the Senate Judiciary Committee. A whip's job is to count votes, and Durbin used that position to move the bill through the Senate. He also had a partner in Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham as co-lead, so senators took up the bill as a measure from both parties rather than one.

The DEFIANCE Act would not add a new law to the federal books. Congress would instead rewrite one that already exists. Under the bill, the changes would go into 15 U.S.C. 6851, an existing section of the U.S. Code, and would extend it to cover what the bill calls "intimate digital forgeries," according to Congress.gov. With that language, the statute would name sexual deepfakes outright. A victim would then bring her claim under a section of federal law that already deals with intimate images rather than under a statute written from nothing.

The statute Congress would amend is recent. Congress enacted it as Section 1309 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2022, a large spending package, and the DEFIANCE Act amends that section rather than replacing it with a separate law. Congress is being asked to broaden a remedy it has already enacted, not to design one from the start. That shapes the decision in front of the House. Members would not be debating whether federal law should address intimate-image abuse at all, because the 2022 law already exists. They would be deciding whether that remedy should name forged images explicitly. For victims, the change would place a deepfake claim inside a section of law that has been on the books since 2022, not in an untested new statute.

A single fixed award cannot fit every case of deepfake abuse, and the DEFIANCE Act would let victims seek other kinds of compensation as well. A winning victim could recover actual losses and the defendant's profits and could ask a court to order the images removed, according to Congress.gov. Under that remedy, a person who makes these images to sell could be ordered to hand over what the sales earned and would be left with nothing to show for the work. The removal order addresses the rest of the harm. A payment alone would leave the image online, where people could keep finding it and the injury to the victim would continue.

Courts could also punish a defendant on top of repaying the victim. Punitive damages are among the remedies, which means the law would treat a sexual deepfake as wrongdoing to deter rather than as a debt to settle. The cost of the case would not stay with the victim, either. A right to sue means little to someone who would spend more on the lawsuit than a win would return. A victim who prevailed could make the defendant cover her lawyer's bill and the expenses of bringing the case, so her own savings would not pay for holding someone to account.

A federal claim would give victims the same standing in every state. In January 2024, only ten states had criminal laws against nonconsensual deepfakes, and Morelle's criminal bill had seen no action since its introduction, according to TIME. A civil suit in federal court would not depend on where a victim lives or on what her state legislature has passed. The bill's backers present it as a right that belongs to the victim, not as a crackdown run by the government. "Innocent people have a right to defend their reputations and hold perpetrators accountable in court," Sen. Josh Hawley, one of four lawmakers who introduced the bill, said.

A lawsuit can make a person pay, but it cannot by itself remove an image from the internet. A victim could win her case and still find the picture online. Keeping deepfakes off social media will take a commitment of resources from the companies that run those sites, and legislation alone will not do it, according to comments by Nina Brown, a Syracuse University professor of media law and technology, reported by TIME. The bill would give a victim leverage over the person behind an image, but not over the sites that host it.

That leaves an open question: whether a victim can identify and reach the person she needs to sue.

The bill also puts a dollar figure on a win. Damages under the DEFIANCE Act would start at $150,000, according to Bloomberg Law figures reported by Congress.gov. A victim and her lawyer would have that figure in hand when deciding whether a case is worth the time and the exposure of going to court. Taken together, the remedies would make a deepfake expensive for whoever made or spread it, from the removal order through the punitive award.

The bill pairs a way to get the image offline with a real cost for the person behind it.

Under the DEFIANCE Act, a victim of a sexual deepfake would have 10 years to sue, according to Congress.gov and the University of Cincinnati Law Review. That period would not begin on the day someone first posted the image. Under the bill, it would start on whichever comes later: the day the victim discovers the image or the day she turns 18. A deepfake that appears long before its subject learns of it would still be grounds for a lawsuit when she finally finds it.

The two starting points protect two groups of victims. A person depicted as a child would not lose any of her time to sue while she was still a minor. Her period would begin at adulthood, so she could decide for herself, as an adult, whether to go to court. A person who finds an image years after it surfaced would keep the full period from the moment she learns of it. That matters for a harm that spreads through copies a victim may never see until a friend, an employer or a search result turns one up. Under a deadline tied to the first posting, those victims could lose their right to sue before they knew they had a case.

The 10 years would also give a victim room to find a lawyer, gather evidence and weigh whether to go forward. She would not have to make that choice in the first weeks after a painful discovery.

A victim who learns of a deepfake late would not, under this bill, find that she had also learned of it too late.

The holdup does not run along party lines. The bill has bipartisan support, and its House cosponsors include Rep. Laurel Lee, a Republican from Florida, alongside Ocasio-Cortez, according to Parade. Advocates have therefore turned from winning votes to winning a place on the House schedule. The bill does not need more supporters. It needs House leaders to bring it to the floor.

Until they do, the Senate's unanimous support remains a promise to deepfake victims rather than a right they can use.

Paris Hilton argues for the DEFIANCE Act as a victim first and a spokesperson second. An intimate video of Hilton leaked in 2003, when she was 19, according to Congress.gov. Hilton says that the law offered her no protection then and that the harm had no name. A lawsuit she could file on her own behalf is exactly what she lacked at 19, and it is what this bill would create.

The 2003 leak explains how Hilton came to the cause, but the harm behind her advocacy is happening now and keeps growing. Over 100,000 explicit AI deepfake images of her exist, according to Hilton's own count reported by ABC News, and no one has checked that figure independently. Each new image brings the harm back. Hilton said that "each time a new one appears, that horrible feeling returns, that fear that someone somewhere is looking at it right now and thinking it's real." Her injury comes from what a stranger might believe about each image as well as from the image itself, so it returns with every new copy. That makes her a victim whose case is still open, not a survivor recalling an old scandal.

Hilton has pressed the issue in Washington before. ABC News reports that in 2022 she took her case to officials at the White House under President Joe Biden. She also holds the title of chief advocacy officer at Loti AI. Her return to Washington years after that meeting makes her case harder for lawmakers to dismiss as a publicity stop.

For Hilton, the bill is about the next new image as much as the video that leaked in 2003.

The bill's backers are not asking Congress to imagine a harm that, by Hilton's count, has already reached many of its own members.

A victim of a sexual deepfake can already see an abuser charged with a crime and can make a platform remove the image. She has no federal right to take the creator to court herself. Victims have lived with that gap since the TAKE IT DOWN Act became law in May 2025, according to the NYU Annual Survey of American Law. That law makes publishing intimate depictions, including sexual deepfakes, a crime, but it gives victims no civil cause of action. Prosecutors and platforms hold the controls under the existing law. The DEFIANCE Act would give victims a civil suit of their own, according to Congress.gov. That makes the bill a companion to TAKE IT DOWN rather than a rival, and the case for it rests on what the first law leaves undone.

A takedown moves quickly once a platform learns of an image, but the clock does not start before then. Under TAKE IT DOWN, platforms face a 48-hour takedown requirement that begins when they are notified, the NYU Annual Survey of American Law reports, and someone has to find a copy and report it first. Each removal erases one copy and costs the person who made it nothing. Under the DEFIANCE Act, the defendants would be the creators and distributors of an image. Sites that host the images keep broad protection for what their users post under Section 230, at 47 U.S.C. § 230, so the bill aims at the people behind an image rather than the sites that carry it.

A right to sue gives victims an option, not a fix for every case. Many victims want the image gone and nothing more, and many would rather stay away from police and courtrooms altogether, according to comments by Carrie Goldberg, an attorney and image-based abuse expert at the firm C.A. Goldberg, reported by the NYU Annual Survey of American Law. Victims are best served by having both laws. A takedown serves the victim who wants the image gone, and a suit would serve the victim who wants its maker held to account.

Federal law already offers removal, and the DEFIANCE Act would let a victim go after the person who made the image.

The Senate's unanimous vote means that no senator tried to stop the bill, which is a narrower kind of support than the word "unanimous" suggests. The Senate Judiciary Committee reports that no senator objected to its passage. That result shows that no senator was willing to oppose the bill openly. It does not show how hard any senator would work to see it through. For a victim waiting on the right to sue, the clean Senate result signals goodwill but guarantees nothing.

Durbin treated the Senate win as half the job. "Now, let's pass this in the House and make it the law of the land," Durbin said, as reported by the Senate Judiciary Committee. The senator who carried the bill through his own chamber knows that the vote there does nothing for victims until the House votes too.

That leaves the bill's fate with the House, the chamber that has not yet voted.

Victims cannot use the rights in the DEFIANCE Act unless the House passes a bill of its own, and House members have already introduced one. The House version of the DEFIANCE Act carries the number H.R. 3562, according to Congress.gov, which gives readers a specific bill to follow. As a companion bill, it asks House members to take up the same protections the Senate bill contains rather than write a new approach to sexual deepfakes. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., is one of its two leaders. Rep. Laurel Lee, R-Fla., leads it with her, so a lawmaker from each party has put her name at the top of the House bill.

That pairing means neither party in the House can treat a deepfake victim's right to sue as the other side's cause. A lead sponsor from each party still sets no date for a floor vote, though. Lawmakers can introduce a bill and stand behind it for months without the House ever taking it up. Backing for H.R. 3562 is already in place, and the decision to bring it to a vote has not been made. Until the House makes that decision, the federal right to sue over a sexual deepfake that the DEFIANCE Act would create remains out of reach for victims.

For anyone waiting on that right, H.R. 3562 is now the bill to watch.

Until the House passes the change, the 2022 statute stays as written, without the words "intimate digital forgeries."

A sexual deepfake usually damages a victim's reputation, safety and peace of mind, and that kind of harm rarely shows up on a pay stub or a medical bill. Under the DEFIANCE Act, a victim would not have to prove any financial loss to seek damages of $150,000, according to Congress.gov. The harm would count even when it cost her nothing she could measure. A woman who kept her job and lost no income but still has to live with the image would have a claim worth bringing. If damages depended on proven losses, she would have had little to claim.

That sum works as a limit on the standard award, and the difference matters to anyone weighing a lawsuit. The University of Cincinnati Law Review describes $150,000 as the cap for standard liquidated damages, so a court could award that much but not more in an ordinary case. A victim should treat the figure as the most the basic award offers, not as a set check she can expect to collect.

A court could award more when the image is part of a wider campaign against a victim. When a deepfake is connected to stalking, harassment or a sexual assault, the cap rises to $250,000, according to the University of Cincinnati Law Review. The higher limit depends on danger to the victim, not on how far the image spread. The victims facing the most physical risk could recover the most.

Any award is a judgment against a person, and many creators of sexual deepfakes post from anonymous accounts that are hard to trace. Kennedy Aikey, an associate member of the University of Cincinnati Law Review, argues that the bill needs added tools, such as provenance metadata and identity checks on high-risk AI tools, to put the remedy within reach. "Without such measures, the civil remedies promised by the DEFIANCE Act may remain largely symbolic, offering recognition of harm without a realistic path to justice," Aikey wrote. A victim would no longer have to prove loss, but she would still have to find the defendant.

Whether she can name the person to sue matters more than the size of the award, and these dollar limits do nothing to answer that question.

Instead of one sum for everyone, a court could match the award to what a particular victim lost and what a particular defendant gained.

Under the DEFIANCE Act, calling a sexual deepfake fake would not protect the person who made it. The easiest defense open to a maker is to admit the image isn't real and argue that nobody is harmed when nobody is fooled. The bill rejects that argument: a disclaimer saying the image is fake would not make it lawful, according to Congress.gov. A maker who stamped a label on the picture would face the same lawsuit as one who passed it off as genuine. The injury, in practice, becomes the sexual depiction of a real person without consent, and whether a viewer believes the image is real would not decide the case.

For a victim, the rule removes a fight before it starts. She would not have to prove that anyone mistook the image for a real photograph, and that proof would be hard to supply when the image is openly labeled as fake. The rule also takes away an easy workaround for anyone who would otherwise caption an image "parody" or "AI-generated" and keep sharing it. Under the bill, that caption would offer no legal cover. A victim's case would turn on what the image shows and on whether she agreed to it, not on how a stranger might read it.

A maker's honesty about the forgery would earn no protection under the bill, and only the victim's consent would.

The protection covers only the person who brings the suit. It keeps the plaintiff's identity private, and it says nothing about the identity of the person who made or shared the image. A victim who files under a pseudonym would still have to name a defendant, and many creators of sexual deepfakes post through anonymous accounts. The pseudonym provision gives a victim no help in learning who that person is.

Under the bill, a victim could keep her own name out of the case, but the person who harmed her could stay unnamed as well.

#5364. I’ve coached the world’s most marketable athlete for 8 years. New CEOs should copy how her team handles expert advice

There are a lot of new CEOs coming into the market right now. Challenger, Gray & Christmas counted 1,337 CEO exits in the first nine months of this year, including 111 in September. On September 1, John Ternus took over at Apple, with Tim Cook staying on as executive chairman.

When someone takes over a new leadership role, they’re getting a ton of advice. Even the good advice is often too much. “This is what worked really well for us.” “This has been a problem this whole time.” It comes from staff members and even the former CEO.

It’s from the experience and knowledge of all these other people, which is fantastic. But the problem I see is it’s an overdose. You start to lose touch with your own instincts, your own gut. And when you must make the tough decisions your gut already knows, you hesitate.

For the past eight years, I have coached Aryna Sabalenka, a multiple Grand Slam champion who has spent more than 100 weeks at world No. 1. She was just named the most marketable athlete in the world, out of all sports. You can imagine how many people are approaching us these days.

Anton Dubrov is her tennis coach. I am her performance coach. A big part of our job is filtering. Whether we’re speaking with specialists, agents or Aryna directly, we’re constantly filtering what’s getting through and who has the access.

In 2022, her serve was falling apart. She finished that year with 428 double faults, more than anyone else on the tour. In San Jose, she lost the same way, frustrated and crying, talking about how we’d done everything. I remember telling her, “We have done everything except the one thing you’re most afraid of”: addressing her serve. What started as a technical issue had become a massive mental barrier.

So we brought in a specialist, a biomechanist. This guy was amazing. The challenge is that when you bring in someone who’s highly specialized, they can find 20 different things to fix. That’s when advice becomes noise and interference.

He wanted to address the rhythm and timing of her acceleration and where she produced it. Her foot placement, her rotation, where and when she loaded her legs, her toss, her general movement quality. Then he wanted to get into her forehand too. All valid points, and way too much at once.

There’s another thing you have to manage. When someone is given an opportunity like that, it’s natural for them to want to find problems they can fix, or to show how much they know. That’s a common human response, and it adds to the noise.

Nothing in a serve works in isolation. So Anton and I sat down with him and worked out which one or two things would influence everything else. We picked two. The first was her left arm, and the direction it was driving down after her toss. The second was the motion of her right arm and the way her right wrist turned over through contact. Improve those two, and much of the rest would self-correct. Everything else on his list, we held back.

Then we decided who would deliver it, and when. He coached her only at specific practices, and only at specific moments within those practices, with Anton always right there with him. Some weeks he traveled with us, same setup. The rest of the time, Anton delivered the message, with me alongside as an outside eye. Anton and I drove the when, the where and the what.

My job was making sure she had the right amount of coaching and enough time to make it her own, and doing the movement training so she could physically do the work. She is the one performing, so it has to match her personality and her style. She can’t just copy and paste someone else’s ideas.

Aryna heard one clear, consistent message, no matter who was delivering it. That built trust that we were on the right track. If we had allowed him to come in and just give tons of advice, she would have started overanalyzing, lost touch with herself and stopped acting. It would have gotten worse.

Instead, a few months later, she won her first Grand Slam at the Australian Open, and she has been consistently dominating the tour ever since.

I see a lot of CEOs run into the same thing. They’re getting a ton of amazing advice, and they lose themselves in all this information. The noise starts to become interference.

The person bringing you advice brings their nerves and their history along with it. Earlier in Aryna’s career, people on the team brought a lot of anxiety into this space. My job was to stand with Anton and step in between her and that noise. Sometimes it meant asking people to leave the team, or at least leave that room. For a new CEO, that urgency can come from your board, or from old team members still emotionally attached to the old plans.

All this advice can also become a hiding place. More meetings, another deck. Leaders feel like they’re being responsible, but their gut knows there are decisions they’re hiding from.

When I was 13, I was homeless. One of the places that helped me get off the streets and become the person I am today was a dojo, a martial arts school stuck between an adult bookstore and a pawnshop.

The sensei, Jan Sunderlin, used to tell me something I didn’t fully grasp until recent years: “Through loyalty you gain trust. With trust comes freedom. To maintain that freedom, remain loyal.”

I see loyalty as having many layers, and the first layer is loyalty to yourself, to your own code and your gut. That’s what got you this job in the first place. When you have that in place, people around you feel that stability way before you must go out and prove it. This is where real trust comes from. And that trust buys you the freedom to lead the way you need to lead.

Of course the person who got you there needs to grow into the person who keeps you there. But if you let every piece of advice in, it’s going to dilute your code. And when pressure hits, you will hesitate and make decisions that aren’t truly yours.

Before your first big meeting, take a piece of paper and write down who you are. What are the values you hold, even if it’s going to cost you? Write down the one or two things you want to achieve your quarter, then your first year.

Then write down whose voice you’re going to trust to filter the advice coming from all angles, the way Anton and I do for Aryna. That might be a chief of staff, a COO or one board member. If the former CEO is still in the building, agree early on how their advice will reach you.

Every time you get a piece of advice, hold it up against that page and ask yourself: Does this make me more aligned with who I am at my best, or is this advice going to direct me to become someone I’m not?

Early days with Aryna’s team, Anton and I used to share hotel rooms and look for the cheapest flights. There was nobody lining up to give her advice on anything. Now everybody is coming knocking on the door, and the job has not changed. It’s still to protect the person who must perform.

Now that’s your job, but the person you’re protecting is you.

We don’t rise to the occasion. We fall back to the level of our code.

In your first 90 days, make sure that code is still yours.

Jason Stacy is a high-performance coach and keynote speaker who has coached Aryna Sabalenka since 2018. He is the author of The Pressure Code: How Elite Performers Align Their Energy, Emotions, and Environment, with a foreword by Sabalenka. Stacy owns The Coaching Sweet Spot LLC, a performance coaching and speaking business that works with leaders, coaches and athletes. He is also a paid brand ambassador and event speaker for IM8, and is paid in shares of its parent company, Prenetics; Sabalenka is an investor in and ambassador for IM8.

#5363. Uncommon Thinkers: Alexis Harroun aims for space with a new engine — and stays grounded

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 13, 2026 at 7:46 amNovember 17, 2026 at 7:48 am

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

A few weeks after learning that her tiny startup had won a NASA prize to fly its engine in space, Alexis Harroun was camping in Yellowstone, sitting around a fire and looking up at the stars. Satellites kept drifting past overhead — and the news finally sank in.

“I’m like, oh, we’re going to be sending something up and we’re going to be able to see it,” she said. “That was very humbling in a lot of ways and very exciting.”

Harroun is co-founder and CEO of Juno Propulsion, a Tukwila, Wash.-based startup building a new kind of rocket engine. Instead of a steady flame, Juno’s engines use detonation, a supersonic combustion wave that releases more energy from the same amount of propellant.

“It’s essentially like a higher MPG rocket engine,” Harroun said.

The technology has been studied for decades but has never flown in orbit. Juno aims to change that next year, when its engine is set to fly aboard a Momentus satellite in a mission called Project Iris.

That’s a big goal for a company that, when the July 2025 NASA call came, was just Harroun, co-founder and CTO Ari Martinez and a summer intern working out of a one-room office.

If Iris succeeds, Juno’s engines could let satellites run on non-toxic propellants and maneuver far more freely in orbit, something both commercial and defense customers increasingly want. For Harroun, who earned her Ph.D. studying these engines, it would be the payoff of years of work.

Harroun sees the technology as a long-overdue leap. The basic physics behind today’s rocket engines dates to the 1930s and has been refined about as far as it can go, she said, calling it a constraint that’s “been a glass ceiling for too long, in my opinion.”

Harroun grew up south of Seattle in Federal Way. She didn’t come from an aerospace family or spend her childhood dreaming about space. Her dad was a physician and her mom a flight attendant and flight instructor.

What she did pick up at home was an entrepreneurial streak. Her dad ran his own practice for about 20 years, and her mom is now a real estate agent. Harroun said watching them make “something out of completely nothing” has shaped her own path, especially in building Juno.

She calls herself a “late bloomer” who fell for engineering as she was finishing high school and heading to the University of Washington. Sci-fi became an inspiration along the way, and it’s now one of her favorite genres.

She spent all four years at UW working with professor Carl Knowlen, who leads the Aeronautics & Astronautics Department’s Detonation Engines Lab, and she joined the student rocketry team, eventually leading its propulsion group.

Knowlen “sees the potential in everyone,” Harroun said, and the two built a strong relationship that’s still going. Juno’s $1.2 million National Science Foundation grant, awarded this summer, is a partnership with his research group.

Knowlen was also the faculty adviser for the student rocketry team, where he spent “many hot, and sometimes rainy, days” with Harroun and her teammates, test-firing motors and launching high-powered rockets.

“She always was level-headed and led by example,” Knowlen said. “No one worked harder than her to see these tests and launches go off as planned.”

He called her “an exceptional student, natural leader, creative thinker, and very independent,” and said it’s been a great satisfaction to see the engineer she has become.

During college, Harroun interned at NASA, Boeing and Blue Origin. That first stint at Blue Origin, in 2016, set her next move.

“I realized that everyone who had the job that I wanted had gone to Purdue,” she said.

She spent the next six years at Purdue University in West Lafayette, Ind., earning a master’s degree and a Ph.D. Her doctoral research was on the technology Juno is now building. She also met Martinez there. The two shared an office for years.

Harroun never planned to stay in academia.

“That just didn’t feel like my calling,” she said. “I wanted to use that very unique experience to get the technical chops to do the type of engineering that I wanted to do.”

Her doctoral advisor, Purdue professor Stephen Heister, still advises her and the company.

“He was one of the people who really pushed me to think about starting this company,” Harroun said. “I think he saw the potential that I had as a founder, both from a technical and a leadership perspective.”

Heister recalled their first technical discussion, when Harroun arrived as a new master’s student. He went deep on nozzle flows, her thesis topic, and the complications of building a nozzle for a detonation engine.

“At the end of my diatribe, she sat quietly and said, ‘You’ve given me a lot to think about,’” Heister said. “I can’t think of any other 22-year-old student with such a response but I knew she was indeed a special talent.”

He described Harroun as having “the unique ability to think deeply and at length,” and said it’s “terribly gratifying” to watch her commercialize the technology she worked on as a grad student.

After finishing her Ph.D. in 2023, Harroun came back to the Seattle region and started Juno. She knew the territory: her UW lab work and the rocketry team had put her in touch with local industry, and Juno now works with some of the same companies she did as a student.

Interning at Blue Origin was the first time she could say “there’s literally a rocket company in our backyard,” Harroun said. Its presence helped build a regional talent pool, which she described as “a contingent of rocket scientists that just live here.”

Starting a company comes with many unknowns, and coming home crossed one off the list.

“I knew how to go start doing stuff immediately,” she said. “So it made that calculus really easy.”

Harroun’s ambitions reach well beyond one demo flight.

“Our mission is to be the rocket engine provider for the U.S.,” she said. “Think of a Rocketdyne.”

That company built engines for the Saturn V and the space shuttle, and it’s now part of L3Harris. Juno wants to play a similar role with a new technology. It’s starting with in-space propulsion for satellites and plans to expand into engines for upper stages, orbital transfer vehicles and, eventually, the boosters that lift rockets off the pad.

The first step is Project Iris. NASA paid Juno about $500,000 through its TechLeap program to build the payload, and it’s also covering the Momentus spacecraft and the flight. There’s no paying customer yet, but the mission is designed to mimic the maneuvers a real satellite would make.

Japan’s space agency has flown rotating detonation engines on suborbital research rockets, but going to orbit is “a whole ‘nother game,” Harroun said. “Going to space is hard. I can attest to that.”

Building a company has taught Harroun things her Ph.D. didn’t. Handling toxic propellants is so complicated, she learned, that operators can spend more fueling a satellite than on “the propulsion system itself, which is kind of crazy.”

The bigger draw is mobility. For decades, satellites have mostly stayed in the orbit a rocket left them in, she said, and “that’s not really acceptable anymore in today’s world.”

To get there, Juno has raised a $1.4 million pre-seed round led by SOSV, on top of its NASA and NSF awards.

As for going to space herself, Harroun admits it would be hard to say no if she got the opportunity.

But the avid hiker and backpacker is partial to terra firma. Her best-case future is one where Earth is the place humanity gets to enjoy and space is what makes that possible.

“I don’t know that I would be the traveler,” Harroun said, “but I’d definitely like to be the enabler.”

#5362. Bristol Myers Squibb CEO says America’s edge in new drugs is ‘not a birthright’ as the U.S. loses its measles elimination status

On the day the U.S. officially lost its measles-elimination status, Bristol Myers Squibb CEO Chris Boerner had a warning for the country that went beyond one virus.

“It’s a reminder,” Boerner said Tuesday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, after Fortune’s Diane Brady opened their conversation with the news. The U.S. leads the world in new medicines, he said: 90% of them launch here, often two to three years before other rich countries get them. “That’s a real benefit that we have, but it’s not a birthright.”

On Tuesday, the Pan American Health Organization said the U.S. no longer meets the standard it first cleared in 2000: no single chain of measles transmission lasting 12 months or longer. The CDC has counted more than 5,400 cases so far in 2026, after 2,289 last year, many of them in outbreaks that began in close-knit Mennonite communities and spread, CBS News reported. Mexico and Bolivia lost their status too. Canada lost its status last year.

The numbers behind the decision have been building. In the 2025–26 school year, 92.4% of U.S. kindergartners had their MMR shots, CDC data show. That was down from 95.2% before the pandemic and under the 95% that epidemiologists say measles herd immunity requires. Exemptions hit a record 4.2%.

Boerner didn’t name Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. or any specific policy. He did spell out what he thinks keeps the U.S. ahead: a public-private partnership built around the NIH, a deep biotech scene, access to capital, drugmakers that work from discovery to sale, and “an FDA that’s the sort of global standard.” Under all of it, he said, sits “a respect for science.”

“Whenever you undermine any piece of that ecosystem, it impacts the whole,” he said. “If we want to continue to benefit from advanced therapies, including some of the world’s best vaccines, I think we need to be mindful of improving that ecosystem and being very careful about policies that don’t.”

Pressed on how he felt personally, he called it “clearly troubling.”

His restraint stands out against his peers. Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla told investors last December that “science is replaced with political beliefs” at HHS, BioSpace reported. At Davos in January, asked what stands in the way of a better vaccine conversation, Bourla answered: “The Secretary of Health.”

In December 2025, Bristol Myers was one of nine drugmakers to sign most-favored-nation pricing deals with the White House. On Tuesday, Boerner credited the president with getting one big thing “absolutely” right, which is that other countries “are not paying their fair share.” He pointed to the U.K.’s pledge, in its pharmaceutical trade deal with the U.S., to double its spending on innovative medicines over about a decade.

The CDC, for its part, played down the designation. “The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said in a statement Tuesday, pointing to $100 million the agency has sent to state and local health departments.

On cost, Boerner went straight at the system around his industry. Medicines are about 10% to 15% of U.S. health spending and have been for a decade, he said, so “we got to bring the other 85% to the table.” Roughly 50 cents of every dollar spent on a branded drug goes to someone who had nothing to do with discovering or developing it. “That screams inefficiency,” he said, borrowing the president’s word, “middlemen.” He said BMS runs assistance programs for uninsured and underinsured patients that it is “prohibited by statute” from offering to people on Medicare. “That’s unacceptable. We should fix that.” He also said he’d happily be paid more when a drug works and less when it doesn’t. U.S. rules make those deals hard, so BMS does far more of them abroad.

Inside the company, he’s rebuilding how drugs get made. Last week BMS said it will fold research and development into a single organization under chief medical officer Cristian Massacesi starting Jan. 1. Chief research officer Robert Plenge will leave after an advisory stint through March. The traditional boundaries between research and development “are collapsing,” Boerner said in the announcement. AI is part of the reason. He told Brady the technology lets BMS run in parallel work that used to happen in sequence. The company has committed to cutting the time from a drug entering the clinic to approval by 30%. Boerner thinks AI “will beat that by a mile.”

PAHO expects the U.S. to submit a plan in the coming weeks to stop measles transmission. Getting the status back means going at least a year without an unbroken chain of spread. Boerner’s prescription went wider than one virus. “We’ve got to be mindful of the entire ecosystem,” he said, “and treat it like an ecosystem.”

Nick Lichtenberg is business editor and was formerly Fortune's executive editor of global news.

#5361. 10 of the largest stock market debuts, from Tokyo to Tadawul

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A look at 10 of the biggest IPOs in history, from NTT DoCoMo in 1998 to Saudi Aramco in 2019, spanning banks, tech, telecom, insurance, autos and energy

The size of an initial public offering sounds like a simple number, but it rarely is. Two lists of the biggest IPOs in history can put the same deals in a different order, and neither list has to be wrong. The gap usually comes down to what gets counted.

The first variable is the greenshoe, also called the overallotment option. It lets underwriters sell more shares than a company first planned to offer when demand is strong. Some tallies count only the base deal. Others count the full amount raised once the greenshoe is exercised. On a large offering, that choice can move a deal up or down a list.

The second variable is the dual listing. Some companies sell shares on two exchanges at about the same time, often one in mainland China and one in Hong Kong. Combining both portions produces a larger figure than counting either market alone. Currency conversion adds another layer. Many of these deals were priced in riyals, yen, yuan or Hong Kong dollars rather than U.S. dollars. Dollar totals depend on the exchange rate used.

For those reasons, this piece does not offer a definitive ranking. It covers 10 of the largest stock market debuts on record, presented in chronological order rather than by size. The selection runs from a Japanese mobile carrier in 1998 to a Saudi oil producer in 2019.

The deals span six trading venues: the Tokyo Stock Exchange, Shanghai, Hong Kong, the New York Stock Exchange, Nasdaq $NDAQ and Saudi Arabia's Tadawul. They also cross industries. Chinese lenders sit alongside a payment network, a social network, an e-commerce group, an Asia-focused insurer, a carmaker and two Japanese telecom operators.

The reasons behind the offerings varied as much as the companies did. Some were partial sales by state owners or parent companies. Others followed a corporate rescue or a breakup. A few gave public investors their first chance to own shares in a large internet business.

Each slide covers when and where the company went public, how the deal was priced or sized, and what set the listing apart at the time it happened.

NTT DoCoMo, the mobile phone unit of Nippon Telegraph and Telephone, went public in Japan in 1998. The offering was one of the largest IPOs of its era.

The deal turned a wireless division into a listed company of its own. Before the offering, outside investors could gain exposure to the mobile business only through its parent. After the listing, they could buy shares in the mobile operator directly.

DoCoMo remained a unit of Nippon Telegraph and Telephone after the listing. The parent kept its ties to the mobile business even as public shareholders came on board.

This kind of transaction is known as a carve-out listing. A large parent sells shares in one of its businesses while keeping a connection to that business. The parent can raise money this way. The market, in turn, puts a separate price on the unit.

The 1998 date makes DoCoMo's offering an early example of a very large telecom listing. It came years before the Chinese bank, U.S. technology and Saudi energy offerings of the 2000s and 2010s.

Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) raised roughly $21.9 billion in October 2006 through a dual listing in Shanghai and Hong Kong. It was among the first very large Chinese bank listings.

ICBC is a state-owned commercial bank headquartered in Beijing. It is one of the large state-owned lenders at the center of China's banking system.

The bank divided its offering between two exchanges. One portion of the shares listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange in mainland China. The other portion listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange.

Shares of mainland Chinese companies that trade in Shanghai are known as A shares. They are priced in yuan. Shares of mainland companies that trade in Hong Kong are known as H shares. They are priced in Hong Kong dollars. ICBC's offering used both share classes.

Agricultural Bank of China, a state-owned lender, went public in July 2010 in an offering that raised roughly $22 billion. It sold shares on two markets, Shanghai and Hong Kong.

The listing gave public investors on both exchanges a way to own shares in a Chinese state-owned bank.

Published totals for the deal differ from one report to another. The roughly $22 billion figure is an approximation, not an exact sum.

The offering arrived in a busy year for very large listings. AIA Group went public in Hong Kong in October 2010. General Motors $GM returned to public markets in November 2010.

General Motors $GM returned to public markets in November 2010, pricing its common shares at $33 each. The offering ranked among the largest U.S. stock sales of its time.

The listing followed the automaker's 2009 bankruptcy restructuring and a rescue by the U.S. government. That sequence set it apart from most deals on lists of record IPOs.

Many of the largest offerings involve a company selling shares to outside investors for the first time. A state-owned bank, a subsidiary separated from its parent or a privately held tech business would fit that pattern. General Motors had been a public company before its bankruptcy. Its 2010 sale was a return to the market rather than a first appearance.

Alibaba Group's initial public offering on the New York Stock Exchange in September 2014 raised about $25 billion once the overallotment option was exercised. It was the largest U.S. IPO, and the company behind it was not American.

Alibaba is a Chinese e-commerce group. It priced its shares at $68 each for its NYSE debut.

The roughly $25 billion total includes the extra shares sold through the greenshoe. A count limited to the base deal would put a smaller figure on the same offering.

The deal also stood out for where it took place. Alibaba chose a U.S. exchange for its listing rather than a market in China.

That choice meant a foreign company carried out the largest IPO on a U.S. exchange. The record went to a Chinese e-commerce business listing in New York, not to an American company.

Saudi Aramco raised about $25.6 billion when it went public on Saudi Arabia's Tadawul exchange in December 2019. The oil company was valued at about $1.7 trillion at listing.

The shares were priced at 32 riyals each. Aramco sold them on its home exchange. It did not add a listing in New York or Hong Kong.

That choice set the deal apart from several other very large offerings. Some companies went public on a foreign market. Others sold shares on two markets at about the same time. Aramco's offering took place on a single domestic exchange and was priced in the country's own currency.

The $25.6 billion figure counts the greenshoe. Aramco's total reached that level only after the overallotment option was exercised. Any comparison with another offering depends on whether that deal's total was measured the same way.

The two-market structure gave the bank access to two separate pools of investors. Domestic buyers could take part through Shanghai. Foreign investors faced limits on buying mainland-listed shares at the time. They could take part through Hong Kong instead.

The listing made ICBC a publicly traded company. The Chinese state remained its controlling shareholder after the offering.

Visa $V went public on the New York Stock Exchange in March 2008, selling shares at $44 each. The offering raised about $17.9 billion, making it the largest U.S. IPO at the time of its listing.

Visa runs a payment network. Its system carries transactions between the banks that issue Visa-branded cards, the merchants that accept those cards and the cardholders who use them.

Visa does not lend money to cardholders. The banks that issue the cards handle the lending. Investors in the offering were buying into the network that moves card payments, not a lender holding consumer debt on its own books.

Before the IPO, Visa was owned by the financial institutions that belonged to its network. Those banks were both its owners and its customers. The offering changed that arrangement. Outside investors could now hold a stake in the company alongside the banks that had built it.

The $44 figure was the offer price. Investors who received shares in the offering paid that amount. The price was set before the stock began trading. After the opening, the share price moved with buying and selling on the exchange.

The amount an IPO raises reflects the cash the offering brings in. It is not a measure of what the whole company is worth. Visa's total described the money raised from the shares it sold, not a valuation of the business.

The record Visa set applied to U.S. exchanges. No earlier IPO on a U.S. exchange had raised as much when Visa listed. The mark belonged to that moment rather than standing as a permanent high for U.S. offerings.

The timing also set the deal apart. Visa listed in the same month that Bear Stearns agreed to a sale to JPMorgan $JPM Chase in a rescue backed by the Federal Reserve. A record-size offering went ahead while U.S. financial markets were under heavy strain.

AIA Group, an insurer focused on Asia, went public on the Hong Kong stock exchange in October 2010 and raised about $20.5 billion. The listing followed AIA's separation from its former parent, American International Group (AIG).

That separation set the deal apart from a typical IPO. In a standard first-time offering, a company that built itself up independently sells shares to outside investors. AIA had a different history. It was an established insurance business that operated inside a larger U.S. group before it became a standalone company.

A listing of this kind is often called a carve-out. A parent takes a business it already owns and sets it up as a separate company. Investors are then offered shares in that business directly. In a carve-out, the seller of the shares can be the parent group rather than the business being listed.

For AIA, the result was an independent insurer with its own shares trading in Hong Kong. Before the split, an investor who wanted a stake in its operations had to buy into AIG as a whole. After the listing, AIA could be owned on its own.

That change gave investors what markets often call a pure play. AIA's share price would track the results of one Asian insurance business, not the wider mix of operations held inside AIG.

The choice of exchange matched the company's footprint. AIA's business is concentrated in Asia. A Hong Kong listing put its shares on an exchange inside the region where it operates.

The amount raised is the reason the deal appears among the largest IPOs on record. At about $20.5 billion, the AIA offering reached a size more often associated with state-owned banks, large technology companies and national energy producers. Among the 10 offerings in this selection, it is the only one from the insurance industry.

The offering came after the bankruptcy process and the government rescue. It put the carmaker's common shares back in front of public investors.

Accounts of the total amount raised differ. The gap depends on whether preferred shares sold in the deal are counted alongside the common stock. The $33 price for common shares is the figure that stays consistent across those accounts.

The deal shows that a place on lists of the largest stock market debuts does not always mean a company was new to investors. A carmaker coming out of bankruptcy appears in the same company as banks and tech businesses that were going public for the first time.

Facebook $META went public on Nasdaq $NDAQ in May 2012, pricing its shares at $38 each. The offering raised about $16 billion and valued the social network at roughly $104 billion at pricing.

Those two figures measure different things. The $16 billion is the cash raised by selling shares in the offering. The $104 billion is the value that the $38 price placed on the whole company.

Seen together, they show that the IPO was a partial sale. Public investors bought a portion of the business, not the entire company. Existing shareholders kept the rest.

The $104 billion figure was also a snapshot taken before trading began. It reflected the offer price, not a price set by buyers and sellers on the open market. Once the shares started trading, the company's market value moved with the stock price.

Facebook also stood apart from many large IPO candidates. It was a consumer service known well beyond the investment world. The listing gave public investors a way to buy shares in the social network on an exchange.

The company chose Nasdaq over the New York Stock Exchange. Nasdaq has long been the listing venue for many large U.S. technology companies. That choice tied the debut to Nasdaq's own trading systems.

The first trading session did not run smoothly. Technical problems at Nasdaq disrupted the debut and affected trading in the new shares. The trouble drew attention to the exchange's systems as well as to the stock.

By the close, Facebook shares had finished close to the $38 offer price. The stock ended its first session with little change from the level set in the offering. Investors who bought at the offer price ended the day with little gain or loss on paper.

The company that sold those shares now operates as Meta Platforms. The May 2012 offering marks the point at which the social network first became a publicly traded company.

SoftBank Corp, the mobile carrier unit of SoftBank Group, went public on the Tokyo Stock Exchange in December 2018. The offering raised roughly $23.5 billion, which made it one of the largest IPOs ever.

The shares sold belonged to the carrier, not to its parent. SoftBank Group is a Tokyo-based conglomerate founded by Masayoshi Son. Son started the group in 1981. It holds stakes in technology businesses around the world. The mobile network is one business inside that group, and it was the part offered to public investors.

The carrier traces its roots to the group's 2006 purchase of Vodafone's Japanese mobile business. SoftBank rebranded that operation under its own name. By the time of the listing, it was one of Japan's three major mobile carriers, alongside NTT DoCoMo and KDDI. It also sells plans under the Y!mobile brand.

A parent company can sell shares in a subsidiary while its own stock stays listed. The deal raises cash from a business the parent already owns without selling the whole group. SoftBank Group kept majority control of the carrier after the offering. Buyers of the new shares gained direct exposure to the carrier's operations. They did not gain a claim on the parent's wider portfolio of investments.

The Tokyo Stock Exchange is Japan's largest equity market. Japan had seen a large mobile listing before. NTT DoCoMo, the mobile arm of Nippon Telegraph and Telephone, went public in Japan in 1998. Both companies were mobile units of larger Japanese telecom groups.

SoftBank Corp's debut followed Alibaba's 2014 listing in New York. It preceded Saudi Aramco's December 2019 share sale on Saudi Arabia's Tadawul exchange.

The valuation and the amount raised measure different things. The roughly $1.7 trillion figure put a price on the whole of Aramco. The $25.6 billion figure is the money raised from the shares on offer. Investors in the IPO bought only a small slice of the company.

The two numbers sit on different scales. One is counted in trillions of dollars, the other in billions. That gap is what a small sale of a very large company looks like on paper.

It also explains how one listing could sit among the largest stock market debuts on record while most of Aramco's shares stayed out of public trading. The offering set a market value for the entire oil producer, even though the cash came from selling only part of it.

#5360. Araceli raises $4.5M for drug discovery tools aimed at reducing animal testing

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 13, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 4:38 pm

Araceli Biosciences, a Portland-area biotech company, has secured $4.5 million in funding to help commercialize technology and develop new products that support using human cells instead of animal studies to test new drugs.

The Tigard, Ore., startup offers instruments and software for creating images of cells and automating analysis. Its technologies fall under the umbrella term “New Approach Methodologies,” which includes human-tissue models, computer simulations and AI-based approaches that reduce or avoid experimentation on animals such as mice, rats and monkeys.

Supporters of the methods, known as NAMs, argue that they can yield better outcomes because animals are not a perfect substitute for humans and can generate irrelevant findings. That can lead to costly, time-intensive development of drugs that fail to perform in people. Advocates also promote the alternatives as more humane.

The National Institutes of Health announced $84 million in September to build infrastructure for NAMs research at 10 sites nationwide.

“[T]he efforts signal a significant investment into human-based technologies as the future of preclinical science, aiming to make research faster, more predictive, and more directly relevant to human health,” the NIH said in a release.

Araceli said it has raised a total of $22.7 million from investors. The new round was led by William Cortelyou and included Fluke Venture Partners, according to PitchBook. The company disclosed Thursday that businessman and animal welfare advocate Jeff Swickard was also an investor.

Swickard owns 54 auto dealerships across Western states and is a commercial real estate investor with $250 million invested in Portland properties.

Shawn MacDonald, chief financial officer for Araceli, said Swickard’s “support reflects a belief that we share, which is that better science and more humane science go hand-in-hand.”

Araceli launched in 2023 as a spinoff from Phoseon Technology, which makes UV LED units for industrial curing and life sciences applications.

The company said that companies and institutions using Araceli technology include the Max Planck Institute and Evotec in Germany, the Wertheim UF Scripps Institute in Florida, VALID Therapeutics in Boston, and Ginkgo Bioworks, as well as large pharmaceutical companies. It has 30 employees.
