#5359. 10 stock market debuts that rose, closed flat or fell on their first day

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These 10 IPO first-day pops and flops, from VA Linux and Netscape to Facebook and Peloton, show how far a first trading day can move from the IPO price

An initial public offering has two prices that matter on day one. The first is the IPO price, which the company and its underwriting banks set shortly before trading begins. The second is the closing price at the end of the first session. That close comes after a full day in which public investors could trade the shares freely for the first time. The distance between those two numbers is what traders call a pop or a flop.

A large pop looks like a win, and for investors who received shares at the IPO price, it is. For the company, it can mean something else. Every share sold below what the market proved willing to pay is money the company did not collect. A flop sends the opposite signal. The price was set higher than public demand could support on the first day.

This list of IPO first-day pops and flops gathers 10 stock market debuts that show both outcomes. It is a selection, not a complete ranking. Every percentage is rounded and measured the same way, from the IPO price to the first-day close. Opening trades and intraday highs are left aside. Each debut is judged on that single measure.

The first six slides cover gains, ordered from the largest percentage move to the smallest within this group. They run from VA Linux Systems, whose December 1999 debut opens the list, to Netscape, which went public in August 1995. Between them sit The Globe.com, Beyond Meat, Airbnb $ABNB and Snowflake $SNOW.

The last four slides cover debuts that disappointed. Facebook $META comes first, because its shares closed almost exactly at the $38 IPO price in May 2012. That was a flat result rather than a loss. It still fell short of the expectations that surrounded the offering. Uber $UBER, Robinhood and Peloton follow, and each closed its first session below its IPO price.

The dates cluster in two periods. Three of the gains came between 1995 and 1999, during the run-up in internet stocks. Six of the remaining seven debuts took place between 2019 and 2021, with Facebook's 2012 offering the exception. Each slide stands on its own figures: the IPO price, the first-day close and the percent move between them.

VA Linux Systems priced its IPO at $30 a share on December 9, 1999, and closed its first day of trading at $239.25. That rise of about 698% is widely cited as the largest first-day gain for a U.S. IPO.

In dollar terms, each share added $209.25 in a single session. An investor who received stock at the offer price held shares worth nearly eight times their cost by the closing bell.

The company did not create Linux. It built and sold computer hardware, chiefly servers and workstations, configured to run the Linux operating system. Linux is open-source software, meaning its code is free to use, copy and modify.

Finnish programmer Linus Torvalds released the first Linux kernel in 1991. By the late 1990s, the system had become a common choice for running web servers. VA Linux sold machines built for that kind of work.

VA Linux was not the first Linux-focused company to go public that year. Red Hat, which distributed a commercial version of the Linux software, held its IPO in August 1999. VA Linux offered public investors a hardware route into the same open-source trend four months later.

The Globe.com priced its initial public offering at $9 a share on November 13, 1998. The stock closed its first trading day at $63.50, a gain of about 606% over that offering price.

That close left each share $54.50 above the price set for the offering. Put another way, the stock ended its first session worth a little more than seven times its IPO price.

The company began on a college campus. Stephan Paternot and Todd Krizelman founded the site while they were students at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York.

The Globe.com was an online community. Members could build personal home pages, talk in chat rooms and post on message boards. Much of what appeared on the site came from its own users. That model was an early version of what later became known as social networking.

Airbnb $ABNB priced its IPO at $68 a share on December 10, 2020, and the stock closed its first trading day at $144.71. That was a gain of about 113%, more than double the offering price.

The $68 price came after Airbnb raised its target range for the offering. The shares listed on Nasdaq $NDAQ under the ticker ABNB.

Airbnb went public during the COVID-19 pandemic, at a time when travel demand had collapsed. Border closures, lockdowns and quarantine rules cut into the short-term stays at the center of its business.

Netscape Communications priced its shares at $28 on August 9, 1995, and closed its first trading day at $58.25. That close left the stock about 108% above its offering price.

The $28 price was a revision. The company had first planned to sell shares at $14, then doubled the price before the stock began trading. Netscape listed on Nasdaq $NDAQ under the ticker NSCP.

Netscape made Navigator, a web browser. Navigator gave ordinary computer users a point-and-click way to view pages on the World Wide Web. In 1995, it was the product most people linked to the company's name.

Marc Andreessen was a co-founder. Before Netscape, he co-wrote Mosaic, an early graphical browser built at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications at the University of Illinois. His co-founder was Jim Clark, who had earlier founded Silicon Graphics.

Uber $UBER Technologies priced its IPO at $45 a share on May 10, 2019, and closed its first trading day at $41.57. That left the stock down about 7.6% from its offering price.

The gap worked out to $3.43 a share. An investor who bought at the IPO price and held through the close had a paper loss on each share.

The offering raised about $8.1 billion. The shares trade on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker UBER.

Garrett Camp and Travis Kalanick founded Uber in San Francisco in 2009. It began as a service for booking black cars through a smartphone app. It later added lower-cost ride-hailing, food delivery through

Peloton priced its IPO at $29 a share on September 26, 2019, and closed its first day of trading at $25.76. That put the stock down about 11% from its offering price in its Nasdaq $NDAQ debut.

The shares finished the session $3.24 below the price set for the offering. Investors who bought at $29 ended the day holding stock worth less than they paid.

On Wall Street, a debut that closes under its offering price is known as a broken IPO. Peloton's listing fit that description at the end of its first session.

The company traded under the ticker PTON. Its business combined two things: connected exercise bikes and subscription classes streamed to those machines. That mix made Peloton part equipment maker and part media company.

The company traced its roots to VA Research, which Larry Augustin co-founded in 1993 while a graduate student at Stanford University. The business adopted the VA Linux Systems name before going public.

VA Linux listed on Nasdaq $NDAQ under the ticker LNUX. Nasdaq was the main listing venue for technology and internet companies of the era.

The debut came near the height of dot-com enthusiasm. The offering priced about three months before the Nasdaq Composite index reached its peak in March 2000.

The company later moved away from the hardware business that defined its IPO. It became VA Software in 2001 and SourceForge in 2007, taking the second name from the software development website it operated.

The business sold no physical product and no packaged software. What it offered advertisers and investors was an audience, gathered in one place by the content its members made themselves. Like many websites of that period, it earned revenue by selling advertising on the pages those members visited.

The 606% move is the second-largest percentage gain among the six pops in this selection. Only VA Linux Systems, which listed a little more than a year later, closed its first day further above its IPO price. Netscape, the oldest debut in the group, gained about 108% in August 1995. Netscape sold browser software, and its first-day move was a fraction of The Globe.com's.

The listing came in late 1998. That was more than a year before the Nasdaq $NDAQ Composite index reached its dot-com peak in March 2000. The Globe.com debut arrived while investor appetite for internet shares was still building toward that high point. In that market, a site whose main asset was user traffic closed its first day far above the price its own offering had set.

Beyond Meat priced its initial public offering at $25 a share on May 2, 2019, above its marketed range, and the stock closed its first trading day at $65.75. That was a gain of about 163% over the IPO price.

The plant-based meat maker listed on Nasdaq $NDAQ under the ticker BYND. An investor who received shares at the offering price held a $40.75 per-share gain by the close.

The company and its underwriters had marketed the offering to investors at a lower range. Setting the final price above it showed that orders exceeded what the original range had assumed. The first-day climb meant buyers who missed an allocation paid well above even that higher price in the open market.

Beyond Meat makes meat substitutes from plant ingredients rather than animal protein. Its best-known product is the Beyond Burger, a patty made mainly from pea protein and designed to cook and look like ground beef. The company sold it in the meat case of grocery stores, alongside conventional beef, rather than in a separate vegetarian aisle. It also sold plant-based links under the Beyond Sausage name.

Restaurant chains had added the product before the listing. Carl's Jr. began offering a burger made with a Beyond Meat patty in early 2019.

Ethan Brown founded the company in 2009, and it was based in El Segundo, California. Its private backers before the IPO included Bill Gates and Leonardo DiCaprio. Tyson Foods, one of the largest U.S. meat processors, had also invested and then sold its stake before the offering.

At the time of the debut, Beyond Meat's best-known rival, Impossible Foods, was privately held. Public stock investors could not buy shares in Impossible Foods directly.

Both companies were pushing into fast food that spring. In April 2019, Burger King began testing the Impossible Whopper in St. Louis, built on an Impossible Foods patty. Plant-based burgers from both companies were on mainstream chain menus in the weeks before the BYND shares began trading.

The company made cuts of its own that year. In May 2020, co-founder and CEO Brian Chesky announced that Airbnb would lay off about 1,900 employees, roughly a quarter of its staff. In the same message, Chesky said Airbnb expected its 2020 revenue to come in at less than half of its 2019 total.

The listing plan predated the crisis. Airbnb said in September 2019 that it expected to become a public company in 2020. It filed its registration statement publicly with the Securities and Exchange Commission in November 2020, weeks before the shares began trading.

Airbnb was founded in San Francisco in 2008 by Brian Chesky, Joe Gebbia and Nathan Blecharczyk. The idea began in 2007, when Chesky and Gebbia rented air mattresses in their apartment to visitors in town for a design conference. The early name, AirBed & Breakfast, came from that setup. The startup went through the Y Combinator accelerator in early 2009.

The company runs an online marketplace rather than a hotel chain. Hosts list homes, apartments and private rooms, and guests book them through the platform. Airbnb earns revenue from service fees on those bookings. It does not own the properties listed on its site.

Airbnb's debut came one day after another large consumer-tech listing. DoorDash, the food delivery company, began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on December 9, 2020.

Snowflake $SNOW priced its IPO at $120 a share on September 16, 2020, and closed its first trading day at $253.93. That was a gain of about 112%, or $133.93 per share above the offering price.

The offering raised about $3.4 billion. At the time, that made it the largest software IPO. The shares listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker SNOW.

Snowflake sells a cloud-based data platform. Companies use it to store large volumes of business data and to run queries and analysis on that data. The service runs on the major public clouds, including Amazon $AMZN Web Services, Microsoft $MSFT Azure and Google $GOOGL Cloud, rather than on hardware Snowflake owns.

That setup also puts Snowflake in competition with its hosts. Amazon, Microsoft and Google each sell their own data warehouse services, such as Amazon Redshift and Google BigQuery.

A core part of Snowflake's design separates data storage from computing power. Customers can scale each one up or down on its own. Snowflake charges largely by consumption. Customers pay for the computing they use instead of buying a fixed software license.

The company was founded in 2012 by Benoit Dageville, Thierry Cruanes and Marcin Żukowski. Dageville and Cruanes had previously worked at Oracle $ORCL, the database company. Frank Slootman was chief executive at the time of the listing. He had earlier run Data Domain, a data storage company, and ServiceNow $NOW, a maker of IT workflow software. Both of those companies went public while he was in charge, Data Domain in 2007 and ServiceNow in 2012.

Two outside investors were tied to the offering. Berkshire Hathaway $BRK.B, the conglomerate run by Warren Buffett, bought shares in a private placement at the IPO price. That meant Berkshire paid $120 a share, the same price set for the public offering, rather than the first-day closing price.

Berkshire seldom invests in newly public companies, and its purchase drew wide attention for that reason. Salesforce $CRM, the customer relationship management software company, also invested in Snowflake.

Netscape was founded in 1994 under the name Mosaic Communications Corp. It took the Netscape name later that year after a dispute with the University of Illinois over the Mosaic name. The company was based in Mountain View, California.

Netscape had not turned a profit when it went public. Investors were buying into a young company whose value rested on the growth of web use rather than on earnings.

The Netscape IPO is often cited as the start of the dot-com boom.

Microsoft $MSFT released the first version of Internet Explorer later in August 1995. The rivalry between Navigator and Internet Explorer became known as the browser wars. In 1998, the U.S. Justice Department filed an antitrust case against Microsoft. The case focused in part on how Microsoft bundled Internet Explorer with Windows.

Netscape released Navigator's source code in 1998, and that project became Mozilla. The Mozilla project later produced the Firefox browser. America Online agreed to buy Netscape in November 1998. The deal closed in 1999, ending Netscape's run as an independent public company.

Facebook $META priced its IPO at $38 a share on May 18, 2012, and closed its first trading day at $38.23. That was a gain of about 0.6%, or 23 cents a share above the offering price.

The offering raised about $16 billion. At $38 a share, the social network carried a valuation of roughly $104 billion. Morgan Stanley $MS led the group of banks that underwrote the deal.

Mark Zuckerberg started Facebook in 2004 with several of his Harvard classmates. The company filed for its IPO in February 2012. It went public eight years after its founding. Its shares listed on Nasdaq $NDAQ under the ticker FB.

Zuckerberg rang Nasdaq's opening bell from Facebook's headquarters in Menlo Park, California, rather than from the exchange in New York. The ceremony went ahead on schedule. The trading did not.

Trading in Facebook shares had been scheduled to begin at 11 a.m. Eastern time. Technical problems at Nasdaq delayed the start by about half an hour. The same problems left some brokers and investors waiting to learn whether their orders had been filled, and at what price.

The episode drew a regulatory response. In May 2013, the Securities and Exchange Commission charged Nasdaq over its handling of the Facebook offering. The exchange agreed to pay a $10 million penalty to settle the charges.

Buyers who received shares at $38 did not lose money on the first day. The debut is still described as a flop because the shares delivered almost none of the first-day gain that investors had expected.

For Facebook, the flat close meant it sold its shares at close to the price public buyers were willing to pay that day. For investors who bought at the offering price, it meant almost no immediate return.

The company has since changed its name. Facebook's parent became Meta Platforms in October 2021. Its stock ticker switched from FB to META in 2022.

The company stayed private for about a decade before listing. In that time it raised money through a long run of private funding rounds. Its backers included the venture firm Benchmark, Japan's SoftBank and Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund.

Many early investors had bought shares years before the listing. The IPO gave them a public market in which those shares could eventually be sold. Public buyers on May 10 came in at a price set after years of private fundraising.

Leadership had changed before the listing. Kalanick resigned as chief executive in 2017. Dara Khosrowshahi, who had run Expedia $EXPE, became CEO that year and led Uber through the IPO.

Ride-hailing already had a public reference point. Lyft $LYFT, Uber's main U.S. rival, went public on Nasdaq $NDAQ in March 2019, weeks before Uber. Uber's own debut gave investors a second listed ride-hailing stock to weigh.

Drivers also drew attention to the offering. On May 8, 2019, two days before the IPO, drivers in several U.S. cities and other countries staged protests over pay and working conditions.

Robinhood Markets priced its IPO at $38 a share on July 29, 2021, and closed its first trading day at $34.82. That left the stock down about 8.4% from its offering price.

Each share finished $3.18 below where it started. Robinhood had marketed the deal to investors in a range of $38 to $42 a share. The final price landed at the bottom of that range.

Robinhood listed on Nasdaq $NDAQ under the ticker HOOD. The company runs a brokerage app built around commission-free trading of stocks, options and cryptocurrency. Vlad Tenev and Baiju Bhatt co-founded the company, which is based in Menlo Park, California.

The offering departed from a common IPO practice. Most new shares in a typical deal go to institutional investors such as mutual funds and hedge funds. Robinhood set aside part of its offering for its own retail customers. They could request shares through the app before trading began.

That structure matched the company's pitch to small investors. It also meant that some of the buyers at the offering price were individual users of the app. Those who bought at $38 and held through the close ended the session with a paper loss.

The listing came about six months after the January 2021 surge in GameStop $GME and other meme stocks. During that episode, Robinhood temporarily restricted purchases of several heavily traded stocks. The move drew complaints from users. Tenev testified about it before the House Financial Services Committee on February 18, 2021.

Robinhood's revenue model also faced scrutiny before the IPO. Much of its income came from payment for order flow. Under that arrangement, market makers pay a broker to route its customers' trades to them. In December 2020, Robinhood agreed to pay $65 million to settle Securities and Exchange Commission charges. The charges centered on how Robinhood had described those payments to customers.

Each bike carried a touchscreen that played instructor-led cycling sessions. Riders could join a class live or choose from a library of recorded workouts. An on-screen leaderboard let riders see how their output compared with others in the same class.

Owners paid a monthly fee for access to that class library, on top of the upfront cost of the equipment. The fee gave Peloton recurring revenue alongside its hardware sales.

John Foley, a former Barnes & Noble executive, co-founded Peloton in 2012. The company was based in New York City and filmed many of its classes in its own studios there. Before it had a product on the market, Peloton raised early money for its first bike through a Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign in 2013.

By the time of the IPO, the product line reached beyond cycling to a treadmill called the Tread. It used the same streamed-class format as the bike.

Peloton also sold a digital membership through its app for people who did not own its equipment. App users could stream classes such as strength training, yoga and meditation on phones and other devices.

#5358. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. serves Trump Jollibee in a moment of culinary diplomacy

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said he sent President Donald Trump a “taste of Manila”—sending fried chicken from Jollibee, the Philippines’ largest fast-food chain, to the U.S. president and his delegation as a late-night snack on Tuesday, ahead of their bilateral meeting in Manila on Wednesday.

“Jollibee is a very, very popular chain, and one of their main products is fried chicken,” Marcos said at the opening of his bilateral meeting with Trump on Wednesday. “We are very proud to say that we have surpassed KFC in the United States in terms of popularity.”

While in Manila, Trump announced that he’d agreed “a very big trade deal, the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made so far” with the Philippines, yet offered no details. Marcos’s office has not confirmed the agreement of a trade deal.

The delivery was culinary diplomacy for a chain that’s become a national symbol at home and has ambitions to break into the U.S. market.

Started in 1975 as an ice cream parlor by Filipino businessman Tony Tan Caktiong, Jollibee is best known for its “Chickenjoy” fried chicken and a sweet-style spaghetti topped with sliced hot dogs. The chain has more than 1,600 stores across 17 countries, according to its website.

Its parent, Jollibee Foods Corporation, runs a portfolio of about 20 brands—including Chinese-food chain Chowking, dim sum chain Tim Ho Wan, and U.S. burger chain Smashburger—with more than 10,000 stores and cafés across 33 countries. With $5.3 billion in annual revenue, Jollibee ranks No. 71 on the Fortune Southeast Asia 500.

In January, Jollibee said it would separate its domestic and international businesses; in September, the company named the international unit Jollibee Foods Corporation International (JFCI) and chose Hong Kong for its proposed listing.

Marcos may be overstating his claim about Jollibee’s popularity in the U.S. Jollibee has just over 100 stores in North America, including Canada. KFC, by comparison, has over 3,500 U.S. locations, according to its official website. Yum Brands, KFC’s parent company, reported $8.2 billion in revenue last year.

Jollibee has become an obligatory stop for visiting leaders.

New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon ate at a Jollibee in Manila’s business district on the first day of an official visit in April 2024; Marcos posted his own Jollibee order—hamburgers, fried chicken, and palabok, a Filipino noodle dish—to Facebook afterward.

On Nov. 15, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese visited a Jollibee restaurant as the chain announced plans to expand into Australia, where more than 400,000 people were born in the Philippines, making the Filipino-born population the country’s fifth-largest diaspora community, according to a statement from Albanese’s office.

#5357. Blue Origin puts its space station plans on hold to concentrate on moon missions instead

by Alan Boyle on Nov 13, 2026 at 2:35 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 2:35 pm

Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin space venture has decided not to seek further NASA funding for its Orbital Reef space station project in order to tighten its focus on lunar missions.

For the past five years, Blue Origin has played a lead role in Orbital Reef, alongside partners including Sierra Space and Boeing. In late 2021, Blue Origin won a $130 million contract from NASA in the first phase of the space agency’s Commercial Low Earth Orbit Destinations program, or CLD.

Now NASA is seeking proposals for the next phase of the program, which will fund the development of orbital outposts to replace International Space Station in the 2030s. Proposals are due on Dec. 8, with contracts expected to be awarded next spring.

Blue Origin indicated that it will not submit a bid.

“Blue Origin’s mission is to build a road to space for the benefit of Earth so that millions of people can live and work in space. Establishing a sustained human presence on the moon is a critical step toward that future,” the company said in an emailed statement.

“As our role supporting NASA’s Artemis and Moon Base missions continues to grow, we’re focusing resources on capabilities that directly advance our lunar projects,” Blue Origin said. “By sharpening that focus, we can move faster on the technologies and infrastructure needed to make lunar permanence a reality.”

Orbital Reef was once touted as a “mixed-use business park” in space — and was even slated to star in a sci-fi thriller titled “Helios.” But much like that delayed film project, the space station is now on the back burner.

Orbital Reef isn’t the only initiative Blue Origin has put on hold to prioritize moon missions. In January, the company suspended its suborbital New Shepard program for at least two years for similar reasons.

Blue Origin is building landers for delivering cargo and crews to the lunar surface for NASA. An uncrewed Blue Moon Mark 1 lunar lander is scheduled for launch early next year, and a crew-capable Mark 2 version is scheduled for testing in low Earth orbit next year during NASA’s Artemis 3 mission.

Last week, NASA awarded Blue Origin a $94 million base contract, plus a $140 million option, to deliver a nuclear-powered rover to the lunar south pole. Blue Origin also won a spot in NASA’s broader lunar cargo delivery program. In addition, Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin subsidiary, will contribute to a lunar power-generating project known as miniCAST.

Blue Origin is pursuing several other moon development initiatives, including a program called Blue Alchemist that aims to use lunar materials to manufacture solar cells and electrical wire.

Several competitors are still working on commercial space stations. Voyager Technologies, Airbus and Northrop Grumman lead the Starlab consortium, which received CLD Phase 1 funding from NASA and is expected to put in a proposal for Phase 2.

Axiom Space and Vast are also developing outposts that could take the place of the ISS. Meanwhile, Marysville, Wash.-based Gravitics is building space station hardware for Axiom and an orbital carrier for the U.S. Space Force.

#5356. 11 flood safety steps, from the first alert to emotional recovery

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Learn the difference between a flood watch and a warning, and 9 more safety steps for before, during and after a flood.

Staying safe in a flood depends on moving early, because a whole community faces the same flood at the same time. Many people picture a flood as a private emergency at their own front door, judged by the hour when the water stands highest. In practice, neighbors reach for the same roads, the same supplies and the same help all at once. In a single Ottawa flood, the number of basements reported underwater topped 6,000, according to CBC News. The roads out fill up as well, and the CDC advises evacuees to expect heavy traffic on evacuation routes. A household that waits to see what everyone else does has already waited too long, so the useful work has to happen before the water rises.

The danger also lasts long after the water drains away. A falling waterline feels like the end of the emergency, and that is the moment many people relax. The harm keeps coming in the weeks that follow. People face contaminated water and spoiled food, mold in walls nobody dried in time, fumes from generators run in the wrong place, injuries during cleanup and the strain of living through all of it. The signals people rely on are easy to mistake for an all-clear. A flood alert, a line on a flood map and a depth at which water turns dangerous each show where danger starts, not where safety begins. A person on the safe side of any of them can still be at risk. Staying safe means acting before the official signal turns urgent and staying careful well after the flood looks finished.

The American Red Cross laid out flood safety advice that runs from reading the first alert to recovering emotionally afterward. That advice covers the difference between a watch and a warning, the mold that grows in a home left wet, the carbon monoxide that no one can see or smell, and the emotional toll that stays with people after the repairs are done. Taken together, the guidance forms a timeline that starts before the first raindrop and continues well past the cleanup. The reader's job along that timeline is to act sooner at the start and to stay careful longer at the end.

Many people hear "watch" and "warning" as two levels of the same alert, but the real difference between them is time. A watch means flooding is merely possible, while a warning means flooding is occurring now or soon, according to the American Red Cross. A household that knows which one is in effect knows whether it still has time or has to act immediately. The CDC says that people should evacuate when a flood warning is issued or when authorities direct them to leave. A warning is the moment to go. Anyone who starts getting ready at that point has already lost the hours the work required.

The watch stage sounds like permission to wait, but most of the preparation belongs there. During a watch, the CDC's National Center for Environmental Health advises households to fill their vehicle's gas tank, put essential documents in waterproof material and set aside enough water to last at least three days. A full tank lets a family drive out before anyone tells it to go. The papers and the water are already packed when it does. Flooding is only possible during a watch, but that is when nearly all of a household's preparation should happen.

Authorities can also order people to leave, and once they do, a household has no decision left to weigh. "Never ignore an evacuation order," the CDC said.

A household that finished its work during the watch can follow that order in minutes, while one that waited spends the warning packing as the water rises.

Flood risk can change from one block to the next, so the question that matters is whether a particular house is exposed, not whether the region floods. The American Red Cross directs residents to FEMA's Flood Map Service Center, where anyone can search for a home's flood zone by its address. The answer is only as current as the map behind it, and Harris County, Texas, last gave its floodplain maps a comprehensive overhaul in 2007, according to the Houston Chronicle. A house labeled as outside the floodplain is not necessarily free of risk, and the label is where a homeowner's research should begin.

When officials redraw a map, the label on file can change for a great many homes at once. The Houston Chronicle reports that draft maps could shift more than 420,000 properties in the Houston area to a higher-risk rating. If those drafts take effect, the rating those owners have known would no longer describe their risk. The change would not be spread evenly. In Hunterwood, about 85% of parcels, 650 of 764, may be moved to higher risk, the highest share among Houston's super neighborhoods. An owner or buyer should therefore check how the drafts treat the surrounding neighborhood, along with the zone listed for the address.

A flood-zone line also determines what some homeowners must pay. Inside the 100-year floodplain, owners whose mortgages are federally backed are required to buy flood insurance. For those households, a change on a map becomes a new bill. The maps are drafts, and any single home's label could change before they take effect.

The sensible move is to look up the address today and plan as if the higher-risk label already applied, rather than waiting for a final line or treating the old one as protection.

Most flood safety advice assumes there will be some time between the first alert and the arrival of the water, enough time to understand the threat, weigh the options and move. A flash flood may come with little to no warning, according to the American Red Cross. People caught in one may have no time at all to decide where to go. That changes what preparation means. A household facing a flash flood can't count on an alert to start its planning. The decisions it made in advance are the only ones it can rely on once the water starts to rise.

The plan this threat calls for is simple: choose a spot of higher ground ahead of time, one the household can reach quickly. Speed is the test that matters most. When there is little or no warning, a hill or upper floor that takes too long to reach does nothing for the people who can't get there in time, however high it is. A family should judge each option by how fast everyone in the household could get to it on foot or by car, and pick the closest one that is truly above the water. That choice has to be made on a dry day, when people have time to look at the routes, compare the options and settle on a single place. Every person in the home should know where it is, so no one has to stop and discuss it when the time comes.

A household that already knows where it is going needs no warning time to start moving.

When forecasters predict a river flood or a storm surge, many households decide to stay put and wait to see how high the water gets. The American Red Cross advises households to learn whether their area is prone to these floods and to review their evacuation plan so they can leave quickly. The first of those steps belongs well before any alert. A family that learns only on the day of the flood that a river or the sea can reach its home has already lost the head start the rest of the plan depends on. The second step sets the standard for readiness: a plan reviewed in advance turns leaving into a matter of minutes instead of a debate at the kitchen table. A household in a flood-prone area should treat departure as a real possibility and have it worked out before officials make the call. The real decision is made days earlier, and the hours before the water comes should go to carrying it out.

Leaving early also keeps people out of the water itself, and contact with floodwater carries risks that have nothing to do with its depth or speed. Most people judge floodwater by whether it can knock them over or sweep them away. But what is in the water is a hazard of its own, and the safer course is to stay out of it entirely rather than guess how clean or shallow it looks. Some coastal waters naturally carry vibrio bacteria, and a cut exposed to that water during a flood can become infected, according to the CDC. The risk weighs most on anyone who already has a cut, scrape or wound. For them, leaving before the surge arrives keeps broken skin away from water that may hold those bacteria.

A household that gets out ahead of a river or the sea keeps its members clear of the current and of whatever the water carries.

A flooded road rarely looks dangerous, because the water seems shallow and a car feels heavy enough to push through it. Yet a person can be knocked off their feet in 6 inches of fast-moving water, and 12 inches is enough to float a vehicle, according to the American Red Cross. The weight of a car gives no protection in water that shallow, and a driver who stays behind the wheel is inside the vehicle once it floats. The Red Cross places this advice among the steps for the middle of a flood, when the time for preparing has run out. At the water's edge, a driver faces one decision and has seconds to make it: drive in or turn back.

Those figures are not a limit to measure the road against. A number invites a driver to treat anything under 6 inches as safe to cross, and that reading is the trap. The CDC's National Center for Environmental Health sets no safe depth for moving water at all. Taken together with the Red Cross thresholds, that position shows what the figures really mark. They show how quickly floodwater turns deadly, not a level below which wading or driving is safe. The numbers are worth knowing only as proof that very little water is enough to kill.

Two separate safety agencies reduce this advice to a rule rather than a measurement. The Red Cross sums up the point in a short slogan, and the CDC uses the same four words. "Never drive in flooded areas—turn around, don't drown!" the CDC said. The word "never" leaves no exception for a driver who thinks a few inches can be crossed.

The decision that counts is made before the tires touch the water. Once a car is in the current, the driver has few good choices left.

The American Red Cross offers a free phone app, the Red Cross Emergency App, that a household can install on its own before a flood arrives. The app costs nothing, so no household has to go without it because of price. The Red Cross also offers a Spanish version, and families who read Spanish rather than English can use the app as well. A household needs to install it before the forecast turns, while there is still time to act ahead of everyone else.

Red Cross help also covers the weeks after the flood, when people feel they should be coping on their own. The Red Cross lists the Disaster Distress Helpline, 1-800-985-5990, under taking care of yourself after a flood. The line is free and takes calls or texts, so anyone can reach help for flood stress from home, without waiting for an office to open or a shelter bed to free up. A household that saves the number when it installs the app will have both ready before anyone needs them.

Local recovery help through the Red Cross can come with a fixed end date and a spending limit. On July 15, 2026, Ottawa's city council voted to fund Red Cross recovery work after a local flood, but only for six months and with no more than $400,000 from the city, according to CBC News. Ottawa residents who expect that help to last as long as their own repairs may find it gone before the work is done.

A household that sets up the app and the helpline today, and plans its repairs without counting on local help to last, will be ready on both counts.

People need protection before they begin cleaning up after a flood, because the cleanup is where much of the harm happens. Once a house is dry enough to enter, many people go straight back in to clear it, as if the dangerous part were over. The property can stay hazardous long after the flood, with electrocution risk, falling trees and debris among the dangers, according to the American Red Cross. Clearing a home puts people directly among those hazards. "Many injuries happen during cleanup," the Red Cross said. Cleanup workers and volunteers should be up to date on tetanus shots, ideally before cleanup begins, according to the CDC. That protection has to be in place on the first day of work, and a tetanus check belongs on the to-do list before the cleanup weekend, not after someone gets cut.

After a flood, the wound to worry about is the one that gets dirty, even if it doesn't look serious at the time. The tetanus concern lies with wounds contaminated by floodwater, soil, waste or saliva, not with contact with the water itself, according to the CDC. Crushing damage also carries a higher chance of infection than a slice through the skin. A finger or foot caught under shifting debris therefore deserves more attention than an open gash that looks worse. Anyone hurt during cleanup should watch a dirty or crushed wound until it heals rather than dismiss it on the day it happens.

A household can finish clearing the house while a wound from that work is still at risk of infection.

The health risk from a flood stays behind after the water drains, in everything the water soaked. "Stay away from floodwaters. They may contain sewage, sharp items, and chemicals that can make you ill," the American Red Cross warned. For that reason, the CDC says that anything edible the flood or storm reached belongs in the trash. Contact alone is enough to make the food unsafe. After losing so much, people want to save what they can, but food the water reached is a loss, and no amount of cleaning brings it back.

A kitchen the water never reached can be lost as well. The CDC advises throwing out perishable food that sat unrefrigerated through a power outage, and for anything uncertain it gives the same rule as the Red Cross: if you aren't sure the food is safe, discard it. A refrigerator on a dry upper floor may therefore need emptying as surely as the flooded basement. With that standard, a household has to know food is safe before keeping it rather than prove it spoiled before tossing it. Anything nobody can vouch for after the outage belongs in the trash.

A home the flood never entered can still have unsafe water. Surface water can contaminate groundwater, the CDC reports, and that can affect private wells as well as city systems that draw on groundwater. A household with a private well in a flooded area needs to have the water tested before using it, and the well owner is the one who has to confirm it is safe. Until then, suspect water is off-limits for far more than drinking: mixing baby formula, making ice, cooking, washing hands or dishes and brushing teeth all have to wait. People who would never drink a glass of that water can still be exposed through those routine tasks.

Owners have only hours to dry out a flooded home, and many use up that time before they reach the front door. Most people expect cleanup to begin once the water is gone and they are back inside with time to work. The American Red Cross says a house still wet after 24 to 48 hours should be treated as moldy. Families kept away by an evacuation or a blocked road who can't get back within that time should walk in expecting mold rather than hoping they can still prevent it. For a household that evacuated, those hours may pass before anyone has seen the damage.

The rule asks owners to act before they see any mold. The 24-to-48-hour mark is a reason to assume mold and act. It is not a confirmed finding that a particular home has mold, so a clean-looking wall after that point is no sign that the room is safe. Owners who wait for visible proof will act too late. The safer habit is to treat any part of the home that stayed wet past that mark as moldy. Before that point, owners should keep air moving through every damp room so it has a chance to dry in time. Some losses also have to be accepted early. Anything soaked that can be neither fixed nor dried out should go out with the debris. Keeping those things in the hope that they recover only delays the rest of the work.

When mold is measured in hours, airing out the house and clearing out what can't be saved belong at the top of the cleanup list.

After a flood, people head for the nearest dry, enclosed space, and that instinct is where the carbon monoxide risk begins. The American Red Cross rules out the home itself as a place to run anything that gives off carbon monoxide. Getting back inside a house is therefore not the same as being safe inside it. A garage can feel connected to the outdoors, but it is on the same prohibited list, and a wide door does not make the air in it safe to breathe. Families who move into a camper while their repairs go on face the same rule, because a camper is named too. The home, the garage and the camper are the places a displaced family is most likely to shelter, and the rule covers all three.

An open window does not solve the problem either, and setting equipment outdoors near an open window is also prohibited. People cannot judge this danger for themselves. "Carbon monoxide can’t be seen or smelled, but it can kill you fast," the American Red Cross said. A person's own body gives the main signal, and anyone who begins to feel ill, lightheaded or weak may be breathing the gas. Those complaints are ordinary enough to pass for the tiredness of a long day of cleanup. The gas can kill quickly, so those symptoms leave little time to act. The safer course is to keep this equipment out of every place on the list, including the ground just outside an open window, from the first time anyone switches it on.

A household can dry its walls and confirm that its tap water is safe and still not be finished with the flood. The people who lived through it may stay shaken long after the house is livable again, and that reaction is an expected result of the disaster, not a personal failing. "It's normal to have a lot of bad feelings, stress, or anxiety," the American Red Cross said. Anyone who feels that way is not overreacting and has no reason to wait until the strain gets worse before dealing with it. Disaster stress has its own dedicated source of help, the Disaster Distress Helpline, so reaching out is a standard part of flood care rather than a last resort. The helpline is free, which means repair bills that already stretch a household's budget are no reason to put off a call.

Recovery from stress starts with ordinary care of the body. Eating healthy food and getting enough sleep both help a person cope, and those basics deserve the same priority as drying out rooms or replacing spoiled food. They should not get only the time left over once the house is handled. The helpline number, 1-800-985-5990, belongs in a phone now, before the strain arrives, so that reaching out later takes a single step.

A flood isn't over for a household until the people in it have recovered too.

#5355. Does the Nvidia turmoil spell trouble for the Gulf’s AI ambitions?

The downfall of Jensen Huang following revelations of extramarital affairs—including one involving a suspected Chinese spy—and the turmoil that has engulfed Nvidia in its wake have gripped the world’s attention over the past week.

Given their national AI ambitions are strongly tied to investments in Nvidia and access to its coveted chips, Gulf countries will be vulnerable to any dramatic changes in its future strategy.

During U.S. President Donald Trump’s Gulf tour in May 2025, the UAE unveiled plans to develop a 5-GW joint AI Campus in Abu Dhabi. Once complete, it will be the largest facility of its kind outside the U.S. At the heart of the project is Stargate UAE, a 1-GW computing cluster developed by Abu Dhabi-backed G42 in partnership with a host of U.S. companies, including Nvidia, which will supply its Grace Blackwell chips (GB300s).

Nvidia has also forged a strong commercial alliance with Saudi Arabia, with Huang among a select group of U.S. tech leaders invited to meet with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman during his much-feted visit to the White House last November.

During the visit, Elon Musk announced a 500-MW data center in partnership with Saudi government-backed AI company, Humain, which will be powered by Nvidia’s computing chips.

Trump also hosted Mohammed bin Salman, alongside Huang and Elon Musk, at the U.S.-Saudi Investment Forum on November 19 last year.

Just hours later, the U.S. Commerce Department authorized the export of up to 35,000 Nvidia Blackwell GB300 chips to both G42 and Humain. Earlier in the day, Humain said it planned to purchase 600,000 Nvidia AI chips.

This relationship was deepened last month when Humain announced plans with Nvidia to deploy around 27,000 GPUs and develop up to 84-MW of AI computing capacity in the kingdom across a multi-phase program starting in the fourth quarter of this year and followed by planned large-scale deployments beginning in mid-2027.

While the existing partnerships Nvidia holds with the UAE and Saudi are unlikely to be threatened by Huang’s departure, it could weaken the relationship’s momentum, according to Mohammed Soliman, senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, where he focuses on technology and geopolitics.

“The relationship with Nvidia is pretty solid and institutional at this point,” he said. “The deals with G42 and Humain sit on government-to-government agreements that were already in place. That said, Jensen matters a lot and his leaving will have an impact. The overall direction doesn’t change, but losing him as the main driver takes something off the table.”

Sam Winter-Levy, a senior fellow in the Technology and International Affairs program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, expects that the change in leadership at Nvidia could make the company more circumspect in its business dealings with the Gulf.

“Huang was the public face of Nvidia’s sovereign AI pitch and had his own relationships with Gulf leaders, which will be hard to replace quickly,” said Winter-Levy, whose research focuses on the geopolitics of AI.

“I would assume Nvidia will honor its existing contracts with the Gulf, probably with more attention to compliance and things like end-use checks, but to make fewer splashy announcements of new deals.”

In July, Washington relaxed export restrictions on the UAE, granting approved organizations greater access to Nvidia chips and other advanced technologies.

For Gulf governments, a more immediate concern is whether the upheaval at Nvidia could make Washington more reluctant to approve further exports of advanced chips, thereby slowing the pace of the region’s AI buildout.

The upheaval has given U.S. lawmakers fresh ammunition to push for the inclusion of a series of chip-control bills, such as the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act and the MATCH Act, in this year’s National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).

Last week, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer urged Congress to pass the bills, while House Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar called for chip export controls to be included in the annual defense policy bill.

“Congress has limited direct power here, since export licenses lie with the executive branch, and the administration has removed many of the license requirements that slowed chip deliveries to the UAE in the past,” said Winter-Levy.

“But oversight raises the political cost of new Gulf deals, and Congress can attach conditions such as chip location verification to new bills like the NDAA.”

Chip location verification is a technical and regulatory method used to track the physical location of advanced processors—such as GPUs—to ensure they do not get smuggled or diverted to restricted countries.

However, on Monday, the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, issued an interim rule that requires companies to obtain licenses to export, reexport, or transfer AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if the equipment could be used by a list of 22 embargoed countries, which includes China. The move aims to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia’s computing power from data centers in third countries.

“The new remote access rule primarily affects Gulf companies if they are renting large amounts of compute to Chinese-parented firms, but otherwise does not fundamentally change the situation for the UAE,” said Winter-Levy.

“It does, however, signal that the administration is increasingly prepared to crack down on chip diversion and remote access if it becomes politically salient enough.”

In the future, it seems increasingly likely that the Gulf will become more vulnerable to U.S. export controls given that, even before Huang’s abrupt departure, Democratic lawmakers had already pushed back against what they viewed as its preferential treatment. They frequently cited fears that China could obtain backdoor access to sensitive U.S. technology through the Gulf.

“There will probably be more political noise out of Washington that could slow some deliveries or stretch timelines,” said Soliman.

However, the region’s growing role in financing and supporting America’s AI infrastructure could also give the region some leverage in return, according to Winter-Levy.

“The dependence isn’t entirely one-way,” he said. “Gulf capital is now part of the American AI buildout, which gives them some leverage. And if U.S. companies come to rely on large quantities of compute housed in the Gulf, that will give the Gulf a degree of leverage over those companies. But the asymmetry is large, since Washington can slow the Gulf’s AI plans with a regulatory notice.”

Ultimately, Nvidia’s upheaval is unlikely to derail the Gulf’s AI ambitions, but it exposes just how dependent those ambitions remain on decisions made in Washington and Silicon Valley.

The UAE and Saudi Arabia have invested heavily in positioning themselves as global AI powerhouses, but their ability to deliver on those plans hinges on continued access to U.S. technology and political goodwill.

As scrutiny of chip exports intensifies, the challenge for both countries will be to maintain their strategic partnerships while reducing their exposure to shifting U.S. political priorities. For the Gulf, the question is no longer simply whether Nvidia can deliver the chips, but whether Washington will continue to let them.

Melissa has specialized in covering the region for 20 years, during which time she has worked for a range of well-known publications including AGBI, MEED, Forbes Middle East and MEES. #5354. Officials blame aging FAA telecom gear as U.S. airspace reopens, see no link to Microsoft or AI

by Todd Bishop on Nov 13, 2026 at 3:04 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 7:58 pm

Updated with officials’ explanation of the cause and the reopening of U.S. airspace.

The nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. commercial air travel Friday was not caused by the Microsoft 365 outage that began a day earlier, federal officials said at an evening news conference, blaming aging FAA telecom equipment that was overloaded with data.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened the news conference by raising the Microsoft outage himself. “I want to make sure everybody understands that there is no connection between this and Microsoft,” he said. “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy likewise ruled out a role for SMART, the FAA’s new AI traffic-planning tool, saying it isn’t connected to the core systems controllers use to track flights.

“There was no possible way SMART would have impacted what happened today,” he said.

The FAA reopened U.S. airspace at 5:15 p.m. Pacific, more than four hours after the problems began, Duffy said. He said flights would resume slowly, depending on whether airlines had crews available, and some may not depart until Saturday morning.

Microsoft confirmed in a statement that it had no indication the FAA ground stop was related to its service disruption.

Asked whether a cyberattack or “rogue AI” could be ruled out, Mullin said there was “nothing completely certain right now,” but “it appears that this was mechanically driven.” He said he could not rule out the possibility of a cyberattack but said there was “zero evidence” of one so far.

What happened: Duffy said the FAA began seeing unstable radar and communications data at air traffic control facilities across the country at 12:36 p.m. Pacific. Aging switches and routers in the agency’s telecom network “got overloaded with data” and began producing inconsistent information, he said, adding that the FAA still relies on “1980s little copper lines.”

“Our new IP switches did not go down. It’s the old hardware that went down,” he said. The FAA restored service after deploying fixes to reduce the overloading on its switches, he said.

Mullin said the overload appeared to have been triggered by new equipment the FAA was installing. As the agency put “patches into the system” and added “new equipment and new technology,” he said, it “was overwhelming the older system.” Neither official said exactly what that equipment was.

The FAA is in the middle of replacing its legacy telecom network with a modern internet-protocol network. AT&T took over the lead role on that project in August with an initial $74.3 million award, as the FAA works toward a goal of finishing by the end of 2028.

Duffy and Mullin used the briefing to press Congress for money to finish rebuilding the air traffic control system. Mullin said President Trump has declared the situation a national emergency.

The administration has asked Congress for an additional $30.1 billion for aviation infrastructure, AeroTime reported. Duffy said at the evening news conference that he wants $50 billion.

Earlier in the day, Mullin had said officials were looking into a possible link to SMART, including through DHS’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). The FAA said Tuesday it was expanding the system to the airspace managed by all 22 of its en route air traffic control centers.

The agency describes SMART as a cloud-based system that pulls in about 200 data streams, including weather, flight paths and controller staffing, to recommend flight schedules and routes. FAA specialists review its recommendations, and local facilities decide whether to act on them.

SMART is part of a 12-year, $875 million FAA contract with Boston-based Air Space Intelligence, which denied any connection to the issue. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said.

The FAA halted departures nationwide shortly before 1 p.m. Pacific. More than 3,500 planes were in the air at the time, Duffy said. It’s the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11 attacks, after a January 2023 failure of the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system.

FlightAware counted nearly 7,000 flights delayed or canceled as of Friday afternoon.

#5353. Akash’s Solana Migration Clears November 2 Vote at 97%, With Four More On-Chain Decisions Ahead

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

But a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

Proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration plan and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

The technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It shows how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository says a yes vote does two things:

It also says plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain."

A no vote would stop the whole plan. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis."

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 showed an expected result of "Will PASS":

Turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

The tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC showed almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

The portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks."

Why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

The spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

At launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence shows what that requirement means on-chain.

So Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

For now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":

The second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the plan goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

#5352. Booking Holdings is combining its partner businesses into a new B2B travel division

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Booking Partner Division will combine Booking.com Strategic Partnerships and Rocket Travel by Agoda starting in January 2027

Booking Holdings $BKNG announced a new global business-to-business organization on Wednesday that will merge the partner operations of Booking.com and Agoda. The unit, called Booking Partner Division, will be operational from January 2027, the company said.

The division builds on Booking.com Strategic Partnerships and Rocket Travel by Agoda. It will work with banks, financial institutions, airlines, online travel companies, travel technology platforms, affiliates, advertisers and publishers. Teams and leadership from both units will join the organization, which will operate across the Americas, Europe, the Middle East and Asia-Pacific.

Its solutions span White Label, API, Branded Solutions and Chain B2B Rates Distribution. The company said the portfolio covers more than 4.7 million properties and over 33 million accommodation listings, along with upwards of 500 airlines and 200-plus car rental providers. Existing partners can continue to rely on current relationships and capabilities as the organization comes together, it said.

Omri Morgenshtern, CEO of Booking Partner Division, will lead the unit. He is also the CEO of Agoda, according to CNBC.

"By bringing together the strengths we've built and developed within Booking Holdings, we can bring more of what we do best to partners and their customers today, while creating the focus and agility to innovate faster, harness emerging technologies like AI, and build the solutions they need to thrive," Morgenshtern said in a statement.

Glenn Fogel, CEO of Booking Holdings, said in a statement that connecting the company's strengths "in new ways" would help it "accelerate innovation, open up new opportunities for growth and ultimately deliver more for partners, their customers and travelers."

Morgenshtern told CNBC that focusing on both product and go-to-market efforts could let the company "grow faster and serve better partners." He would not put a figure on what the division might add to Booking Holdings' revenue and profit, and he pegged the size of the total addressable market at $2 trillion, according to CNBC.

The company said the division will develop AI capabilities to help partners build more personalized travel experiences. Booking expects those tools to build on what it already knows about travel, while keeping token costs low, according to CNBC. Morgenshtern told CNBC he is "super optimistic" about a vertical agent that Booking will offer partners.

#5351. Nvidia’s earnings boom meets a governance test

Good morning. Nvidia’s third-quarter earnings call, the first for CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, came less than a week after Jensen Huang resigned. The company delivered stronger-than-expected results, but the leadership transition and a new emphasis on board oversight put governance and regulatory compliance front and center.

“Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing,” Kress said Tuesday on the call.

Board Chair Harvey Jones ended speculation about Huang’s return. “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said. The board is conducting an independent investigation after Huang disclosed personal behavior inconsistent with company standards.

Heidrick & Struggles has been retained to conduct an internal and external search for Huang’s permanent replacement. Jones said the board is “enhancing our oversight capacity going forward.” He noted the formation of the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee to oversee national security policies, export-control compliance and global trade risks. Nvidia’s national security and trade compliance teams will report directly to the committee and to Kress for day-to-day operations.

The move underscores the growing importance of compliance for Nvidia and its new leadership amid questions about the potential diversion of advanced AI chips to China.

The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security announced Monday an interim final rule addressing remote access to advanced computing technology through overseas data centers. Developed at the direction of the Treasury Department and National Security Council, the rule is intended to prevent companies in restricted countries from bypassing export controls through remote computing.

At the center of the issue are questions about whether advanced Nvidia chips supplied through Megaspeed were diverted to China. U.S. export rules have allowed certain overseas data centers to provide remote computing services to Chinese customers, a distinction from unauthorized transfers of restricted physical chips, Fortune reported.

Kress said third-quarter sales of licensed Hopper data center products to China totaled $2.4 billion. However, she added: “Our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China.”

For CFOs and corporate directors, Nvidia’s predicament illustrates a broader challenge: As companies expand into strategically sensitive markets, financial performance increasingly depends on the strength of their compliance systems, third-party oversight and internal controls.

For the third quarter ended Oct. 25, Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% year over year, and data center revenue of $107.6 billion, up 110%.

Nvidia also raised its fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to approximately 75%, up from its previous projection of 70% and based on a higher fiscal 2027 revenue base, Kress said. Shares rose about 4% in overnight trading.

Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director of Yorkville Ives & Co., wrote in a note Wednesday morning that the board had drawn a line on Huang’s reinstatement, Kress had raised the number that matters most, and the financing discipline investors wanted appeared unprompted. The firm maintains its outperform rating and $225 price target.

“The CEO search, the investigation, and the 15% special meeting threshold are the open questions we are still waiting on,” he added.

With a growth engine that remains powerful, the more difficult test for Nvidia’s new leadership will be showing that the company’s governance and compliance structures are equally capable of managing the risks.

#5350. Gov. Ferguson seeks $10M to help develop Eastern Wash. clean-energy hub

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 13, 2026 at 4:32 pmNovember 16, 2026 at 10:09 am

Gov. Bob Ferguson is proposing $10 million to fund basic infrastructure needed for the Northwest Advanced Clean Energy Park, a master-planned industrial area in Eastern Washington that will foster development of large-scale clean energy, advanced manufacturing and supply chains. The proposal will be included in his 2027–29 capital budget.

If approved by lawmakers, the funding would support sewer, water, electrical and road infrastructure at the park.

“This investment will support thousands of good-paying jobs in the trades and advanced industries, and unlock billions in private investment,” Ferguson said in a statement.

The 1,641-acre site was formerly part of the Hanford Nuclear Reservation, a sprawling federal property along the Columbia River near the Tri-Cities that is undergoing a massive environmental cleanup. Hanford was established during World War II to produce plutonium for the Manhattan Project.

Mel Clark, president and CEO of the CleanTech Alliance, an industry trade group, welcomed the news as the state struggles to get clean power plugged into the grid.

“Washington needs more energy generation, more clean energy, and more manufacturing,” Clark told GeekWire via email. “We’re excited to see the Governor take action to change our last-place ranking in building new clean energy projects.”

According to the governor’s office, two projects have committed to locating at the park once infrastructure construction is complete: Atlas Agro’s low-carbon fertilizer production plant and the utility-scale Ruby Flats Solar Farm.

State officials said General Matter is also considering the location for producing advanced nuclear fuel for small reactors. That siting could potentially be beneficial for another project planned for the same area: Amazon, X-energy and Energy Northwest are developing plans for the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility, a nuclear plant comprised of clustered, small reactors.

In 2024, the Norwegian company Cenate expressed interest in building a factory at the park to produce lithium-ion battery components, according to the Tri-Cities Area Journal of Business, ultimately withdrew its plans.

The Tri-Cities is also attracting fusion-energy investment. Last year, Seattle startup Avalanche Energy landed a $10 million grant from the Washington State Department of Commerce’s Green Jobs Grant Program to develop FusionWERX, a commercial-scale testing facility for fusion technologies. The project is being developed in an existing Port of Benton building in Richland.

Washington is heading into its 2027–29 biennial budget with a multibillion-dollar shortfall, but officials have not yet settled on a definitive public estimate.

Ferguson has acknowledged the scale of the gap but has not publicly specified an amount. The shortfall concerns the state’s operating budget, which is separate from the capital budget funding proposed for the energy park.

Editor’s note: Comment from CleanTech Alliance President and CEO Mel Clark added 11/16.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5349. Hackers Hijack 178 Major Websites, Including BBC, Zoom, CNN, HSBC, and Ledger

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Hackers have turned some of the world’s most recognizable websites into potential crypto theft traps after compromising a third-party platform used by 178 major organizations. The attack injected malicious JavaScript through Optimizely, a website experimentation platform trusted by companies including BBC, Zoom, CNN, HSBC, Salesforce, IKEA, and crypto hardware wallet maker Ledger.

Visitors could unknowingly load malware simply by opening an affected webpage, and the consequences go far beyond stolen browsing data. The malicious code can replace crypto wallet addresses copied to the clipboard, redirecting payments straight into attackers’ wallets. Security researchers have already identified $7,040 in crypto received by wallets linked to the campaign.

🚨 BREAKING: Ledger and 177 other major organizations, including Zoom, CNN, and Salesforce, were affected by a massive JavaScript attack.The malware stole cryptocurrency, payment card details, and user data, while also targeting iPhones with exploit kits.

The investigation by cybersecurity firm Report URI identified 188 infected JavaScript snippets belonging to 178 organizations after examining 1,611 Optimizely scripts. The malware operated through trusted website infrastructure, making the attack particularly dangerous. Rather than breaking into every company’s servers individually, attackers injected malicious code into Optimizely customer projects.

Affected websites continued loading JavaScript through Optimizely’s legitimate content delivery network. Visitors had little reason to suspect that a familiar website was serving malicious instructions. This is a dangerous clipboard hijacking mechanism.

The malware searched webpages for crypto wallet addresses and replaced legitimate destinations with addresses controlled by attackers. It could also intercept copied addresses, meaning someone browsing an affected website could potentially paste a fraudulent wallet address elsewhere.

The attack targeted several major crypto networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, TRON, and Litecoin.

A victim could believe they were sending funds to an exchange, another wallet, or a friend. Instead, the transaction could land directly in an attacker’s wallet.

Report URI identified $7,040 in receipts across attacker-controlled wallets by November 16. The funds included Bitcoin, Litecoin, Ethereum, TRON, and stablecoins.

The scale of the incident raises questions about how much trust businesses place in third-party website services. The affected organizations span several industries, including banking, technology, media, retail, and crypto.

HSBC was among the financial institutions affected, alongside Equifax and other major organizations. BBC, CNN, Fox News, Zoom, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, and Air France-KLM also appeared in Report URI’s investigation.

Ledger’s inclusion makes the incident particularly concerning for crypto users. The company is known for its hardware wallets, which help customers store private keys away from internet-connected devices. However, the incident demonstrates how threats can reach users through ordinary browsing activity, outside the hardware wallet itself.

The malicious campaign also contained capabilities targeting Apple devices. Researchers identified exploit infrastructure associated with Coruna and DarkSword, two iOS exploit kits designed to target vulnerabilities in iPhones and iPads.

This means the operation was not limited to stealing crypto or payment information. It also carried tools capable of targeting mobile devices through malicious webpage content.

Optimizely confirmed that attackers exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation account signup flow to inject malicious JavaScript into customer projects. The company said it blocked access to the vulnerable pathway, deployed a fix, removed injected code, revoked active tokens, and reset access for affected accounts.

Earlier today, Optimizely identified and contained a security incident affecting some Optimizely Web Experimentation customers. The vulnerable path is blocked, the injected code was removed, and customers have been contacted directly. Updates: https://t.co/ptZHZviIeC

However, the incident raises serious questions about third-party website security. Report URI’s investigation found that even Optimizely’s own websites carried the malicious code. Researchers also observed the attacker rebuilding the malware 26 times during the campaign, adding capabilities and additional cryptocurrency wallets.

Most infected snippets were subsequently cleaned up, with Report URI finding only one remaining infected snippet in its final November 16 sweep.

But the financial damage and potential exposure remain difficult to measure. Researchers have identified crypto receipts, but the number of affected visitors, compromised payment cards, and exposed browser sessions remains unknown.

The bigger problem is that website visitors rarely know which third-party scripts are running behind the pages they trust. A familiar banking website, news outlet, or crypto platform can become an unexpected entry point for malicious code without its visitors noticing anything unusual.
