#5348. 10 of the best-selling video games of all time, from Tetris to Minecraft

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A selection of 10 best-selling video games of all time, from Tetris to Minecraft, with publisher-reported sales figures where available and the history behind each title

A falling-block puzzle created in the Soviet Union in 1985 and an island-building life simulation released on the Nintendo Switch in 2020 have something in common. Both are among the best-selling video games of all time. The 35 years between them cover several generations of consoles and a wide range of genres.

This article gathers 10 of those games. It is a selection, not a complete ranking, and the titles appear in order of first release rather than by sales. That order also tracks the hardware they arrived on. The earliest entries ran on the Nintendo Entertainment System and the Game Boy. Later ones launched on the Wii, the Switch and consoles from Sony $SONY and Microsoft $MSFT.

Game sales figures are moving targets. Most of the totals here come from the publishers or their parent companies. Those totals keep climbing as new copies sell. A number reported in one year can be out of date the next. Each figure in this piece is tied to the company that reported it.

The figures do not always measure the same thing. Take-Two Interactive $TTWO, the parent company of Rockstar Games, reports units shipped for Grand Theft Auto V and Red Dead Redemption 2. Shipments and sales are separate measures. Nintendo, Microsoft and CD Projekt describe their totals as copies sold. Most figures in this piece carry the phrase "more than." That wording marks each one as a floor at the time it was reported, not a final count. Nintendo's figure for Wii Sports is an approximate one instead. Two entries, Tetris and the original Pokémon games, appear without any sales figure.

Hardware bundles shaped several of these totals. When a game comes packed in the box with a new console, every system sold in that package adds a copy to the game's count. Nintendo paired Super Mario Bros. with the NES this way. Wii Sports came with the Wii in many regions. In 1989, Nintendo also packed a version of Tetris with the Game Boy.

The selection also spans many genres. It moves from puzzle and platform games to creature-collecting role-playing, motion-controlled sports and sandbox building. It also includes open-world crime, fantasy role-playing, kart racing, a frontier western and a life simulation. Each slide that follows covers what the game is, who made it and when it arrived.

Tetris is a falling-block puzzle game that Alexey Pajitnov created in the Soviet Union in 1985.

The whole game rests on one mechanic. Blocks drop into the playing area, and the player arranges them on the way down. There is no story to follow and no cast of characters to learn.

In 1989, Nintendo put a version of Tetris in the box with its Game Boy handheld. That pairing carried a puzzle game designed in the Soviet Union to Nintendo's portable audience.

Tetris did not stay tied to the Game Boy. Versions of the game have been released on many platforms. Its popularity carries across those machines rather than resting on any single one.

Super Mario Bros., which Nintendo released for the Nintendo Entertainment System in 1985, has sold more than 40 million copies, according to Nintendo. The game established the side-scrolling platformer format that later Mario games built on.

Many of those copies came from bundling. Nintendo packaged Super Mario Bros. with the NES console itself. Many players got the game in the hardware box instead of buying it as a separate cartridge.

That history affects how the figure compares with other best-selling Nintendo games. The total tracks the reach of the NES as much as demand for Super Mario Bros. as a stand-alone purchase.

Super Mario Bros. is also the only 1985 release in this selection with a reported sales total. Tetris arrived the same year, but it carries no figure here.

The design is the game's other lasting contribution. In a side-scrolling platformer, the screen moves sideways as the player runs through a level. The player jumps between platforms to reach the end.

Super Mario Bros. built its levels around that structure. Later entries in the Mario series returned to the template that the 1985 NES release had established.

Pokémon Red, Green and Blue are the Game Boy games that launched the Pokémon series. Game Freak developed them, and Nintendo published them. They first went on sale in Japan in 1996.

The work was divided between the two companies. Game Freak built the games. Nintendo released them on its own hardware.

Each version centers on one activity. The player catches creatures called Pokémon and then trains them. That catch-and-train loop places the games in the creature-collecting role-playing genre.

The Game Boy was Nintendo's handheld console. It ran on batteries rather than plugging into a television. A player could carry the whole game in a pocket and keep building a collection away from home.

Wii Sports has sold about 82.9 million copies, according to Nintendo. The company released the game in 2006 alongside its Wii console.

The disc collects five sports: tennis, baseball, bowling, golf and boxing. Every event runs on the Wii's motion controls. Players swing, throw and punch with the controller in hand. The game turns those physical movements into actions on screen.

That design made the game inseparable from its hardware. Each event was built around the Wii's motion-sensing controller, so Wii Sports could only be played on the console it launched with.

In many regions, buyers did not pick up Wii Sports as a separate purchase. Nintendo packed it in the box with the Wii. In those markets, the game reached every household that bought the console in that package.

That means its sales total reflects demand for the Wii as well as demand for the game itself. Both the design and the distribution of Wii Sports traced back to the same machine. It is one of the best-selling Nintendo games.

Minecraft had passed 300 million copies sold, Microsoft $MSFT said in 2023. The game is commonly cited as the best-selling single video game.

Mojang Studios released the full version of Minecraft on November 18, 2011. That finished release came three years before Mojang changed hands.

Minecraft is a sandbox game. Players dig into the world to mine resources. They then turn those materials into structures of their own design.

That loop of gathering and building is the core of the game. The player decides what to collect, where to dig and what to make from it. In a sandbox, the player sets the goals.

Microsoft bought Mojang, the studio behind Minecraft, in 2014. Microsoft reported the 300 million milestone nine years after that acquisition. The total therefore covers copies sold both before and after the game came under Microsoft's ownership.

Grand Theft Auto V has shipped more than 200 million units across its platforms, according to Take-Two Interactive $TTWO.

Rockstar North developed the open-world crime game. Rockstar Games published it.

The game launched on September 17, 2013. Its first release came on two consoles — PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360.

Take-Two's shipment total combines every platform the game has appeared on. It does not describe sales on any single console.

The story takes place in San Andreas, a fictional state. Instead of following a single lead, players control three protagonists.

Those three characters are Michael, Franklin and Trevor.

CD Projekt has reported sales of more than 50 million copies of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt. CD Projekt Red released the fantasy role-playing game on May 19, 2015.

The game is based on the Witcher books by the Polish author Andrzej Sapkowski. Its setting and characters come from that series of novels.

That literary source sets it apart from the other nine games in this selection. Each of those began as an original video game property. None was adapted from a book series.

Mario Kart 8 Deluxe is the best-selling game in Nintendo's Mario Kart series. Nintendo has reported sales of more than 60 million copies.

Nintendo released Mario Kart 8 Deluxe on the Nintendo Switch on April 28, 2017. That reported total counts copies of the Switch edition.

The game did not begin life on the Switch. It is an expanded version of Mario Kart 8, a kart racer that first came out on Nintendo's Wii U.

Its place at the top of the Mario Kart series came from that expanded version. Nintendo's best-selling kart racer is a reworked earlier release rather than an entry built from scratch for the Switch.

Red Dead Redemption 2 has shipped more than 60 million copies, according to Take-Two Interactive $TTWO. Rockstar Games released the western on October 26, 2018.

The story is set in 1899. Its central character is Arthur Morgan, an outlaw.

Morgan rides with the Van der Linde gang. The player follows events from inside that group, through Morgan's eyes.

Rockstar Games also published Grand Theft Auto V, which launched in 2013. Red Dead Redemption 2 arrived from the same publisher five years later. It traded a modern fictional state for a frontier setting at the close of the 19th century.

Animal Crossing: New Horizons is a life simulation that Nintendo released on the Switch on March 20, 2020. Nintendo has reported more than 45 million copies sold.

The premise is simple. The player arrives on a deserted island and develops it.

That design places the game in the life simulation genre. Progress comes from shaping one place over time rather than from winning a race or finishing a level.

New Horizons is the latest release in this selection. It arrived 35 years after Tetris and Super Mario Bros., which both date to 1985.

It is also one of two Switch games here. The other is Mario Kart 8 Deluxe, which came out on April 28, 2017. Nintendo has reported more than 60 million copies sold for that racing game.

#5346. Current price of oil as of November 17, 2026

As of 8:15 a.m. Eastern Time on November 17, 2026, oil is trading at $94.94 per barrel, based on the Brent benchmark we’ll explain in a bit. That’s $1.74 below yesterday morning’s level and about $30.70 higher than where it stood a year ago.

No one can say for sure where oil prices will go next. Many forces shape the market—but at the core, it’s still about supply and demand. When risks like a potential recession or war ramp up, oil prices can change direction quickly.

When you buy gas at the pump, you’re covering more than the cost of crude oil. You’re also paying for every step in the process, including refineries, wholesalers, taxes, and the markup your local gas station adds.

Even so, crude oil has the biggest influence on what you pay, often making up more than half the cost per gallon. When oil prices jump, gas prices usually climb right along with them. But when oil falls, gas prices often slip much more slowly—a pattern sometimes called “rockets and feathers.”

If an emergency hits, the U.S. keeps a backup supply of crude oil called the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. It’s mainly there to protect energy security during crises, such as sanctions, catastrophic storm damage, even war. It can also help cushion the blow when supply shocks send prices soaring.

It’s not meant to solve long-term problems. Instead, it provides quick relief for consumers and helps keep vital parts of the economy moving, like essential industries, emergency services, and public transit.

Oil and natural gas are two of the world’s primary energy sources. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by extension. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which which increases demand for natural gas.

When looking at how oil performs, two main benchmarks stand out:

Of the two, Brent gives a better picture of global oil performance because it prices a large share of the world’s traded crude. It’s also the go-to for tracking oil’s historical trends. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now relies on Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

If you look at the Brent benchmark over several decades, oil has been far from stable. It has experienced sharp rises tied to wars and supply cuts, along with steep drops linked to global recessions and oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:

To sum up, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s heavily influenced by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, shifting energy policies, and much more.

Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage:

The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic.

The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing.

In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply.

When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf.

#5345. 6 regional park passes and the visitors who get the most from them

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Six regional passes cover parks from Hawaiʻi to Utah to the Oregon coast. See who saves, who doesn't and which limits apply.

Most people hear "fee-free" and picture a park entrance where nobody collects money on one special day of the year. For someone who keeps returning to the same corner of the country, the more dependable way in is a single pass, bought once and honored by parks that sit near one another. These arrangements are still changing. A yearly pass from Crater Lake, Lassen Volcanic, Lava Beds or Whiskeytown has worked at all four of these parks on either side of the California-Oregon line only since Jan. 1, 2023, according to the National Park Service. Hawaiʻi's three-park pass changed how visitors buy and sign it on Jan. 1, 2024, according to the Hawaiʻi Tourism Authority, so what a traveler heard about these passes a year or two ago may not hold now. At least one regional deal has also been the cheaper way in. When the four western parks joined forces in 2023, their shared annual pass cost $55, while the nationwide interagency annual pass cost $80. On the Atlantic shore, the seashore and the wildlife refuge each sold their own yearly pass for $45 in 2020, according to 47abc. The savings go to people who keep coming back to one region, not to someone crossing the country once.

A regional pass is a bargain only for a certain kind of visitor, and at some of these parks the children in the car were never paying in the first place. Visitors under 16 enter the four California and Oregon parks free, according to the National Park Service. In Arizona, Recreation.gov reports that Sunset Crater Volcano National Monument charges no one younger than 16 to get in. The decision about a pass falls on the adults. For adults who travel widely, the nationwide pass can make a regional one a waste of money. "Do NOT purchase a site pass now if you have a valid America the Beautiful annual or lifetime pass OR are planning to get one," Recreation.gov, the federal reservation and pass site, said. Anyone planning trips across several regions should weigh the nationwide pass first. Choosing a regional pass is a bet on how many trips a visitor will take and how many of them will stay within one cluster of parks.

The National Park Service set out to show which annual passes work across several parks or sites. These passes cover very different kinds of places, so the right one depends on which landscape a visitor keeps returning to. They reach from Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park to Arches National Park in Utah. One covers the state and federal sites along Oregon's coast, and another belongs to a seashore whose pass the wildlife refuge next door accepts. Each pass carries a single name, but what it covers, who can use it and what it cost when last priced differ more than that name suggests. Whether a pass pays off depends less on its price than on how often a visitor comes back to the same place.

A visitor who keeps coming back to the volcanic and sacred landscapes of Hawaiʻi can buy the Tri-Park Pass once and enter Haleakalā, Hawaiʻi Volcanoes and Puʻuhonua ʻO Hōnaunau for a year, according to the National Park Service. The year is counted from the day of purchase rather than from Jan. 1. A buyer who comes for a spring trip can still use the pass on a return visit the following winter. Someone who visits once and never returns gets little from it, while a traveler who goes back to the crater, the lava fields or the place of refuge within those 12 months gets its full value.

Visitors can settle entry to all three parks before they leave home instead of sorting it out at the first entrance station. The Hawaiʻi Tourism Authority reports that travelers can get a digital version of the pass from Recreation.gov before their trip. That puts the pass on the packing checklist rather than among the arrival-day errands, and a traveler can buy it before boarding the flight.

The pass covers three federal parks, not the rest of the islands. A beach day outside those parks can still cost money, and the county charges for parking at Kahaluʻu Bay, according to the Hawaiʻi Tourism Authority. Travelers $TRV who mix volcano days with beaches and county stops should expect to pay at other lots. For them, the pass covers only the national park share of the budget.

The traveler who gets the most from the pass is the one who returns to these three parks again and again within the year.

The Southeast Utah Parks Annual Pass puts two quieter national monuments on the same purchase as the region's famous parks. Arches and Canyonlands national parks, along with Natural Bridges and Hovenweep national monuments, all accept this single yearly pass, according to the National Park Service. In 2014, St. George News reports, the pass covered those same four sites, so its reach has held steady even where other terms are hard to confirm. A visitor headed for Arches or Canyonlands can add the two monuments to the year's travels without buying another pass.

The real savings went to people who kept coming back. In 2014 the annual pass cost $25, while paying separately at the four sites came to about $32, according to St. George News. For a visitor who paid those separate fees, the pass saved only a small amount. A pass holder who returned later that year paid nothing more at the gate. That made the pass a better deal for people who live within driving distance and visit these canyons again and again than for a tourist passing through once.

Anyone counting on that bargain should check it first. The National Park Service gives no price, validity period or vehicle terms for this pass, though it does for some other group passes. The $25 price dates from 2014, according to St. George News, and there is no current price to compare against it. A buyer should confirm the price and terms with the parks before planning a year of visits around the pass.

For the Utah visitor who keeps returning to these canyons and monuments, this is the pass to ask about first.

Only one pass gets a visitor into all three national monuments around Flagstaff, Ariz. The annual pass gives a year of entry to the three Flagstaff-area monuments for a vehicle or a motorcyclist, according to the National Park Service. Recreation.gov lists those monuments as Sunset Crater, Wupatki and Walnut Canyon. Sunset Crater Volcano, Walnut Canyon and Wupatki are separate national monuments, so a visitor can spread them across different outings during the year. The shorter option is narrower. The seven-day passes cover Sunset Crater and Wupatki only, which means anyone who wants to see Walnut Canyon has to buy the annual pass. A seven-day pass fits a single trip to two monuments, while the annual pass is the one designed for people who come back. A visitor who has decided on the canyon has, in effect, already decided on the full year.

The pass covers a whole carload, but the person who bought it has to come along on every visit. It lets in the holder with everyone riding in one noncommercial vehicle, or with a single passenger on a motorcycle. Recreation.gov reports that only the buyer may use a pass, with photo identification shown at every visit, and that no new one is issued if it goes missing. A neighbor or relative can't borrow the pass for a separate carload, so it serves only the trips its buyer takes. A holder who loses the pass early in its year gives up all the months still left on it.

The Flagstaff pass pays off for someone who lives near these monuments or returns to them often, and who will be in the car on every visit.

The 4-Park Pass is an agreement among four parks, not a single card. Whiskeytown, Lassen Volcanic and Lava Beds in Northern California and Crater Lake in Southern Oregon each honor one another's yearly passes, according to the National Park Service. The parks built the arrangement in stages. The National Park Service reports that they planned a single combined pass for 2024, after they had already begun accepting each other's passes. Each of the four parks sells its own annual pass and accepts the other three, and no separate price appears for the combined pass. A buyer should ask at the entrance which pass they are getting before paying. In practice, a visitor buys one park's pass and uses it at the other three, and the sensible place to buy it is the park they plan to visit first.

Shared passes are simpler to use, but they cost more for regular visitors to one park. The parks set one price for all four passes, and the National Park Service reports that they raised the Lava Beds pass by $10 starting in 2023 to match the others. Before then, Lava Beds sold the cheapest pass of the four, at $45. A visitor who only ever returns to Lava Beds pays more for entry to three parks they may never use. The higher price makes sense for the adult who drives to Crater Lake, Lassen Volcanic and Whiskeytown in the same year.

Seniors have little reason to buy any of these four passes. The national senior annual pass cost $20 in December 2022, according to the National Park Service. That was less than any of the four parks charged for its own annual pass, and the senior pass works at parks across the country.

The four-park agreement is a bargain for adults too young for the senior pass who keep returning to this stretch of the West, and everyone else should look at a different pass first.

Along the Oregon coast, the fee most visitors pay is for parking, and the Oregon Coast Passport lets a driver pay it once for a whole year. The National Park Service describes the passport as one year of paid access to Oregon's coastal state and federal sites, with parking included. Different levels of government run the stops along this shore. Without the pass, a driver heading down the coast road pays at one lot and then pays again at the next. A single passport is honored at both the state and the federal sites, so that driver can stop paying lot by lot. The pass lasts 12 months, and every extra coastal outing within that year lowers the cost of each visit. It makes sense for someone who leaves the highway again and again over the seasons. A visitor who makes one stop on one trip gets little from it.

Some overnight visitors may not need the passport at all. A camper at Shore Acres State Park shows a camping receipt on the dashboard in front of the driver's seat, according to Travel Oregon. With that receipt already in view, the camper may have no use for a separate passport during the stay. The passport's likely buyers at Shore Acres are day-trippers and travelers who sleep somewhere other than the park's campground.

The passport is for the driver who keeps leaving the coast and coming back, while a camper at Shore Acres may already be covered.

The Assateague pass serves one shoreline rather than a network of parks. Assateague Island National Seashore and Chincoteague National Wildlife Refuge each accept the other's annual pass, according to the National Park Service. As of 2020, the refuge and the seashore jointly ran the Virginia end of the island, according to 47abc, so a pass that both sites accept matches how that stretch of beach is managed. The seashore is in Maryland and the refuge is in Virginia, so a single pass works across a state line and at two federal sites. A visitor traveling along the island never has to work out whose land they are on. The pass suits someone who keeps returning to this one island, not someone planning a road trip through several parks.

Drivers gain the most from the pass. In 2020 the refuge waived its entrance fee for hikers, cyclists and riders on the local courtesy shuttle, according to 47abc. Visitors who arrived those ways had no reason to buy it.

A Federal Duck Stamp did not cover beach parking on its own. Stamp holders in 2020 had to buy a separate yearly permit for $20 before they could park at the recreational beach, according to 47abc. Visitors who expect a federal stamp to settle every fee on the island should check what it covers before they arrive.

Buyers should confirm this pass's price before they rely on it. The National Park Service lists no price, validity period or place to buy it. The refuge prices on record were announced in June 2020, according to 47abc, and the two sites may charge something different today.

On Assateague, the pass is worth buying for a driver who returns often to one shared beach, once that driver has confirmed its current terms with the two sites.

#5344. ‘I hope this email finds you’: Microsoft declares outage over as the world digs out of its inbox

by Todd Bishop on Nov 14, 2026 at 10:35 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:28 am

Steven Sinofsky was relieved this week to finally give up a title he never wanted.

“Somewhat happy to say I am no longer responsible for the worst Outlook outage,” the former Microsoft executive posted on X Friday, sharing a May 2000 news story about the “I Love You” worm, which overwhelmed corporate email systems when he ran the Office group.

Later in the day, he aired a pet peeve. After a plumber emailed to say he’d missed an appointment because of the “Outlook outage,” Sinofsky noted that this one wasn’t really the application’s fault. “This time it is the data center layer,” he wrote.

Microsoft’s explanation backs him up. The company says the failure, which cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries this week, was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade in its Microsoft 365 cloud and surfaced after a more recent network change. It hasn’t given more details.

The company said late Friday it had restored service to the remaining customers and regions. The disruption lasted about 30 hours, according to Microsoft’s incident log. Microsoft offered a public apology and promised a detailed post-mortem explaining what went wrong and next steps.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said on X Friday afternoon that “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” made recovery more difficult than normal.

A “thundering herd” isn’t a stampede of frustrated IT admins descending on Redmond, as fitting as that might have been. It happens when huge numbers of devices try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online.

He said the post-mortem would come “shortly,” with a “step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future.” In a reply to another user, he said Microsoft “will be very specific on what happened.” In its notice to customers, Microsoft said it would provide a preliminary post-incident report within two business days and a final report within five.

In the meantime, like prior incidents involving AWS and others, the “Outlook outage” became the latest example of how much depends on one company’s cloud.

Microsoft reported in January that it had more than 450 million paid commercial Microsoft 365 seats, roughly one for every 18 people on Earth.

Among those affected this week were Unity Health Toronto, a hospital network that had to declare a Code Grey, the alert for a systems failure; a Colorado jail that couldn’t take online bond payments; and Pennsylvania lawmakers who went about 18 hours without email. Unity Health said patient care continued without disruption.

In Japan, securities firms and asset managers fell back on fax machines when trade-confirmation emails stopped coming through, Business Upturn reported, citing Nikkei.

In New York, the city’s Emergency Management office warned of delays reaching city agencies. In Singapore, the outage disrupted some government systems, including email, and in London, the UK Supreme Court wasn’t receiving email.

About the only thing that wasn’t Microsoft’s fault was Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop. Federal officials blamed aging FAA telecom gear. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened an evening news conference — before even getting to the news that U.S. airspace had reopened — by saying there was “no connection between this and Microsoft,” adding, “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”

Microsoft itself looked to preempt the speculation a few hours earlier, posting on X that it had “no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services.”

The Microsoft 365 outage was at least the fourth significant one this year. A January outage lasted nearly 10 hours, and in July a bug in Microsoft’s automated network maintenance system disrupted Azure and Microsoft 365 services for hours. On Aug. 31, an Exchange Online outage also hit Teams, OneDrive and SharePoint.

Instead of “I hope this email finds you well,” many people joked, it should just be “I hope this email finds you.” (Consider this our nomination for the “Overworked Twitter Joke of the Week” on The Ringer’s Press Box podcast.)

Microsoft said Friday afternoon that it was watching the backlog of delayed email “to ensure all process successfully before considering the issue resolved.” The University of Washington’s IT department told its users that email delayed during the outage would be delivered as mail queues continued to be processed.

Many people coped with the flood of returning email with a bit of levity.

As the mail started flowing again, CNN chief media analyst Brian Stelter said he was getting “a deluge of emails from PR people pitching their clients to talk about the Outlook outage.” Most were sent during the outage, he noted, “which, fittingly, prevented the pitches from reaching me.”

The security company Malwarebytes captured the paradox in a message to its followers: “We regret to inform you that Teams and Outlook are coming back online after a global outage.”

#5343. Trump said colleges would ‘go to hell very quickly’ without foreign students. New enrollment just fell 18%, costing them billions in tuition

New international students at U.S. colleges fell 18% in the 2025–26 school year, to 228,123, the Institute of International Education said Monday in its annual Open Doors report. The first look at this fall points to a second straight drop. In IIE’s fall 2026 snapshot of more than 800 schools, new international enrollment fell another 15%.

The total looks calmer: 1,146,163 international students, down 3%. But that count includes 335,785 graduates on Optional Practical Training, the program that lets them work in the U.S. after their degree. That group rose 14%, and it pays no tuition. Take it out and the number of international students enrolled in classes fell about 8%, by Fortune’s math. That’s about 73,000 fewer students paying tuition.

The president saw this coming. At a cabinet meeting in August 2025, defending a plan to admit 600,000 Chinese students, Trump said that without them, “our college system would go to hell very quickly and it wouldn’t be the top colleges. It would be colleges that struggle on the bottom.” His base pushed back. Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene said that if keeping Chinese students out made some schools fail, “these schools should fail anyways because they are being propped up by the CCP.”

Since then, his administration has moved the other way. In May 2025 the State Department paused student visa interviews, then restarted them with expanded social media vetting. A travel ban that started with 19 countries grew to 39, plus the Palestinian territory, on Jan. 1. In July, DHS finalized a rule replacing open-ended student status with a fixed four-year limit and called it the end of “foreign student visa abuse.” A federal judge in Massachusetts blocked it in September. Among schools that reported declines this fall, 88% blamed the visa application process and 70% blamed travel restrictions, according to IIE’s snapshot.

The losses were concentrated in one corner of the campus. Graduate students fell 13% to 423,078, and master’s students fell 22%. Doctoral students rose 3%, and undergraduates slipped 0.3%. Indian graduate students, the biggest group, fell 34%.

IIE President and CEO Jason Czyz said the data “reaffirms the enduring importance of international education to the United States.”

Colleges don’t report how much tuition they lost to the drop, so here’s a rough estimate. University of North Texas President Harrison Keller has said each admitted master’s student who didn’t enroll would have brought his school between $20,000 and $25,000. Multiply the roughly 73,000 missing students by that range and you get about $1.5 billion to $1.8 billion in lost tuition. That’s a floor. UNT is a public university, and private schools charge international students much more.

Counting everything students spend, including rent, food and health care, NAFSA estimates international students’ economic contribution fell 7% in 2025–26, to $39.9 billion. That’s about $3 billion less than the year before. NAFSA, the trade group for international educators, puts the cost of this fall’s decline at another $2.4 billion and 31,000 jobs. Its members depend on these students, and its projections rest on surveys.

The money hurts more than the headcount suggests, because these students pay more than their share. Princeton research cited by the Hechinger Report found international students made up 6% of enrollment but 12% of college revenue. They usually pay close to full price and get little aid. In IIE’s survey, 60% of institutions said they recruit them partly for their “financial contributions.”

For most schools, the loss is manageable. Moody’s found in 2025 that a 15% drop in international tuition would barely affect operating margins at 77% of the universities it rates. But 15% of rated universities have more than 15% international students, and some have more than 30%. Under a 20% drop, Moody’s said, 15 universities could lose 2 to 8 points of operating margin. Moody’s and S&P have negative outlooks on higher education for 2026, and Fitch calls the outlook “deteriorating.” “We see revenue growing for the sector next year, but not as much as expenses,” Moody’s analyst Patrick Ronk told The Bond Buyer.

Trump’s “bottom” turned out to include Denton, Texas. UNT projected a $45 million shortfall as international enrollment fell, on top of a $32 million cut in state funding over two years, and it has eliminated 71 academic programs, the Hechinger Report found. “About 60% of UNT’s growth over the last few years has been in international graduate students,” Keller told the board in August 2025. “We’re overexposed compared to other institutions.” UNT had more than 1,300 fewer international students this fall.

The list is mostly private universities in big cities:

The public flagships aren’t immune. International enrollment fell 15.6% at Indiana this fall and 12.7% at Ohio State, Higher Ed Dive reported, and 12% at Pitt, according to the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette.

Domestic students are covering part of the gap. Syracuse, Northwestern, USC and the New School all raised tuition 3% to 4% while losing international students, Hechinger found. “It leaves a really big hole in the budget, which has to get filled one way or another,” UC Santa Barbara economist Dick Startz told the outlet.

College closures are speeding up too, but for a different reason. Hampshire College in Amherst, Mass., will close at the end of this semester, after enrollment fell by almost half since 2015 and it couldn’t refinance a $21 million bond. It’s one of nine colleges set to close in 2026, by The College Investor’s count. Huron Consulting Group says more than 440 of the country’s 1,700 private nonprofit four-year colleges are at risk, as the number of 18-year-olds starts to shrink.

The schools that close are mostly small undergraduate colleges with few international students. The schools losing international master’s students are bigger, and they cut jobs and programs instead. Public institutions “hardly ever close,” Higher Ed Dive noted in covering a Philadelphia Fed model. Fortune reported in August that the country’s high school graduating class is projected to shrink 13% by 2041, so both squeezes are arriving at the same time.

This year, the OPT boom kept the total from looking like a crisis. That’s the program the administration went after next. On Oct. 8, DHS proposed making schools pay $70,000 the first time they recommend a student for OPT and $30,000 for each recommendation after that; schools could pass those costs on to students or employers. In IIE’s survey, 95% of institutions said prospective students would look elsewhere if OPT were restricted. In the fall snapshot, OPT fell 6%, its first decline in five years. The full count for this fall comes in next November’s Open Doors report.

#5342. Who should run Nvidia? Our picks for Jensen Huang’s successor, whether the board likes it or not

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 14, 2026 at 2:10 pmNovember 14, 2026 at 2:10 pm

Nvidia’s board says it’s too early to speculate about who will succeed Jensen Huang. Sorry, we’re having too much fun coming up with names.

The board said in a statement Friday that it’s still choosing a search firm and hasn’t formally engaged any candidates. That came after the Financial Times reported that the board had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas — a name John had presciently floated when we recorded this week’s GeekWire Podcast on Thursday.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation Thursday, a day after the New York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Colette Kress, the company’s longtime CFO, is serving as interim CEO. She spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to run a deliberate search that leaves open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Elon Musk said on X that he was signing a petition to reinstate Huang.

The organizers of one, called “Stand with Jensen,” say it has more than 108,000 names, including more than 5,600 people who identify themselves as current Nvidia employees.

The case for Haas: The Arm CEO spent about seven years at Nvidia, rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm’s CEO in February 2022, when Nvidia’s $40 billion deal to acquire Arm collapsed amid regulatory opposition. SoftBank, Arm’s majority owner, kept Nvidia’s $1.25 billion prepayment.

Arm, based in Cambridge, England, designs processor technology that’s ubiquitous in smartphones, and licenses it to other chipmakers. That includes Nvidia, whose Grace data center CPU, paired with its GPUs in AI systems, is built on Arm cores. Amazon’s Graviton and Microsoft’s Cobalt server chips also use Arm designs.

Haas is one of several candidates, and there’s no guarantee he’ll be offered the job or take it, the FT reported.

He also has a link to Harvey Jones, the longtime Nvidia director named the company’s first board chair this week. Haas was vice president of sales at Tensilica, a chip-design company, from 1999 to 2004, according to his LinkedIn profile. Jones co-founded Tensilica and chaired its board until chip-design software maker Cadence acquired it in 2013.

Haas has also seen Huang’s resistance to succession planning firsthand. “He didn’t like the idea,” Haas said in a 2024 interview, as quoted by the New York Times this week. “He felt it would create competition among executives and be divisive.”

One complication: SoftBank named Haas CEO of SoftBank Group International in April, helping coordinate chip and AI companies in its international portfolio while he continues to run Arm. The FT reported that the appointment was aimed at pushing forward Project Izanagi, SoftBank’s AI chip effort launched to compete with Nvidia.

He knows Nvidia from the inside, but he also knows what it’s like to run a public company — which matters for a board searching in the middle of a crisis.

John’s argument on the podcast: Nvidia needs someone who can shepherd a company through turmoil, not just a great technologist. Think Alan Mulally going from Boeing to Ford, or Dara Khosrowshahi moving from Expedia to Uber after Travis Kalanick’s ouster.

What the betting markets say: On Kalshi, Ian Buck, the Nvidia vice president who created the CUDA software platform, was the favorite at midday Friday. By midday Saturday, Haas had overtaken him, at 25% to Buck’s 18%. Kress was at 10%.

The Axios list of 11 names also includes Apple Executive Chair Tim Cook, for whom President Trump lobbied on Truth Social (“A Legend replaces a Legend!”), along with AMD CEO Lisa Su and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian.

A Northwest wildcard: Analysts have also floated Sanjay Mehrotra, CEO of Boise, Idaho-based Micron Technology, whose memory chips power Nvidia’s AI servers. Mehrotra co-founded SanDisk in 1988 and has run Micron since 2017.

The AWS chief: Matt Garman has run Amazon Web Services since June 2024, overseeing a business with a $142 billion annual revenue run rate at the end of last year. He started at Amazon as an MBA intern in 2005, joined AWS full time in 2006 as one of its first product managers, and later led its compute business and then its sales and marketing organization.

Another Amazon pick: We’d also look at Peter DeSantis, who now leads a new organization that includes Amazon’s AI models, custom chips and quantum computing, reporting directly to CEO Andy Jassy.

DeSantis joined Amazon as a software developer in 1998. He led the EC2 team from Cape Town, South Africa, through its 2006 launch, and spearheaded Amazon’s 2015 acquisition of Annapurna Labs, the Israeli chip designer behind its custom silicon.

In 2018, DeSantis unveiled Graviton. In June, he told Bloomberg that AWS was in talks to sell its Trainium AI chips to other companies for their own data centers.

He knows chips, data centers and AI infrastructure at enormous scale. The catch, as John noted: he’s never been a CEO, and the board may want that experience given the circumstances.

The other Amazon name: Dave Treadwell took over AWS compute and machine learning services in August. Treadwell spent 27 years at Microsoft, where he worked on Windows NT, .NET and Xbox and rose to corporate vice president, before joining Amazon in 2016.

The Microsoft bench: On the podcast, Todd ran through a few Microsoft executives who would bring relevant experience:

The insider with Microsoft roots: Nick Parker, a 26-year Microsoft sales veteran, joined Nvidia in August as executive vice president of worldwide field operations, with a pay package worth more than $40 million. He’s new, but he already runs the team that sells Nvidia’s chips to the world’s largest companies.

One more angle: Whoever gets the job will face a growing list of customers trying to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, including Amazon. In his annual shareholder letter in April, Jassy wrote that Amazon’s chips business would have an annual run rate of about $50 billion if it sold chips to AWS and other third parties the way other chipmakers do.

Jassy said it’s “quite possible” Amazon will sell racks of them to third parties in the future.

In a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14, Huang said he hoped his successor was already inside the company. The board has said it will consider both internal and external candidates.

Listen to our full discussion on this week’s GeekWire Podcast.

#5341. U.S. export controls and Nvidia’s leadership transition remain key watchpoints for the Gulf

Nvidia’s solid third-quarter results will no doubt reassure Gulf investors that the U.S. chipmaking giant is on course to maintain a healthy growth trajectory despite the resignation of Jensen Huang.

Nvidia reported revenue of $116 billion for the three months to October, up 103% from a year ago, and above Wall Street estimates of $109 billion. It has beaten estimates in each of the last five quarters.

For the Gulf states, which are betting big on AI to help move their economies away from oil and rely on Nvidia’s advanced chips to achieve that, the company’s future success is critical.

Huang’s affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy has heightened political pressure to tighten export controls amid long-running concerns in the U.S. that China’s access to advanced American AI chips could undermine national security.

It is also likely to sharpen scrutiny of Nvidia’s future dealings with the Gulf as part of a broader effort to prevent China from accessing banned American technology via intermediaries.

Such concerns have previously made securing Nvidia’s advanced chips an uphill battle for regional AI champions such as PIF-owned HUMAIN and Abu Dhabi-backed G42.

In July, the U.S. Department of Commerce loosened export restrictions on the UAE so that approved government agencies and entities—including its tech champion G42—can receive advanced computing hardware, including from Nvidia, under broader license exceptions. The rule change set no caps on how many chips or other sophisticated goods can be sold to those entities.

Democratic China hawks have frequently raised the alarm over the large-scale sales of AI chips to the Gulf region, arguing they could give China backdoor access to U.S. technology. Last May, Democratic senators demanded that AI chip deals with Saudi Arabia and the UAE contain adequate guardrails to prevent the leakage of sensitive technology to China.

Both Gulf countries maintain strong commercial ties to Chinese tech entities.

In September, Chinese tech giant Alibaba Cloud announced plans to ramp up its data center capacity and expand localized AI services across the UAE. Meanwhile, in Riyadh, Lenovo unveiled its first laptop made in Saudi Arabia at its sprawling 200,000-square-meter manufacturing facility, developed as part of a $2 billion partnership with Alat, a subsidiary of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF).

In its first policy response to the Nvidia scandal, on Monday the U.S. Commerce Department introduced an interim rule requiring overseas data centers to obtain a government license before supplying “significant volumes of computing power” to firms with headquarters in 22 embargoed countries, including China. The move aims to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia’s computing power from locations in other countries.

With Democrats holding majorities in both chambers of Congress from January next year, increased congressional scrutiny of Gulf AI deals is likely.

More broadly, the Gulf’s exposure to the volatility in AI stock prices has been further rattled by Jensen’s resignation amid a broader sell-off in AI tech stocks over the past few months, on the back of valuation and investment bubble concerns.

While not all Gulf funds disclose their individual investments, publicly available filings suggest that Gulf sovereign wealth funds, such as Mubadala, have relatively limited direct exposure to Nvidia shares compared to the scale of their investments in other tech firms.

According to the consultancy, Global SWF, Mubadala ranks among the top institutional backers of AI worldwide.

MGX, a global AI investment fund backed by Mubadala, holds stakes and has participated in funding rounds for OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Databricks, Isomorphic Labs, and SpaceX.

Saudi’s PIF-backed AI venture HUMAIN invested $3 billion in xAI’s $20 billion Series E round in February, shortly before it merged with SpaceX.

Global SWF estimates that Mubadala’s portfolio may have declined by $17.5 billion since the onset of the AI selloff at the end of June, largely driven by a more than 50% drop in chipmaker GlobalFoundries’ share price. PIF, meanwhile, is estimated to have suffered a $5.6 billion decline in the value of its AI-related holdings, largely attributable to its stake in SpaceX.

“Indirectly and strategically, Gulf wealth funds are exposed to the current market turbulence,” Sam Winter-Levy, a senior fellow in the Technology and International Affairs program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told me.

“MGX and other Gulf vehicles hold large stakes in AI labs, data center platforms, and other companies whose valuations depend on the AI boom—and Nvidia, of course, is central to that boom. The Gulf’s national AI strategies are built on Nvidia hardware. I think a prolonged loss of confidence in Nvidia would hit the Gulf relatively hard.”

In a research note published on Monday, London-headquartered Capital Economics warned that the ongoing shakeout in the AI sector is setting the stage for a larger downturn in the U.S. equity market over the next year.

With Nvidia considered a bellwether for the AI industry, its results should help to calm the markets and buoy investor sentiment ahead of Anthropic’s planned listing on Thursday.

You can read my piece here, which takes a closer look at what the potential fallout from the Nvidia crisis could mean for the Gulf’s AI ambitions, particularly in terms of its planned data center buildout.

Melissa HancockAnd as ever, thanks for reading, and do keep in touch with your thoughts and ideas.melissa.hancock@fortune.com

Abu Dhabi-backed Masdar has completed its $950 million Lockhart Solar and Storage complex in California, marking another major step in the clean energy giant’s growing U.S. renewables push.

With 365-MW of solar generation and 173.7MW of battery storage, the project can produce electricity to meet the annual needs of about 350,000 homes and businesses.

Commercially, the project is backed by a hybrid of long-term power purchase agreements with California utilities and corporates.

The project was developed by Terra-Gen, which is owned jointly by Masdar and U.K.-headquartered global infrastructure manager, Igneo Infrastructure Partners.

Masdar operates a major part of its U.S. footprint through Terra-Gen, an independent U.S. renewables developer and operator, in which Masdar acquired a 50% stake in 2024 alongside Igneo.

Masdar has already invested around $3 billion in renewable energy projects across the U.S., with a portfolio reaching 6.3 GW across onshore wind, solar, and battery energy storage systems as of Sep. 2026.

It is targeting an expansion of its portfolio by as much as 25-GW by 2030, capitalising on rising power demand from data centers, industrial electrification, and expanding domestic manufacturing.

Globally, Masdar is also pressing ahead with its ambition to reach 100-GW of portfolio capacity by the end of the decade.

Its U.S. expansion comes despite the federal rollback of clean energy incentives under the Trump administration. Trump declared a national energy emergency on his first day in office last year, stating that inflation was driven by overspending and high energy costs. He officially launched the "drill, baby, drill" policy to extract domestic "liquid gold."

According to a report released in July this year, the scaling back of incentives has led to the cancellation ​or delay of $83 billion in investment across hundreds of projects.

A strong recovery in global oil supplies helped the market return to a surplus in October, the first time since the outbreak of the U.S.-Iran war.

Inventories climbed by 2.3 million barrels per day (bpd) to 105.4 million bpd last month, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA), as "Gulf exports recovered much faster than global oil demand."

The higher export rates prompted the Paris-based agency to "significantly" raise its expectations for global oil supply for the remainder of 2026, with fourth-quarter estimates now 3.3 million bpd higher.

The IEA forecasts fourth-quarter supply will average 105 million bpd, exceeding projected demand by 1.7 million bpd.

The oil market is "straightening out" and "showing tentative signs of rebalancing,” it said.

It follows seven months of disruption to global oil flows, as the ongoing war choked off shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical shipping route that normally carries around a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supplies.

However, Capital Economics sounded a note of caution about the future path to recovery given that the EIA data also shows that the stock of commercial oil inventories in the OECD plunged by 101 million barrels between February and October.

“Rebuilding depleted oil stock inventories–which is key to allowing oil prices to trend lower–will require oil flows sustaining sizeable surpluses into 2027,” it said in a research note published on Monday.

The research firm’s working assumption is that conditions in oil and natural gas markets largely normalize by the end of 2027 and that prices and spreads fall back further.

“But there is an obvious risk that things either fail to improve, or even get worse,” it added.

On Monday, Yemeni pro-government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, said they were withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea, to reinforce positions around Aden and neighbouring areas.

Their retreat follows weeks of intensified fighting with the Iran-backed Houthi movement.

Saudi Arabia has relied heavily on the Bab al-Mandab Strait as a critical oil export route in light of ongoing disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

At least 10 ships were hit in the first 10 days of November, following a record 37 strikes in October—the highest monthly total since the conflict began, according to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.

The amount that DIP Holding raised in its IPO on the Dubai Financial Market last week, the UAE’s first stock market listing of 2026. Shares began trading on Nov. 11 under the ticker symbol DIP and gained up to 7% during their market debut. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund and a unit of Blackstone were among foreign investors that participated in the offering, according to Bloomberg.

Dubai tycoon Hussain Sajwani expects his investments in three AI firms—OpenAI and SpaceX and Anthropic—to generate billions of dollars in returns. In recent years, Sajwani’s Dubai-based real estate firm, Damac Group, has broadened its investment portfolio to include technology and data centers. In 2025, Sajwani pledged to invest $20 billion in U.S. data centres, making the announcement while standing alongside Donald Trump at a press conference in Mar-a-Lago, Florida. He told Bloomberg last week that about $9 billion of that amount had since been deployed.

#5340. Binance’s $6.3B Hack Fix Is Coming Tomorrow: Why the ZK Math Doesn't Tell the Whole Story

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data shows the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

At the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot shows its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

Blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham says those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

If Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

The FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

It shows how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own users. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

While the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now shows:

The first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what users hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:

Why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:

The striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

Compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, showed BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:

Not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

How Binance says it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

What the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It shows the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

Binance says the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest update says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:

The design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

What it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

What customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

Binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.

#5338. Authentic Brands treats the Super Bowl like ‘a business summit.’ It’s hosting a private weekend for executive meetings, ad panels and a brand showcase

For Authentic Brands Group, whose brands drive more than $38 billion in global annual systemwide sales, Super Bowl weekend has as much to do with business as it does with football.

Authentic’s roster spans more than 50 brands, ranging from Reebok, Sports Illustrated, and Care Bears to Shaquille O’Neal, David Beckham, and Kevin Hart, and it’s taking over the Waldorf Astoria Beverly Hills from Feb. 11-13, 2027, Authentic told Fortune exclusively.

The three-day, invite-only event called Authentic House will fill the hotel’s 170 guest rooms and more than 20 programming spaces with executive meetings, conversations with chief marketing officers about Super Bowl ads, and a presentation of Authentic’s brands and upcoming projects.

“For us, Super Bowl is more than just a game. It’s like a business summit and a hospitality experience,” Corey Salter, CEO of entertainment at Authentic, told Fortune. “We’re just really trying to create our own headquarters for the biggest weekend in sports.”

Authentic House was created by Authentic Live, the company’s experiences division, which is also behind Shaq’s Fun House and SI: The Party. Authentic Live hosted more than 50 events in 2025, drawing about 65,000 attendees, 324 million social impressions, and more than 35 billion media impressions.

In 2026, the division hosted 58 entertainment events with about 70,000 attendees, generating 643.3 million impressions and 64.4 billion media impressions, which the company attributed partly to the success of O’Neal’s Dunkman. Authentic Live plans to host more than 90 events in 2027. The company declined to disclose revenue.

Unlike those ticketed events, Authentic House is invite-only. Salter said guests won’t be able to just “come buy a table.” Fewer than 300 people will stay at the hotel, he estimated, while likely more than 5,000 will come through over the weekend.

The concept for Authentic House started small. Earlier this year in San Francisco, Authentic took over Quince, a three-Michelin-star restaurant. That version included a live recording of The Big Podcast with Shaq featuring Bo Jackson and Barry Sanders, along with the SI Swimsuit Digital Cover Party. Guests included Hart, 50 Cent, Ciara, and Russell Wilson.

“We took a leap of faith, and it worked incredibly,” Salter said.

But that restaurant only seated about 120 people, Salter said, so Authentic decided to “take a much bigger swing” this year.

“We believe that content drives commerce,” Salter said. “Our entertainment and lifestyle brands overlap a lot, and we’re in the entertainment capital of the world in Los Angeles.”

But taking over the hotel “was not free,” Salter said. Authentic will host clients and partners in some rooms and sell others to partners. Authentic also has category-exclusive partnerships at Authentic House, which the company said are curated to offer partners “opportunities and access to tastemakers and decision makers across business, entertainment, media and, culture.” The company did not disclose the cost of partnerships.

“Success for us is really making sure that we throw incredible events, that we have a very well-occupied space with good people and good celebrities and good sports people around,” Salter said, adding partners from China, Turkey, Latin America and Australia are expected to attend.

Ultimately, Salter said, the company looks at what it calls total deal value, with the goal of building long-term partnerships.

“It’s not about a quick dollar,” he said.

Programming will include an invite-only dinner hosted by Authentic founder and executive chairman, Jamie Salter, as well as the Authentic Showcase, which Corey Salter called “our version of the upfronts,” the annual events where media companies pitch upcoming programming to advertisers.

USA TODAY will host an Ad Meter Summit with CMOs and its editors, and a Style Studio will let influencers and creators shop brands such as Reebok, Champion, and Juicy Couture. There will also be a Sports Illustrated Swimsuit digital cover launch and a Care Bears Family Day on the rooftop, since over Super Bowl weekend “there’s really nothing for children and families to do,” Corey Salter said.

“Imagine a very overpriced, very expensive birthday party that you would want to do for your kids… and then times it by 10, and that’s what you’re going to see up there,” he added.

Hart, Beckham, and O’Neal are expected to attend, along with a lineup of notable athletes, entertainers, and other talent. Outside the hotel, SI The Party will be held in Century City and Shaq’s Fun House downtown. Authentic’s and partners’ brands will also appear throughout the hotel, including in minibars and guest rooms, at a cafe by the entrance and in a gifting suite, Salter said.

“It’s not going to be like in-your-face branding,” he said, “but it’s going to be really, really nice touchpoints.”

Sydney Lake is an associate editor at Fortune, where she writes and edits news for the publication's global news desk.

#5337. Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 15, 2026 at 8:13 amNovember 15, 2026 at 8:14 am

The world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy. Sure, the feature that took a quarter to build back in 2023 takes a mere AI-fueled weekend in 2026, but many AI startups are running on FOMO, caffeine and tokens without a clear strategy.

A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line.

Sam Altman’s Startup Playbook puts the speed creed in one line: “I have never, not once, seen a slow-moving founder be really successful.” I was singing from the same hymnbook earlier this year. In my column on ten commandments for AI startups I wrote that “velocity is the new moat.” Then everyone got fast, and I stopped singing.

Here are the five arguments usually made for that creed.

The window is closing. Each model release opens a gap that the frontier labs close within a release cycle or so. But if the labs will close it anyway, speed merely buys you a nicer funeral. The argument supports picking a different direction, not running faster in this one.

Competitors are everywhere. AI makes building cheap, so clones show up in weeks. True, and that’s the reason velocity isn’t a moat. When building is cheap, defensibility matters more than being first. Peter Thiel’s last-mover argument from Zero to One is stronger today than when he wrote it. In his words: “It’s much better to be the last mover—that is, to make the last great development in a specific market and enjoy years or even decades of monopoly profits.”

The data flywheel. Early users generate data that improves the product, so get there first. Except that each new model generation resets the flywheel, and data that taught a fine-tuned model something in 2024 is worth little once a frontier model does the task out of the box.

The data that matters is data the labs can’t easily get: clinical records, industrial sensor readings, proprietary transactions. Access to proprietary data often comes through trust and partnerships, which take time, and moving too fast can cost you the trust required to obtain that precious data.

Momentum attracts capital and talent. That’s true. However, capital raised on growth hype may be planting the seeds of its own demise. A high valuation can box you into the growth story that justified it. Startups that raise at a saner pace retain the option to change direction.

Learning speed. Fast iteration finds product-market fit sooner. This one holds, but there are two kinds of speed.

Fast iteration means cheap experiments: a prototype, a pilot, a feature shipped to 20 users and pulled if it flops. Fast scaling means hiring ahead of revenue, signing multi-year contracts, buying compute and raising at a valuation you then have to grow into.

Iteration should be as fast as you can make it, because each cycle is cheap to undo. Scaling should come more slowly, because each step is a major commitment that’s hard to unwind, and scaling too early is one of the most expensive mistakes a startup can make: a 2011 study of more than 3,200 high-growth technology startups blamed premature scaling for about 74% of internet startup failures.

Jeff Bezos drew a similar distinction in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders. A few decisions are one-way doors, irreversible once you walk through, and deserve deliberation. Most decisions are two-way doors, and those should be made fast by a small group. A startup’s experiments are two-way doors. Its big commitments, a large raise, a long contract, a hiring spree, are not.

At AI House, Sri Chandrasekar, one of our managing directors, puts it this way: “We don’t hand founders a thesis. We expect them to find the right problem, and that takes judgment, not speed. Building is nearly free now, so run every experiment fast and manually, and only build the machine once something works.”

Finding the right problem takes iteration, acumen and judgment. Speed helps with the first and does little for the other two. A hamster on a wheel at 200 mph has plenty of speed and no chance of progress. Even Altman’s playbook says Y Combinator looks for “businesses that get more powerful with scale and that are difficult to copy.”

Prof. Herbert Simon, the Nobel laureate who helped invent AI at Carnegie Mellon, advised his graduate students to pick important problems for which they had a secret weapon, because they would win only “by having access to some knowledge or research methods the others do not have.”

Swap students for founders and research methods for data and relationships, and the advice holds. A startup’s secret weapon is an asset you hold that a competitor can’t acquire by moving faster: a dataset nobody else can assemble, a relationship that took years to nurture.

Farecast, the airfare prediction company I founded in 2003, developed a secret weapon by gathering a massive amount of labeled data. By 2007 we were mining more than 175 billion airfares, and every prediction we made was later scored against what the fare actually did, so the labeled set grew every day, and it grew only by waiting for fares to play out.

A startup that signs a data agreement with a hospital network has the same kind of weapon. So does a payments company whose fraud labels come from its own transaction stream. In each case the data is the asset a faster rival can’t copy.

Laurence Peter, of Peter Principle fame, said it decades ago: “If you don’t know where you are going, you will probably end up somewhere else.”

So pick a direction where frontier labs won’t go and clearly articulate why. Run experiments fast but make commitments slowly. Jim Collins, the Good to Great author, called it firing bullets before cannonballs: cheap shots to find the range, then the one big shot once you have it.

Chase the data and the relationships the labs can’t buy and accept that trust is the slow road to both. Raise at a pace that leaves you the option to pivot when the next model lands. And name your secret weapon in one sentence.

To repurpose an old joke: two bulls stand on a hill above a herd. The young one says, let’s charge down there. The old one retorts: charge and they scatter. Walk, and they’ll be waiting when we arrive.

In AI right now, everyone is charging. The founders who end up with the prize will be the ones who are more judicious.

#5336. Amazon loses 40 Leo satellites in ULA Vulcan launch failure — a new setback for its Starlink rival

by Todd Bishop on Nov 15, 2026 at 1:41 pmNovember 17, 2026 at 2:31 pm

Update, Tuesday Nov. 17: ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests Vulcan’s first stage underperformed just after liftoff. Read our follow-up story for details. This story has been updated with ULA’s preliminary findings.

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed to reach orbit Sunday, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle company’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service.

It was ULA’s first total mission failure since the Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture was formed in 2006, Spaceflight Now reported. The flight was Vulcan’s first in nine months, and the first of 38 Vulcan launches that Amazon has purchased.

ULA said Sunday that it didn’t yet have specific data on what went wrong, and that it would work with Amazon and others to find the cause and return to flight as quickly as possible.

Amazon Leo said in a post on X that “there is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01.” It added, “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

The rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET (9:40 a.m. PT), after two days of delays and a countdown hold with 20 seconds left on the clock to resolve a technical issue. It isn’t known whether that issue played any role.

The rocket’s six solid rocket boosters, made by Northrop Grumman and the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appeared to perform normally and burned out less than two minutes after liftoff, according to Space.com and Spaceflight Now.

The first stage, powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin, fired from liftoff before separating from the Centaur upper stage, which carries the payload the rest of the way to orbit.

ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to reach orbit. The Centaur, powered by two RL10 engines made by L3Harris, appears to have started normally and couldn’t make up for the shortfall. ULA appears to have lost telemetry and the mission about 10 minutes into the flight.

Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned, and that a telemetry-driven animation showed the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in its burn. ULA hasn’t said what caused the shortfall.

Impact on Amazon Leo: Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based satellite internet network, formerly known as Project Kuiper, on 14 missions since April 2025. Its last successful launch was in July, when ULA flew the last of eight Leo missions on its Atlas 5, the older rocket that Vulcan is replacing.

The larger Vulcan carried 40 satellites on Sunday, compared with 29 on the last Atlas 5 launch, and is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Melissa Wuerl, Amazon Leo’s director of launch systems, called it the program’s “primary workhorse over the next several years” in a preview of the mission. Amazon had said the second Vulcan mission could fly within weeks of the first. That flight now has to wait for ULA’s investigation.

Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on Blue Origin’s New Glenn, which has been grounded since a May ground-test explosion, and has booked others on Arianespace’s Ariane 6 and SpaceX’s Falcon 9.

In June, the Federal Communications Commission gave Amazon permission to keep deploying satellites even if it missed its July 30 deadline to put 1,616 into service. Satellites that weren’t operational by then temporarily lose priority in key spectrum bands.

Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy and operate all 3,232 first-generation satellites. Amazon has said it plans an initial rollout of commercial internet service this year.

Vulcan’s track record: Sunday’s mission was the fifth for Vulcan, which debuted in January 2024, and the first with six solid boosters. Boosters suffered nozzle failures on the second flight in October 2024 and on a national security mission in February. Both reached orbit, but the Space Force paused Vulcan national security launches after February.

ULA flew Sunday’s mission with an improved nozzle design. The rocket’s BE-4 engines had also been retrofitted to fix the oxygen valve problem behind the New Glenn explosion in May, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight, CBS News reported.

ULA is also under new leadership. Longtime CEO Tory Bruno left last December for Blue Origin, and Peller, who led Vulcan’s development, was named CEO in August.

Amazon’s next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for Nov. 23 at the earliest.
